papers.title: Domain-Specific Constitutional AI: Enhancing Safety in LLM-Powered Mental Health Chatbots
papers.abstract: Mental health applications have emerged as a critical area in computational health, driven by rising global rates of mental illness, the integration of AI in psychological care, and the need for scalable solutions in underserved communities. These include therapy chatbots, crisis detection, and wellness platforms handling sensitive data, requiring specialized AI safety beyond general safeguards due to emotional vulnerability, risks like misdiagnosis or symptom exacerbation, and precise management of vulnerable states to avoid severe outcomes such as self-harm or loss of trust. Despite AI safety advances, general safeguards inadequately address mental health-specific challenges, including crisis intervention accuracy to avert escalations, therapeutic guideline adherence to prevent misinformation, scale limitations in resource-constrained settings, and adaptation to nuanced dialogues where generics may introduce biases or miss distress signals. We introduce an approach to apply Constitutional AI training with domain-specific mental health principles for safe, domain-adapted CAI systems in computational mental health applications.
papers.summary: General-purpose AI safeguards do not cover the risks specific to mental health chatbots. These include getting crisis intervention right, following therapeutic guidelines, and noticing subtle signs of distress in vulnerable users. The authors propose applying `Constitutional AI` (CAI) training with a set of **domain-specific mental health principles** to build safer, domain-adapted systems for therapy chatbots, crisis detection, and wellness platforms. The abstract gives no quantitative results.

papers.title: ChemBART: Pre-training a Reaction Language Model for Comprehensive Synthesis Planning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated transformative potential across diverse fields. However, in computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP), current LLM methodologies are often restricted to single-molecule representations, limiting their application to isolated, single-task scenarios such as precursor prediction. Addressing this gap, we present ChemBART, a BART-based language model that adopts a reaction-centric pre-training strategy. By leveraging a mask-filling pre-training task on holistic reaction expressions (Reactant > Reagent > Product), ChemBART effectively solves a variety of chemical problems, including precursor/reagent generation, temperature-yield regression, and molecular property classification. Building on these capabilities, we demonstrate the integration of ChemBART with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) for multi-step synthesis route design, where the model serves to optimize the policy and value functions within a reinforcement learning framework. Beyond single-molecule pre-trained LLMs that are constrained to specific applications, ChemBART unifies diverse chemical tasks to facilitate synthesis planning with comprehensive implementation information. Most significantly, the proposed multi-step synthesis routes and reaction conditions were validated in the wet lab, confirming the discovery of shorter synthetic pathways with a >20% yield improvement over established literature benchmarks. Our work highlights the potential of reaction-focused pre-training and showcases the broad utility of ChemBART in closing the loop between in silico prediction and wet-lab synthesis.
papers.summary: Most language-model approaches to computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) represent single molecules and handle one task at a time, such as predicting precursors. `ChemBART` is a BART-based model pre-trained with mask filling on whole reaction expressions (reactant, reagent, product). A single model then handles precursor and reagent generation, temperature and yield regression, and molecular property classification. Combined with Monte Carlo tree search (`MCTS`) as policy and value functions, it plans multi-step routes, and the proposed routes were validated in the wet lab, giving shorter pathways with **more than 20% higher yield than established literature routes**.

papers.title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.
papers.summary: Decision models return normalized probabilities over candidate choices, but being calibrated on single-answer tasks does not show that those probabilities are reliable when several choices are correct. The authors evaluate `Jev`, `Liquid d1`, and `GPT-6 Luna Decisions` on `MetaTool`, `HotpotQA`, and `ECtHR`. Even when a model ranks every correct choice above every distractor, **in 28% to 50% of those lists at least one correct choice gets less than the uniform probability 1/n**. Given five identical copies of a correct choice, the models assign them probabilities with mean gaps of 17 to 79 percentage points, so a probability threshold can rank correct choices but cannot reliably recover the full set.

papers.title: Do Machine Learning-Guided Proactive Full Capacity Protocols Mitigate Emergency Department Overcrowding? A Simulation-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract:
Objective: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding threatens care quality, yet Full Capacity Protocols (FCPs) are typically activated only after crowding thresholds have been exceeded. This study evaluated whether machine learning-guided proactive FCP activation improves ED crowding control compared with conventional reactive activation.
  Materials and Methods: We developed and validated an integrated machine learning and discrete-event simulation framework representing ED patient flow and capacity management. An embedded machine learning model predicted hourly waiting-room crowding six hours ahead and triggered proactive FCP activation. Using empirically calibrated operational parameters from a large US hospital, we compared proactive and reactive deployment strategies over a 365-day simulation horizon with 10 independent replications. Outcomes included ED length of stay, wait time, percentage of time above the crowding threshold, number of FCP activations, and protocol duration.
  Results: Proactive deployment produced statistically significant reductions in the percentage of time above the crowding threshold and average protocol duration across all threshold settings. It also reduced crowding variability and extreme congestion events, resulting in smoother ED operations. Although proactive deployment generally improved ED length of stay and wait time, these differences were not statistically significant.
  Conclusion: Embedding machine learning predictions within an operational simulation enables proactive, prediction-guided capacity management before severe congestion develops. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of proactive FCP deployment as a decision-support strategy for improving ED crowding control and provide evidence to support prospective implementation in clinical practice.
papers.summary: Emergency department (ED) Full Capacity Protocols (FCPs) are normally activated only after crowding thresholds are already exceeded. The authors embed a machine learning model that predicts hourly waiting-room crowding six hours ahead inside a discrete-event simulation calibrated to a large US hospital. They then compare proactive and reactive FCP activation over a simulated year with 10 replications. Proactive activation **significantly reduced the share of time above the crowding threshold** and shortened protocol duration at every threshold setting, while improvements in length of stay and wait time were not statistically significant.

papers.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols
papers.abstract: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per-phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round-trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. Round trips are not the whole bill: when an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, handshake cost scales with the counterpart's capability inventory at 24-107 tokens per capability, so a 200-capability counterpart spends 11% of a 200k-token context window before the agent reads its own task. MCP's own 2026 revision cuts its handshake from three round trips to two and, with era pinning, to zero on warm reconnects, protocol evolution that corroborates the cost we measure. We release the full harness, raw data, and analysis at https://github.com/pvarshh/handshake-benchmark.
papers.summary: Agent protocol surveys list handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, but none had measured it. Using each protocol's official SDK, this benchmark splits the handshake into phases for `MCP` (the 2025 initialize and 2026 discover versions), `A2A`, and `ACP`, and measures round trips, latency, bytes on the wire, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios. Round-trip count dominates: at 50 ms RTT, legacy `MCP` takes three round trips and 230 ms, while `A2A` takes one round trip and 61 ms. When an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, cost grows by 24 to 107 tokens per capability, so **a 200-capability counterpart consumes 11% of a 200k-token context window** before the agent reads its own task.

papers.title: baseVultra: Compact Nonlinear Recurrence with Reallocated Capacity
papers.abstract: Nonlinear recurrent networks remain useful for streaming sequence modeling, yet gated cell design is still dominated by LSTM and GRU. We study whether recurrent computation can be reallocated away from gate transforms and toward candidate generation. We propose baseVultra, a compact recurrent cell that concentrates the dense recurrent budget on a single H x H candidate-generation matrix, while replacing recurrent gate matrices with O(H) diagonal interactions. The candidate update combines this dense branch with two low-rank auxiliary branches, an EMA cache, and learnable output blending; the gates additionally receive lightweight second-order access to h_{t-2} through diagonal terms. On TinyShakespeare character-level language modeling, baseVultra achieves a validation loss of 1.594 in the compact one-layer 200K setting, compared with 1.604 for a parameter-matched LSTM and 1.616 for a parameter-matched GRU, while its dense recurrent matrix-vector computation is about 54% of GRU under matched hidden size for this configuration. On text8, a roughly 45x larger benchmark, baseVultra is competitive with full-gate cells (1.854 bpc vs. 1.849 for GRU and 1.837 for LSTM). On formal-language probes, the largest gains appear under constrained hidden-state capacity (0.991 vs. 0.761 GRU and 0.691 LSTM OOD2 accuracy on Counter at H=16) and vanish as hidden size grows. These results characterize where and when candidate-focused recurrent capacity allocation helps: the benefit is concentrated in compact regimes, while full-gate cells remain competitive at scale.
papers.summary: `baseVultra` is a compact recurrent cell that puts its dense recurrent budget into a single candidate-generation matrix and replaces the gate matrices with cheap diagonal interactions. It also adds low-rank auxiliary branches, an exponential-moving-average cache, and second-order access to the hidden state from two steps back. On `TinyShakespeare` at about 200K parameters, it reaches a validation loss of 1.594, compared with 1.604 for a parameter-matched `LSTM` and 1.616 for a `GRU`, using about 54% of the GRU's dense recurrent computation, and it is roughly on par with both on `text8`. **The gains concentrate in small hidden-state regimes** and disappear as hidden size grows.

papers.title: MCP vs CLI for AI Agents: A Comparative Analysis of Tool Integration Strategies for Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: AI agents require interfaces to interact with external systems such as files, APIs, databases, and cloud services. Two competing paradigms have emerged: CLI (Command Line Interface), where agents execute shell commands directly, and MCP (Model Context Protocol), a structured JSON-RPC protocol providing governed, typed tool access. This paper presents a comparative analysis across 14 evaluation dimensions, supported by worked examples, security assessment against established compliance frameworks, and economic modeling. Our analysis indicates that CLI provides superior efficiency for single-user, local-only workflows, while MCP addresses requirements that CLI fundamentally cannot satisfy, including fine-grained access control, credential isolation, structured audit, and multi-tenant governance. We further examine how progressive disclosure techniques eliminate MCP's historical weakness (context window overhead), yielding token efficiency comparable to CLI while preserving its architectural benefits. A hybrid architecture is recommended for production systems. This analysis draws upon academic, government, and industry sources including NSA formal guidance (CSI U/OO/6030316-26), OWASP security standards, and economic modeling from BCG and Gartner.
papers.summary: AI agents can reach external systems either by running shell commands through a command line interface (CLI) or through the Model Context Protocol (`MCP`), which provides typed, governed tool access over JSON-RPC. The authors compare the two across 14 dimensions using worked examples, security assessment against frameworks such as `OWASP` and NSA guidance, and economic modeling. They conclude that CLI is more efficient for single-user local workflows, while MCP provides access control, credential isolation, structured auditing, and multi-tenant governance that CLI cannot. They also argue that **progressive disclosure brings MCP's token usage close to CLI's**, and they recommend a hybrid architecture for production.

papers.title: Lighthouse: On Building a Trustworthy Digital Assistant for Exploring History with Civil Rights Archives
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), as a decision-support aid, provides new tools for studying history effectively using multimodal data, including text, images, and audio. We present, to our knowledge, the first digital assistant named Lighthouse--commonly called a chatbot--for exploring the Civil Rights period of the United States using data from South Carolina. From an AI perspective, the system's novelty lies in its guiding design principles of (a) focusing on trustworthiness of content and (b) by modeling and reducing potential harm to users from generated answers. It implements these with a neuro-symbolic approach that combines neural learning through a large language model (LLM) with rule-based symbolic solving, balancing risk of answers with generality of coverage. We evaluate Lighthouse with both factual objective questions that admit a single acceptable answer as well as subjective questions. For the latter, a dataset of subjective question-answer pairs (QAs) is created by discovering a "gold standard" by aggregating answers from independent experts. Lighthouse has access to over 18k primary sources from a range of collections and can be easily extended.
papers.summary: `Lighthouse` is a chatbot for exploring the US Civil Rights era through more than 18,000 primary sources from South Carolina archives, designed around content trustworthiness and reducing potential harm from generated answers. It uses a **neuro-symbolic design that pairs an LLM with rule-based symbolic solving** to trade off answer risk against coverage. It is evaluated on factual questions and on subjective questions, for which the authors build a gold-standard dataset by aggregating answers from independent experts.

papers.title: V-JEPA 2 Meets AQA: Phase-Based Scoring and Reference-Based Feedback for Mountain Biking
papers.abstract: We study mountain-bike action quality assessment (AQA) with weak labels and candidate feedback. The training corpus comprises 95 field-recorded jump clips with binary labels denoting good or poor technique. These are coarse categorical labels, not continuous expert quality scores; phase-boundary and aspect-level annotations are unavailable. Our pipeline summarizes four heuristic phases using frozen V-JEPA 2 video features and two-dimensional pose and motion measurements. A small transformer predicts a binary-label score. A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with those of clips labelled as good technique to propose phase, body-parameter, and direction cues. We detail the measurements, network, and evaluation so that the limits of each output are explicit. In five-fold clip-level cross-validation, the full scorer obtained pooled out-of-fold AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812. These are exploratory figures because the reporting fold also selected the neural training epoch and riders were not separated between folds. Removing biomechanical scoring inputs raised AUROC to 0.809. A separate inner-selection run obtained AUROC 0.678, but used about 57 rather than 76 training clips per outer fold, so its difference from the test-selected run does not quantify selection bias. The unsupervised aspect head did not learn distinct factors. On a 17-clip external probe, an earlier checkpoint obtained binary accuracy 0.412 and Spearman association -0.135 with expert scores. Candidate cues had precision 0.118 and recall 1.0 against each of two coaches, with substantial disagreement about direction. These findings do not establish rider-independent scoring or reliable corrective feedback; they identify the empirical work needed to evaluate either use.
papers.summary: The authors study action quality assessment (AQA) for mountain-bike jumps using 95 clips with only binary good-or-poor technique labels. Their pipeline combines frozen `V-JEPA 2` video features with pose and motion measurements over four heuristic jump phases, uses a small transformer to score each clip, and adds a reference layer that proposes corrective cues by comparison with good-technique clips. Cross-validated AUROC (area under the ROC curve) was 0.768, which the authors call exploratory because of selection and rider-leakage issues. **On an external 17-clip probe the scores did not track expert ratings**, and the feedback cues had a precision of only 0.118, so neither reliable scoring nor reliable feedback is established.

papers.title: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots. Assistants based on language models could respond faster and carry out requests such as blocking a card, but only if they give correct information and follow the bank's rules. These rules prescribe a procedure, a set of required steps, such as obtaining a closure quote before closing a deposit. Adapting models to this domain requires measuring how well they follow the procedure, before and after training. Benchmarks usually judge only the records left at the end of a conversation. Many required steps, however, leave the records unchanged, so an assistant that skips them can still be judged successful. We present TauIndianBankBench, an action-oriented benchmark of 1,000 Indian retail-banking tasks where an assistant helps a simulated customer. Besides the final records, it checks that the assistant took every required step and made no unrequested change. For every model, 6.5-12.0% of sessions are judged successful when only the final records are checked, although the assistant skipped a required step or made an unrequested change. Scoring both procedure and outcome shows more accurately how well language models perform in Indian retail banking.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for tool-using conversational agents usually check only the final database state, so an agent that skips a required step that leaves no record can still be scored as successful. `TauIndianBankBench` contains 1,000 Indian retail-banking tasks with a simulated customer, and it also checks that every procedurally required step was taken and that no unrequested change was made. Across all models tested, **6.5% to 12.0% of sessions counted as successful under final-state checking actually skipped a required step or made an unrequested change**.

papers.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.
papers.summary: Model fusion merges several domain-expert models into one, but existing evaluations rarely cover long chain-of-thought reasoning or tool use, and strong average scores can hide the loss of individual capabilities. `FusionEval` provides controlled pools of `Qwen3` and `Llama` experts in math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use, and evaluates fusion methods on eight benchmarks for average and worst-case retention, runtime, and peak GPU memory. **Training-free fusion methods preserve reasoning but substantially degrade tool use**, while `MOPD` keeps tool use and gives a more balanced profile at the cost of extra data preparation, inference, and training.

papers.title: IRAH: Hierarchical Agentic Tree Search for Retrieval Pipeline Optimization
papers.abstract: Optimizing Information Retrieval (IR) pipelines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) requires jointly selecting structural components and numerical hyperparameters under limited evaluation budgets. We introduce the Information Retrieval Agentic Harness (IRAH), which combines Language Agent Tree Search for IR (LATS-IR) with offline meta-learned initialization. LATS-IR performs UCT-guided hierarchical search, first exploring macro-structural pipeline choices and then refining numerical parameters, with natural-language reflections to guide subsequent mutations and provide inspectable search traces. We evaluate IRAH on three in-distribution benchmarks and one out of-distribution benchmark to assess generalization under distribution shift. Under the same meta-learned initialization, LATS-IR outperforms TPE on two of three in-distribution benchmarks, with gains of up to 6.4%, and remains competitive on the out-of-distribution benchmark. Across all four benchmarks, warm-started IRAH achieves the highest average held-out nDCG@10 (0.4816) and improves over its cold-start counterpart. These results establish IRAH as a competitive approach to retrieval pipeline optimization under constrained evaluation budgets.
papers.summary: Tuning information retrieval (IR) pipelines for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means choosing both structural components and numeric hyperparameters on a limited evaluation budget. The Information Retrieval Agentic Harness (`IRAH`) does this with `LATS-IR`, a language agent tree search that first explores pipeline structure and then refines parameters, guided by natural-language reflections and a meta-learned warm start. With the same initialization, it beats Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (`TPE`) optimization on two of three in-distribution benchmarks by up to 6.4%, and **the warm-started version achieves the best average held-out nDCG@10 (0.4816)** across all four benchmarks.

papers.title: Finitely Verifiable Segmentation: Decidability for Every Tokenizer with a Finite-State Verifier
papers.abstract: A segmentation policy assigns to each byte string at most one segmentation into tokens. Call it finitely verifiable when a finite automaton over marked strings, bytes paired with boundary bits, accepts exactly the policy's own segmentations. The automaton judges a proposed segmentation and need not compute one. The paper shows what that hypothesis buys. Four questions that practice settles by folklore become decidable, whether a window certifies a token boundary, whether the boundary gap is bounded, whether a mask keeps generation completable, and whether two policies are equivalent. The last three specialize limitedness, coaccessibility and the equivalence of single-valued transducers. The first refines the synchronizing cut of code theory, and two more ask whether a certified cut, or the cuts of an inventory, let each piece scan alone. The class sits strictly between the online-scannable policies and those with regular domains, and its inner frontier is Choffrut's and decidable in polynomial time. Markings are length-preserving, so the class is exactly the rational segmentation policies, a normal form rather than a restriction, and what the decisions need is a supplied verifier. The class is closed under the operations pipelines use: composition over a labeled stage, restriction, splitting, and byte-fallback union of literal policies. Each composite inherits the six decisions, and certificates transfer between stages under four laws. Under rational, unifilar, almost surely stopping finite-state sources, each mass of the weighted section is an exact rational, and so is each rate where expected length is positive. Maximal-munch lexing, canonical byte-pair encoding and two-mode WordPiece instantiate the interface, and the munch library implements all six decisions. Every theorem carries an executable check, and every reported statistic is a program's own output.
papers.summary: This theory paper studies tokenizer segmentation policies whose outputs can be checked by a finite automaton over bytes paired with boundary markers, and shows that this class is exactly the rational segmentation policies. For such policies, four questions practitioners usually settle by folklore become decidable: whether a window certifies a token boundary, whether boundary gaps are bounded, **whether a generation mask keeps decoding completable**, and whether two tokenizers are equivalent. The class is closed under common pipeline operations, and maximal-munch lexing, canonical `BPE`, and `WordPiece` all fit it. The accompanying `munch` library implements all six decision procedures discussed in the paper.

papers.title: Accelerating Wildfire Hazard Mapping Across Canada with an AI Surrogate Modelling Framework
papers.abstract: Canada's increasing wildfire activity requires frequent national hazard mapping to guide proactive mitigation, including fuel management, land-use planning, infrastructure protection, and evacuation routing. However, process-based wildfire simulation frameworks (e.g., BurnP3 and BurnP3+) rely on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations to model burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. These workflows can take days to weeks to process a single regional modelling unit. To overcome these computational bottlenecks, we present three contributions developed through collaboration between AI researchers and wildfire modelling experts: (a) a standardized framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogate models against process-based wildfire simulators; (b) a multi-task deep learning surrogate trained on national-scale data to emulate burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread at a fraction of the computational cost (seconds); and (c) domain-specific metrics and counterfactual evaluation protocols to probe out-of-distribution generalization. Integrating geospatial data (fuel, terrain, ignition likelihood) and regional weather, our model approximates BurnP3+ simulation outputs, achieving strong performance across agreement, rank-correlation, error, and spatial-overlap metrics. It preserves downstream hazard classifications and produces physically plausible responses to expert-informed counterfactual interventions. On a representative region, the surrogate achieves 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and uses 13% of BurnP3+'s host memory, facilitating rapid scenario analysis.
papers.summary: Process-based wildfire simulators such as `BurnP3+` rely on Monte Carlo runs that can take days to weeks per region, which makes frequent national hazard mapping in Canada impractical. The authors train a multi-task deep learning surrogate on national-scale fuel, terrain, ignition, and weather data to emulate burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. They also provide a standard evaluation framework with counterfactual tests of out-of-distribution behavior. The surrogate closely matches simulator outputs, preserves downstream hazard classifications, and on a representative region gives **an 806-fold end-to-end CPU speedup using 13% of the host memory**.

papers.title: Neural Networks with Differentiable Belief-Function Layers
papers.abstract: Yager's 1987 rule of combination $\boxplus$ was proposed on epistemic grounds: under high conflict, mass should be redistributed to ignorance rather than renormalised onto the class simplex. We observe that backpropagation needs the same rule: Dempster's normaliser $(1{-}\kappa)^{-1}$, where $\kappa$ is the conflict mass, puts a $(1{-}\kappa)^{-2}$ term in the gradient that diverges exactly when evidence sources disagree, while Yager's $\boxplus$ is bilinear and has no such term. Building on this, we construct a deep evidential pipeline in which every mass in the chain from heads to output is a valid Dempster--Shafer mass function, combined by Yager's rule. The output mass on the ignorance set, $m(\Theta)$, serves as the network's ``I do not know'' signal. The network is fit to hard labels and never sees an annotator distribution, yet $m(\Theta)$ orders human disagreement in two modalities, visual and linguistic. Dempster's rises too and ranks contested inputs about as well, but its normaliser divides the conflict out: Yager's vacuity is $9\times$ larger on the most contested CIFAR-10H images, so only Yager's is readable as an amount of ignorance without recalibration. For out-of-distribution detection it is competitive with strong single-pass baselines, while the clamped Dempster variant that scores higher becomes gradient-unstable once the clamp is removed.
papers.summary: Combining evidence with Dempster's rule puts a term in the gradient that diverges exactly when evidence sources conflict, while Yager's 1987 rule, which assigns conflicting mass to ignorance instead of renormalizing, is bilinear and has no such term. The authors build a deep evidential network in which every intermediate quantity is a valid Dempster-Shafer mass function combined by Yager's rule, and use the mass on the ignorance set as an "I do not know" signal. Although trained only on hard labels, this signal orders human annotator disagreement on images and text, and **on the most contested `CIFAR-10H` images it is 9 times larger than Dempster's equivalent**. It is competitive with strong single-pass baselines for out-of-distribution detection.

papers.title: When Stable and Preferred Semantics Agree: A Path-Based Approach
papers.abstract:
We investigate structural conditions under which preferred and stable semantics agree in abstract argumentation frameworks. Our approach is based on suitably chosen sets of paths in the attack graph and binary relations induced by them. We establish a general path-based criterion for semantic agreement and instantiate it with several classes of paths, obtaining sufficient conditions expressed in terms of well-foundedness of the corresponding relations.
  The resulting conditions strictly generalize two principal structural criteria for preferred and stable agreement in the literature: Dung's limited controversiality condition and the SCC-symmetry condition. In particular, Dung's result is recovered as a special case by taking the relevant path set to be the set of even paths. We further introduce two infinite sequences of path sets, each yielding a family of agreement conditions. For the first sequence, a Collapse Theorem reduces the infinitely many associated well-foundedness conditions to three essentially distinct ones, whereas the second sequence gives rise to genuinely distinct conditions with no analogous collapse. Our results apply to both finite and infinite argumentation frameworks, admit simplified formulations in the finite case, and also yield sufficient conditions for the existence of stable extensions.
papers.summary: The paper looks for structural conditions under which preferred and stable semantics coincide in abstract argumentation frameworks. It defines a general criterion based on sets of paths in the attack graph and the well-foundedness of relations those paths induce. This strictly generalizes both **Dung's limited controversiality condition, recovered by taking even-length paths,** and the SCC-symmetry condition. Two infinite families of path sets yield further conditions: one collapses to three distinct conditions, the other does not, and the results hold for both finite and infinite frameworks.

papers.title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Scientific machine learning provides a promising framework for solving complex problems in science and engineering. Notably, physics informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown considerable potential for solving differential equations and modelling engineering systems. Solving time fractional Navier Stokes equations (TFNSEs) on complex domains is challenging due to temporal nonlocality, nonlinear flow dynamics, geometric complexity, and incompressibility constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry gated, divergence-free Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov Arnold network (GeoDiv KAN). The proposed architecture uses geometry dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation to preserve incompressibility by construction. GeoDiv KAN is evaluated for the time fractional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on square, circular, and star-shaped domains. Numerical experiments show that GeoDiv KAN achieves higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN across the considered benchmark problems. To establish practical relevance, GeoDiv KAN is applied to two data driven CFD cases: unsteady flow past a circular cylinder using the \href{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5039610}{Zenodo dataset} and turbulent RANS flow through a complex U bend using the \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/JDecke/ubend-cfd}{U-bend dataset}.
papers.summary: Solving time-fractional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on complex domains is hard because of temporal nonlocality, nonlinearity, irregular geometry, and the incompressibility constraint. `GeoDiv KAN` is a Kolmogorov-Arnold network built on Gaussian radial basis functions that uses geometry-dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation, so the predicted flow is **divergence-free by construction**. On square, circular, and star-shaped domains it is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks (`PINN`), `PIKAN`, and other KAN variants. It is also applied to data-driven reconstruction of flow past a cylinder and turbulent flow through a U-bend.

papers.title: Detecting AI Training in Datacentre Power
papers.abstract: AI governance agreements require methods to detect large model training runs on a monitored computing cluster, without trusting the operator. We develop a method to detect synchronous model training in facility-level power by Viterbi tracking of the wandering iteration cadence. On simulated datacentre power, when the operator makes no attempt to hide, the Viterbi tracker detects at least $96\%$ of training runs against a declared inference workload, at a $1\%$ false-alarm rate and within $0.04$ of the Neyman--Pearson optimum, given a meter that samples at $2$ Hz or faster. Of eight adversarial strategies an operator might use to hide, only extreme variation of the work per iteration evades the tracker. Its strongest form hides training in up to $73\%$ of five-minute observations, but over a day at least $87\%$ of such runs are still caught, at a $0.1\%$ false-alarm rate per run. This adversarial strategy costs no throughput, but in small-scale training the operator needs $93$--$267\%$ more compute to reach the same loss. A modest passive meter is sufficient to make hidden training both detectable and expensive, which makes power metering a promising part of compute verification that does not depend on trusting the operator.
papers.summary: AI governance agreements need a way to detect large training runs on a monitored cluster without trusting the operator. The authors use Viterbi tracking of the wandering iteration cadence that synchronous training leaves in facility-level power draw. On simulated datacenter power with a meter sampling at 2 Hz or faster, the tracker **detects at least 96% of undisguised training runs at a 1% false-alarm rate**, within 0.04 of the theoretical optimum. Of eight evasion strategies, only extreme variation in work per iteration partly succeeds, yet at least 87% of such runs are still caught over a day, and in small-scale experiments the evasion required 93% to 267% more compute to reach the same loss.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling
papers.abstract:
Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries.
  The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository.
  The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair.
papers.summary: Static analyzers miss security bugs when nobody has written detection rules for new frameworks and idioms. `SESAA` starts with no rules and has an LLM agent iteratively write readable `joern` queries, revising them based only on feedback from a second LLM critic that flags likely false alarms and misses without seeing ground-truth labels. On the `OWASP Benchmark` for Python, it reaches **a mean F1 of 0.742**, well above five widely used tools in their default configurations and comparable to the best of them tuned with ground-truth labels. In a pilot on real Python projects, queries induced from code that predated each vulnerability detected 10 of 19 later CVEs.

papers.title: SIGNN++: Robust Graph Neural Star Identification on Earth
papers.abstract: We present SIGNN++, a learning-based star identification (SID) framework for celestial navigation in GNSS-denied nighttime environments. Although researchers have developed learning-based SID methods to improve robustness to observation noise, prior evaluations have focused mainly on synthetic or non-terrestrial environments, leaving their reliability under real terrestrial conditions unclear. To address these limitations, SIGNN++ extends SIGNN, a graph neural network-based SID method, with three components: a more realistic noise model for training data, Fourier Transform (FT) of angular-distance edge features, and RANSAC-based Perspective Star Alignment for identification and attitude refinement. The results show that SIGNN++ is more robust to terrestrial observation disturbances and achieves higher star identification accuracy and solved rates than the original SIGNN and publicly available SID baselines, while maintaining comparable attitude accuracy and practical computation time for continuous operation. The implementation code of SIGNN++ and datasets will be available at https://signnpp.github.io/signnpp/.
papers.summary: Learning-based star identification (SID) for celestial navigation where GNSS satellite positioning is unavailable has mostly been evaluated in synthetic or space settings, so its reliability under real ground-based observing conditions was unclear. `SIGNN++` extends the graph neural network method `SIGNN` with a more realistic training noise model, Fourier-transformed angular-distance edge features, and RANSAC-based star alignment for identification and attitude refinement. It is **more robust to terrestrial observation disturbances** and achieves higher identification accuracy and solve rates than `SIGNN` and public baselines, with comparable attitude accuracy and computation time practical for continuous operation.

papers.title: Agentic Verified Optimization of Real-World Software
papers.abstract: Program optimization aims to improve performance while preserving behavior. Coding agents can already make programs faster by changing algorithms, data structures, and execution strategies. However, existing equivalence checks mostly rely on tests, which agents have been shown to exploit, passing the tests without preserving the intended behavior. We propose agentic verified optimization, in which an agent produces a faster implementation together with a machine-checked proof of equivalence to the existing one. Because the existing implementation serves as the specification, the task avoids the specification-writing bottleneck of verified code generation, and recent advances in theorem proving make the proofs attainable. We formulate the task at the function and repository levels in Lean 4, where programs can be both executed and reasoned about. Few real-world applications are written in Lean, so we develop Aqueduct, an agentic framework that migrates C, C++, Go, and Rust programs into native Lean, validates each port by differential testing against its original. On the 189 reference implementations in Verina, agents produce faster proved rewrites for 156, including algorithmic changes such as replacing exponential recursion with dynamic programming. On 17 migrated applications, their 92 proved rewrites speed up 47 of 51 application scenarios. These application-level gains are smaller than the function-level ones, making the choice of functions to optimize an important problem. Current agents can thus already carry out verified optimization on both standalone functions and applications migrated from real programs. We discuss the remaining challenges and the steps toward verified optimization in production.
papers.summary: Coding agents can make programs faster, but they are usually checked only with tests, and agents have been shown to game those tests without keeping the intended behavior. The proposed task, agentic verified optimization, asks an agent to produce a faster implementation in `Lean 4` together with a machine-checked proof that it is equivalent to the existing code, which serves as the specification. The authors also build `Aqueduct`, an agentic framework that ports C, C++, Go, and Rust programs into native Lean and validates each port by differential testing against the original. Agents produced faster proved rewrites for **156 of the 189 reference implementations in `Verina`**, and on 17 migrated applications, 92 proved rewrites sped up 47 of 51 scenarios, with smaller gains at the application level than at the function level.

papers.title: Why Constrained Updates Still Forget: A Functional-Path Analysis of Continual SFT
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning adapts language models to specialized tasks but can disrupt previously acquired behavior. Existing approaches constrain parameters, gradients, or replay objectives, yet the connection between the protected object, the intervening trajectory, and retained outputs remains unclear. We develop a functional-path account that decomposes old-loss changes along realized updates into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects. The account yields a conditional refresh budget and identifies the restoring direction supplied by informative replay. Matched QLoRA interventions separate constraint granularity from placement before or after Adam: placement strongly affects retention across the studied code-label audits, whereas the granularity interaction depends on the endpoint. Checkpointed generation separates endpoint recovery from higher sampled-path accuracy, and matched replay schedules reveal loss exposure concealed by final scores. A sequential-task comparison extends this distinction to backward transfer: subspace regularization and projection improve average retention while trading off different old tasks; supervised replay protects both more consistently in this setting. Additional response interfaces distinguish content gains from exact-response retention. These findings connect update-level protection to task-wise behavior and motivate mitigation through explicit functional anchors, trajectory evaluation, and joint old/new auditing.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning can erase behavior a language model learned earlier, and existing defenses constrain parameters, gradients, or replay without a clear link to what is actually retained. The authors propose a functional-path account that splits changes in the old-task loss into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects, and use it to derive a conditional refresh budget. Controlled `QLoRA` experiments show that **whether a constraint is applied before or after the `Adam` update strongly affects retention**, while the effect of constraint granularity depends on the endpoint measured. In sequential tasks, subspace regularization and projection improve average retention but trade off between old tasks, whereas supervised replay protects both more consistently.

papers.title: Protection Is Not One Event: A Survey of RAG Protection Research by Measured Endpoint
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems face security, privacy, and copyright risks including content leakage, source reconstruction, unauthorized access, data poisoning, and prompt injection. Yet RAG protection studies use incompatible evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models. We present a systematic survey and human-coded evidence map of 118 full-text-confirmed RAG defense papers, organized by measured endpoint rather than claimed goal or defense mechanism. Our seven-family taxonomy covers content disclosure, formal privacy proxies, access control and suppression, corpus-use detection, and pipeline integrity and attribution. Thirty-two annotators double-coded the papers kappa=0.867. The survey identifies three gaps. First, retrieval reranking and context rewriting each span five or six endpoint families, so mechanisms do not identify protection outcomes. Second, only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary endpoint; under the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% of records have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, and none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, most evaluations use general-purpose question-answering datasets and non-adaptive attacks rather than sensitive data and adaptive, multi-turn extraction. Our controlled RAG testbed shows that preventing verbatim copying does not prevent private-fact recovery: a normalized 8-gram guard reduces 20-token copying to 0.0%, but a three-query adaptive attacker recovers 48.3% of hidden facts on Qwen3-8B. We release the taxonomy, dataset, coding protocols, and testbed to enable comparable, claim-aligned RAG security evaluation.
papers.summary: Studies of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) protection use incompatible metrics, datasets, and threat models, so the authors survey 118 defense papers and double-code them (kappa 0.867) into a seven-family taxonomy organized by the outcome each study actually measures. They find that mechanisms such as reranking and context rewriting span five or six outcome families, that only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary outcome, and that most evaluations rely on general question-answering data and non-adaptive attacks. In a controlled testbed, an 8-gram copy guard reduces 20-token verbatim copying to 0.0%, yet **a three-query adaptive attacker still recovers 48.3% of hidden facts** on `Qwen3-8B`. The taxonomy, dataset, coding protocols, and testbed are released.

papers.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via Generalized Moment Matching
papers.abstract: We study $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private synthetic data for arbitrary databases of $n$ records in $[-1,1]^d$ under a specified integral probability metric (IPM). We introduce generalized moment matching, which estimates moments privately, fits a probability measure, and samples synthetic records. A general error theorem applies when moment error controls the target IPM. This framework extends Chebyshev moment matching for $1$-Wasserstein distance and smooth queries. We apply the framework to maximum mean discrepancy with Matern and Laplace kernels and a two-layer ReLU neural tangent kernel.We also obtain guarantees for sliced Wasserstein-$1$ and the IPM induced by norm-bounded ReLU networks. With sufficiently many synthetic records,these rates are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed dimension.
papers.summary: The work studies how to generate (ε,δ)-differentially private synthetic data for databases of n records in [-1,1]^d, measured against a chosen integral probability metric (IPM). The proposed method, `generalized moment matching`, estimates moments privately, fits a probability measure to them, and samples synthetic records from it, with a general error theorem that holds whenever moment error controls the target metric. It extends `Chebyshev moment matching` and gives guarantees for maximum mean discrepancy with Matérn, Laplace, and ReLU neural tangent kernels, for sliced Wasserstein-1, and for metrics induced by norm-bounded ReLU networks. With enough synthetic records, **the rates are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors** in fixed dimension.

papers.title: Detection Is Not Enough: Reasoning Traces as Testable Program Hypotheses
papers.abstract: When a language model is deployed, no reference solution exists, so the reasoning trace it writes is the only evidence for judging its answer. The reference-free substitutes each fail differently: self-assessment degrades the answer it was meant to protect, sampling agreement measures stability rather than correctness, and perturbation studies read the expected answer off a human-written template, grading a model rather than a trace. We ask how far a single trace can be verified with no reference solution, no judge model and no weight update, and find, for a frozen LLaMA-2-7B-chat on GSM8K, that detection is not what limits such a pipeline. Checking a trace against itself reaches an AUROC of 0.741 and stops there for a structural reason: two thirds of wrong traces state no false equation, having executed a mistaken plan correctly, and on wrong-plan failures the detector flags a wrong trace less often than a right one. A candidate-derived metamorphic probe exposes many of these failures: we abstract the trace into a program over the question's quantities, perturb one quantity, execute the program, and ask the model the rewritten question once, so every trace supplies its own test. Valid perturbations exist for 937 of 1,319 test questions (71.0%); among the 847 that also have a parseable first trace, supported traces are correct 60.6% of the time against a 31.6% base rate, although the probe also refutes 45.5% of correct traces. No tested policy yields a statistically significant improvement in accuracy. A flag earns its retry only when detector precision exceeds D/(R+D), where R and D are the rates at which a retry repairs a wrong trace and damages a correct one; our repair rate is so low that, at the same retry budget, even a perfect detector would recover an estimated 66 of 1,319 questions. Repair, not detection, is the open problem.
papers.summary: In deployment no reference solution exists, so the authors ask how far a single reasoning trace can be verified with no reference, no judge model, and no weight updates, using a frozen `LLaMA-2-7B-chat` on `GSM8K`. Checking a trace against itself plateaus at an AUROC of 0.741 because two thirds of wrong traces contain no false equation: they correctly execute a wrong plan. A metamorphic probe that turns the trace into a program, perturbs one quantity, and re-asks the model raises the accuracy of supported traces to 60.6% against a 31.6% base rate, but it also rejects 45.5% of correct traces. No tested retry policy significantly improves accuracy, and because retries repair so few wrong traces, the authors estimate that **even a perfect detector would recover only about 66 of 1,319 questions**, making repair rather than detection the bottleneck.

papers.title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning
papers.abstract: With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat. Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment. Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads. In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL). Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities. We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives. Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach. The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks. In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models. Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%. Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy. These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.
papers.summary: Prompt injection (PI) hidden in text or images threatens multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and signature- or perplexity-based detectors struggle with sophisticated cross-modal payloads. `MPIDetector` uses few-shot in-context learning (ICL), giving an LLM prompt templates and example attacks so it can judge the semantic intent of inputs without any fine-tuning. On a new benchmark of eight textual and seven visual attack categories plus benign data, tested with `Gemini-2.0-Flash`, `Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct`, and `Doubao-seed-1.6-flash`, it reaches up to 90.91% accuracy with 100% recall on text and up to 99.28% accuracy on images. Against 500 heavily obfuscated web-agent injections from `WebInject`, **it detects up to 99.80%**, outperforming the baselines it is compared with.

papers.title: Feedback That Backfires in Games: Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent's move fails, the harness writes the move and the failure message into the transcript and asks again. In tool calling, this record makes small models more likely to repeat the failed action. We test whether the same holds in games (Sokoban, Connect Four, Othello), where a move can fail by being illegal or by being legal but losing, both verified exactly. On fixed probe items built by perturbing a correct move, the record backfires: pooled over 8 instruction-tuned models (135M-1.7B) it makes the failed move more likely (corrective gain G = -1.38 nats per token), through the move's surface form, for illegal moves but not for losing ones, and not for every model. An exploratory analysis shows what sets the sign: after the record, the failed move's log-probability barely depends on how likely it was before (slope 0.18). Moves the model would not have played become more likely, and greedy decoding starts to produce them; moves it was about to play become less likely, but greedy decoding still repeats 38% of them. A description of the failure that omits the move string keeps the model's preference instead. Along the OLMo 2 1B post-training ladder the inversion is present in the base model and largely removed at the DPO stage. RAGEN's default models invert in RAGEN's own Sokoban format before any RL. A "do not repeat" instruction does nothing, a clean retry is the worst harness, and a decoder ban stops exact repeats but not illegal play. All measurements ran in float32 on a free Colab GPU, which first reproduced the original paper's number.
papers.summary: When an LLM agent's move fails, the harness usually writes the move and the error into the transcript and asks again, and this record was already known to make small models repeat failed tool calls. The authors test the same effect in `Sokoban`, `Connect Four`, and `Othello` across 8 instruction-tuned models (135M to 1.7B parameters) and find that **the failure record makes the failed move more likely** (a corrective gain of -1.38 nats per token), driven by the move's surface form and present for illegal but not for losing moves. Describing the failure without repeating the move string avoids the effect; a do-not-repeat instruction does nothing, and a decoder ban stops exact repeats but not illegal play. Along the `OLMo 2 1B` post-training stages the inversion is largely removed at the `DPO` step, and `RAGEN`'s default models already show it before any RL. All experiments ran on a free Colab GPU.

papers.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.
papers.summary: In long-context inference with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the key-value (KV) cache becomes the memory bottleneck, and existing compression methods built for dense transformers ignore that evicting cache entries can change which experts get selected. `MoEZip` scores context tokens by combining attention weights with a new metric, based on the Fisher information of the routing distributions, that estimates how sensitive expert routing is to perturbation, and it composes this with dense-model eviction scores. **At 10% KV retention, it beats the strongest baseline by 24 and 20 points on average on `LongBench` and `RULER`**, which corresponds to 2.3x and 4.9x higher scores.

papers.title: Spectral Uncertainty Decomposition for Sparse Bayesian Learning
papers.abstract: Estimating distributed neural sources from M/EEG measurements is an ill-posed inverse problem where principled uncertainty quantification remains challenging. The usual conditional Gaussian posterior covariance does not explicitly distinguish uncertainty along likelihood-visible source directions from uncertainty that is invisible to the measurements. We propose a spectral framework based on the singular value structure of the prior-preconditioned forward operator, which provides an exact, interpretable decomposition of the posterior covariance into data-informed and indeterminacy epistemic components. This formulation identifies uncertainty contributions that are reducible by better measurements from those that are fundamentally irreducible by sensing geometry. We further derive an equivalent subtractive decomposition that expresses the prior covariance as the sum of posterior and data-driven reduction terms, enabling precise accounting of uncertainty reduction through Bayesian learning. Together, these complementary representations offer both theoretical insight and practical tools for interpretable uncertainty quantification in M/EEG source imaging for linear-Gaussian Bayesian inverse solvers where the posterior covariance is available in closed form.
papers.summary: Estimating brain sources from magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography (M/EEG) recordings is an ill-posed inverse problem, and the standard Gaussian posterior covariance does not separate uncertainty the measurements can see from uncertainty they cannot. The authors use the singular value structure of the prior-preconditioned forward operator to give **an exact decomposition of the posterior covariance into data-informed and indeterminacy components**, separating uncertainty that better measurements could reduce from uncertainty fixed by sensor geometry. An equivalent subtractive form writes the prior covariance as the posterior plus a data-driven reduction term, which shows exactly how much uncertainty Bayesian learning removes in linear-Gaussian solvers.

papers.title: Prediction Is Not Calibration: Item Parameter Recovery and Representation Coupling in Knowledge Tracing
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) models can estimate item parameters through an item response decoder trained solely for next-response prediction, yet predictive accuracy does not guarantee parameter recovery. We study 2PL, GPCM, and NRM decoders paired with LSTM, Transformer, and DKVMN encoders. Response-model derivatives show why discrimination and option slope updates depend directly on the scale and spread of estimated ability. Affine logit identities show how item-dependent shifts and rescaling in estimated ability are absorbed into item parameters without changing response probabilities. In simulations, difficulty, mean threshold, and correct-option intercept recovery remain high under shuffled order across representation widths, whereas discrimination and keyed option slope contrast recovery require wider item representations and degrade further under fixed item order. Separating the sequence item representation (width $d_S$) from the item parameter key (width $d_M$), and pairing a wide key with a thin sequence representation ($\mathrm{SK}(64,8)$), reduces fixed-order ability distortions and improves recovery and cross-order consistency without sacrificing test accuracy or increasing model size relative to a shared width-64 baseline ($\mathrm{SH}(64)$). On TIMSS and EdNet, widening $d_M$ consistently improves agreement with an offline IRT reference, while the trade-off from narrowing $d_S$ depends on the encoder's reliance on sequence width for prediction. These findings show why item parameters, especially discrimination and option slopes, must be evaluated separately from response prediction.
papers.summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) models can learn item parameters through an item-response decoder trained only to predict a student's next response, but good prediction does not guarantee those parameters are recovered correctly. Studying `2PL`, `GPCM`, and `NRM` decoders with `LSTM`, `Transformer`, and `DKVMN` encoders, the authors show analytically how shifts and rescaling in estimated ability are absorbed into item parameters without changing predictions, and in simulations **discrimination and option-slope recovery need wider item representations** while difficulty recovery stays high. Separating a wide item-parameter key from a thin sequence representation improves recovery and consistency without hurting accuracy or adding parameters, and on `TIMSS` and `EdNet` a wider key consistently brings estimates closer to an offline item response theory (IRT) reference.

papers.title: AI Mindmeld: A Latent Interconnect Protocol
papers.abstract:
LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training.
  The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility.
  Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld
papers.summary: When LLMs act as scientific agents, specialist models must pass information to them as text or other media, which is a bottleneck between rich internal representations. The proposed `Latent Interconnect Protocol` (`LIP`) trains only small connectors that map specialist representations directly into a frozen LLM's internal states, so new specialists can be added without retraining the LLM or existing connectors. Connecting three protein and three small-molecule specialists to `Gemma 3` (4B and 12B) and `Kimi K2.6`, the authors show that independently trained connectors answer familiar and new question types about unseen objects and **transfer zero-shot to cross-domain tasks without joint training**, with gains growing as the LLM gets more capable. They note that current LLMs are not trained to use such inputs, so access does not guarantee the information is used reliably in reasoning.

papers.title: When Reconstruction Is Not Enough: Doubly Robust Counterfactual and Interventional Mediation Analysis with Learned Multimodal Representations
papers.abstract: Learned representations of high-dimensional multimodal health records are increasingly used to adjust for confounding, yet they are usually trained to reconstruct the data rather than preserve the information that causal identification requires. We study counterfactual outcomes under alternative treatments, including phenotype-specific effects and patient-level counterfactual risk profiles of the kind digital twins provide, and interventional direct and indirect effects under exposure-induced intermediate confounding. We give conditions under which a representation preserves identification and show that interventional mediation is more demanding than counterfactual comparison. We prove that no covariate-only training objective, whether reconstruction, contrastive, or physics-informed, can certify that a representation is sufficient, and that, in a linear structural model, a representation can lose arbitrarily little reconstruction accuracy yet induce arbitrarily large bias. We decompose the error of cross-fitted doubly robust estimators into a first-order representation bias, which neither double robustness nor cross-fitting removes, and a second-order remainder of nuisance-estimation errors, so coverage worsens as the sample size grows when the representation is insufficient. We propose a workflow combining modality-specific variational autoencoders trained outside the estimation sample, cross-fitted doubly robust estimators, locked phenotypes, select-then-confirm pathway analysis, portable representations, and diagnostics for representation insufficiency, exposure leakage, and sensitivity. In simulations, discarding a rare, moderately strong confounder gave indirect-effect intervals with 2% coverage at n = 3,000; reconstruction loss missed the problem, and a simple predictive diagnostic flagged it in every replicate.
papers.summary: Learned representations of multimodal health records are often used to adjust for confounding in causal analyses, yet they are trained to reconstruct the data rather than to preserve the information needed to identify causal effects. The authors give conditions under which a representation preserves identification for counterfactual and interventional mediation effects, and prove that **no objective trained only on covariates, whether reconstruction, contrastive, or physics-informed, can certify that a representation is sufficient**. They show that a first-order representation bias survives doubly robust estimation and cross-fitting, so confidence-interval coverage worsens as the sample size grows. In simulations, dropping a rare confounder gave indirect-effect intervals with 2% coverage at n = 3,000; reconstruction loss missed this, while a simple predictive diagnostic in their proposed workflow flagged it every time.

papers.title: How Prompt Style Affects AI Accuracy and Speed in Competitive Programming
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in competitive programming, and their outputs are sensitive to how a prompt is phrased. Prior work has compared prompt strategies for accuracy on competitive programming, but not for runtime speed, and has not situated the results against human performance. In an exploratory study of one prompt in each of nine styles on GPT-5.5 across three accuracy tasks from the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and two NP-hard speed tasks, we found that no single prompt was best: the strongest prompt depended on the task type and on whether results were summarized by the mean or the median, suggesting that, at least for these tasks, prompt style should be matched to the objective rather than treated as universal. Many differences in mean scores came from a few outlier runs, showing that evaluating prompting by a single metric can obscure how much its effectiveness varies. Compared descriptively with human IOI contestants, who worked under different conditions, the AI was neither strictly better nor strictly worse, exceeding the average contestant on one task but falling short on the other two. By extending prompt comparison from accuracy to runtime speed and grounding it against human performance, this study gives a broader picture of how prompt style affects competitive programming performance.
papers.summary: LLM outputs on competitive programming depend on how the prompt is phrased, but earlier comparisons looked only at accuracy and not at runtime speed or human baselines. This exploratory study tests one prompt in each of nine styles on `GPT-5.5`, using three accuracy tasks from the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and two NP-hard speed tasks. **No single prompt style was best**: the winner depended on the task type and on whether results were summarized by mean or median, and many mean differences came from a few outlier runs. Compared descriptively with human IOI contestants, who worked under different conditions, the model beat the average contestant on one task and fell short on the other two.

papers.title: GANet: A Lightweight Group Attention Network for Plant Disease Identification on Embedded Systems
papers.abstract: Global warming and climate change are major catalysts for plant diseases, significantly affecting food production worldwide. Addressing this issue requires continuous monitoring and early detection of plant diseases. While recent advancements in deep learning offer potential solutions, most models demand high processing power and struggle to perform efficiently on low-end electronic hardware. Furthermore, many existing works focus on specific crop diseases, limiting their broader applicability. This paper presents a lightweight Group Equivariance Attention Network (GANet) designed for the prediction and monitoring of 38 types of plant diseases. GANet introduces a novel Group Attention block and Group-Wise Feature Fusion block, making it both sparse and efficient. With only 0.001M parameters, the model achieves an impressive 99.99% accuracy on the PlantVillage dataset. Additionally, GANet is optimized for deployment on edge devices such as the Raspberry Pi 4b and Jetson Nano, where it reaches 5 FPS and 11 FPS, respectively, demonstrating its potential for real-time plant disease monitoring on low-power devices.
papers.summary: Most deep learning models for plant disease detection need more compute than low-end hardware provides, and many target only a single crop. `GANet` is a lightweight group-equivariance attention network that uses new group attention and group-wise feature fusion blocks to classify 38 plant disease types. The authors report **99.99% accuracy on `PlantVillage` with only 0.001M parameters**, and 5 and 11 frames per second on a Raspberry Pi 4B and a Jetson Nano.

papers.title: Benchmarking Model Compression Techniques Across Heterogeneous Edge Platforms: A Predictive Maintenance Use Case for Rotating Machinery
papers.abstract: To enable Industry 5.0, where autonomous systems are widely adopted and integrated with people to promote sustainable development in industries, it is imperative to adapt complex deep learning models to operate efficiently on resource-constrained hardware for edge inference. However, adapting these models remains challenging due to the hardware heterogeneity of edge computing in industrial settings, performance degradation caused by model compression, and the lack of clear guidance on which compression techniques are practical and effective for applications such as predictive maintenance.
