To address these challenges, this paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four state-of-the-art model compression techniques applied to a high-performance convolutional neural network for predictive maintenance using a real-world dataset of rotating machinery, equipment typically used in industry. The compressed models were evaluated across a heterogeneous set of nine computing platforms, ranging from highly constrained edge computing devices to general purpose and high-performance processors, reflecting the diversity and fragmentation typical of industrial edge environments. By jointly prioritizing classification performance, inference speed, and compression ratio, we found that compression using knowledge distillation emerged as the most effective approach. The model had more than 90% speedup across all devices while maintaining a 91.22% balanced F-score, with a very small drop in predictive performance relative to the uncompressed model, along with a 98.9% size reduction. Through successful deployment across multiple edge platforms and a systematic comparison of compression strategies, we demonstrated a clear path to achieving Industry 5.0 targets, drastically cutting computational costs and, consequently, energy consumption without sacrificing predictive performance.
papers.summary: Industrial edge hardware is varied, and it is unclear which model compression techniques work best for tasks such as predictive maintenance. The authors compare four compression techniques applied to a convolutional neural network that diagnoses faults in rotating machinery from a real-world dataset, measuring the results on nine platforms ranging from constrained edge devices to high-performance processors. Weighing accuracy, inference speed, and compression ratio together, **knowledge distillation was the most effective**: it gave more than 90% speedup on every device and a 98.9% size reduction while keeping a 91.22% balanced F-score, only slightly below the uncompressed model.

papers.title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI
papers.abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) models are often shared without their training data, assuming this protects the patients who contributed them. However, a model can reveal whether a patient's records were used in training, a privacy breach known as a membership inference attack. This risk is usually reported as a cohort average, which can appear negligible while individual patients are almost certainly exposed. Identifying potentially vulnerable records before developing a production model could make privacy assessment more practical. We measured each patient's vulnerability to membership inference attack, across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models. Training choices changed how many patients had high attack scores, but the patients who ranked highest by risk largely stayed the same across the configurations we tested. Stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold, yet largely the same patients remained most at risk across training recipes, architectures and initializations, including foundation models. Therefore, we developed a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to identify patients with high risk of exposure before production-model training. We also assessed if flagged patients could be protected without removing their data. Privacy screening should become incorporated into data preparation for clinical AI.
papers.summary: Medical AI models are often shared without their training data, yet a membership inference attack can still reveal whether a given patient's records were used for training, and cohort-average risk figures hide individual exposure. Measuring per-patient vulnerability across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, the authors find that training choices change how many patients are exposed (stronger weight decay shrank the exposed group up to threefold), but **largely the same patients stay most at risk across training recipes, architectures, initializations, and foundation models**. Based on this, they build a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to flag high-risk patients before the production model is trained, and they test ways to protect flagged patients without removing their data.

papers.title: Edit, Don't Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Visual mathematical reasoning can fail before reasoning begins: when a vision-language model (VLM) misreads a diagram, subsequent reasoning proceeds from false premises. This perceptual bottleneck is especially pronounced in smaller models, while accurate textual descriptions can substantially narrow the gap to larger models. Because obtaining such descriptions at inference requires additional annotation or model calls, we propose minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation. Using reference figure descriptions and verified reference solutions as training-only information, a teacher scores incorrect student rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, and only teacher-disfavored tokens contribute to the corrective loss. Correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. This preserves on-policy supervision while avoiding full-response imitation. Across model scales, the method requires no descriptions at test time and meets or exceeds the corresponding base model supplied with a reference figure description at inference. It also improves perception-oriented performance, particularly low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external mathematics and perception benchmarks. Because the minimal-edit teacher evaluates corrections rather than generating its own solution, the method remains effective with a frozen same-size teacher, although its gains are smaller than with a larger teacher on most metrics.
papers.summary: Smaller vision-language models (VLMs) often fail at visual math because they misread the diagram, and accurate text descriptions of the figure close much of the gap but are costly to obtain at inference time. The proposed `minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation` uses reference figure descriptions and verified solutions only during training: a teacher scores the student's incorrect rollouts under a minimal-edit objective so that only tokens the teacher disfavors contribute to the loss, while correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. **Without any descriptions at test time, trained models meet or exceed their base models given a reference description**, improve low-level geometric perception, and transfer to external math and perception benchmarks. The method still works with a frozen teacher of the same size, though the gains are smaller than with a larger teacher.

papers.title: Breaking the high-degree barrier in Lehmer's problem with a human-AI discovery loop
papers.abstract: While artificial intelligence has made rapid progress in mathematical reasoning, many open problems depend on structure that is revealed only through large-scale computational exploration and analytical synthesis. One such example is Lehmer's problem from 1933. It asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial, which measures how far its roots stray from the unit circle, can be made arbitrarily small. Previously, constructing irreducible polynomials with integer coefficients and small Mahler measure has been carried out systematically only for even degrees $d \le 180$. At higher degrees, Boyd's analytical one-parameter family frequently factors, skipping nearly 50% of target degrees and leaving no general construction for arbitrary $d$. Here, we address the high-degree regime through a human-AI discovery loop, in which we extend the conversational prompting with a fast numerical pipeline, an exact symbolic verifier, and large-scale distributed search. The AI agent prototypes numerical and symbolic solvers locally, launches parallel searches across distributed clusters and works with the human researcher to extract and verify mathematical hypotheses. Through this interactive loop, we derive a five-parameter construction, which we call the Generalized Boyd algorithm. It eliminates degree-skipping and constructs irreducible polynomials with Mahler measure strictly below Boyd's limit point $\alpha_1 \approx 1.255434$ for every target degree. Evaluated across all even degrees up to 2000, our approach improves upon six previously published values and holds 99.6% of all best known records. With this work we release the verified dataset of polynomials with minimal Mahler measure across all studied even degrees.
papers.summary: Lehmer's 1933 problem asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial can be made arbitrarily small, but small-measure irreducible polynomials had been constructed systematically only up to degree 180, and Boyd's one-parameter family skips nearly half of the higher degrees because it factors. The authors run a human-AI discovery loop in which an AI agent builds numerical and symbolic solvers, launches distributed searches, and works with a human researcher to form and verify hypotheses. The result is a five-parameter `Generalized Boyd algorithm` that **produces irreducible polynomials with Mahler measure below Boyd's limit point for every target degree**. Across all even degrees up to 2000, it improves six published values and holds 99.6% of the best known records, and the verified polynomials are released as a dataset.
papers.highlight_summary:
Lehmer's 1933 problem asks whether an integer polynomial's Mahler measure can sit arbitrarily close to 1, but beyond degree 180 nobody had a systematic way to build irreducible polynomials with small measure. Boyd's one-parameter family often factors at those degrees and skips nearly **50%** of them. The authors pair `Gemini` running in Google's `Antigravity` agent environment with a human researcher, fast numerical search, exact irreducibility checks and cloud-scale sweeps, and from what the search turned up they derive a five-parameter construction that reaches every even degree.

- Search workers stream candidates to separate verification workers, which use Mathematica's `IrreduciblePolynomialQ` to check irreducibility exactly while the search keeps running; the searches themselves combine `RL` (a cross-entropy-method policy), evolutionary search, priority search, direct sparse search and periodic tiling with a central defect, and the tiling method accounts for **54.2%** of leaderboard entries.
- Across all even degrees up to 2000, the search produced best-known polynomials for **824 degrees**; on the 91 degrees with published values it matches 85 and improves **6**, including d=178 inside the previously well-searched range and d=188, where the best measure drops from 1.28309 to **1.25208**.
- Multiplying the dense search optima by suitable cyclotomic polynomials cancels their repeating blocks, and **95.5%** of those for d≥30 then reduce to 6–7-term specializations of Boyd's two-variable polynomial `F(X,Y)`; this observation led to the `Generalized Boyd` algorithm, which solves for the exponents and signs `(a, b, k, s0, s1)` needed to hit any target even degree directly.
- `Generalized Boyd` produces verified irreducible polynomials with measure strictly below Boyd's limit point α₁≈1.255434 for **all 995 even degrees from 12 to 2000** (the worst case is 1.25535826 at d=1932), and it holds **99.6%** of best-known records, including every degree d≥166.
- All of these are constructions, so they only show that small measures exist and prove no lower bound: every search method levels off just below α₁ for d≥30, Lehmer's degree-10 record of **1.17628** still stands, and the Mahler measures are computed numerically with `numpy.roots` (only irreducibility is checked exactly), so the paper's talk of "breaking" the high-degree barrier refers to coverage across degrees, not to progress on the conjecture itself.

papers.title: A Quadratic Lens on Muon's Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton-Schulz
papers.abstract: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW, yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD, the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon, on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton-Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon, about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer updates matrix parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains LLMs faster than `AdamW`, but it is unclear when and why this helps. Analyzing `PolarGD`, the orthogonalized update at Muon's core, on matrix quadratics with line search, the authors show that it helps when the gradient is far from low rank and its top singular directions have high curvature, and that it acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate. This means **tiny singular values in the iterate can make it much slower than plain gradient descent**. The few `Newton-Schulz` iterations Muon actually uses treat those small singular values the way gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization, and in a transformer trained with Muon about a quarter of the attention matrices' singular values fall in this regime.

papers.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores. Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.
papers.summary: Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve coding agents, but doing it at every step adds substantial computation and API cost. `SWE-Verifier`, a lightweight generative model trained from `Qwen3.5-4B` on preference data, scores each proposed action to decide when extra candidates are worth sampling, then ranks those candidates before execution. In the `mini-swe-agent` harness it raises resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% for `MiniMax-M2.7` at 1.09x cost, and from 72.60% to 74.27% for `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` without training on that model's actions. **It verifies fewer than 4% of steps** while matching or beating trajectory-level and every-step baselines at much lower cost.

papers.title: Generalizing Metropolis-Hastings for DAG Sampling
papers.abstract: A fundamental challenge in Bayesian network structure learning lies in efficiently approximating the posterior distribution of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). For large, high-dimensional datasets, the task remains beyond the capabilities of current methods. This work advances Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms by introducing novel moves that simultaneously resample the parents for multiple nodes of the DAG. At the core of these moves is duet sampling, a new generalization of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm that selects two proposal distributions from a pool at each iteration. One is used for generating a candidate state of the Markov chain and another for evaluating the return to the current state; both are ingredients of an appropriately crafted acceptance criterion. Pairing different proposal distributions provides additional freedom and enables constructing Markov chains that mix more efficiently than their basic Metropolis-Hastings counterparts, at no additional computational cost. Experiments show that our new moves, both individually and in combination, outperform the previous state of the art, which relies on a more restrictive pool of moves. This advantage persists even when letting the previous methods leverage duet sampling to enhance their performance.
papers.summary: Approximating the posterior distribution over directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in Bayesian network structure learning is still out of reach for large, high-dimensional datasets. The authors add Markov chain Monte Carlo moves that resample the parents of several nodes at once. These moves rest on `duet sampling`, a generalization of `Metropolis-Hastings` that picks two proposal distributions from a pool at each step: one generates the candidate state and the other evaluates the move back to the current state. Pairing proposals this way gives chains that **mix more efficiently at no extra computational cost**, and the new moves beat the previous state of the art even when the earlier methods also use duet sampling.

papers.title: GAV: A scientific experimentation environment for PDE agents
papers.abstract: Reliable feedback is essential for coding agents to develop programs for partial differential equations (PDEs). Yet evaluating these programs on new PDE problems often requires expensive reference computations, while fixed datasets restrict the range of experiments. We introduce Generator-Agent-Verifier (GAV), a scientific experimentation environment that makes new PDE problems verifiable by construction. The Generator learns a distribution of continuous reference solutions using data from numerical simulations or experimental measurements to represent a target physical regime. Using the method of manufactured solutions, it works backward from the generated reference solutions to construct matching PDE problems without a separate numerical solve. The Agent designs experiments, investigates failures, and iteratively improves its program. The Verifier evaluates candidate programs against the reference solutions and provides numerical feedback on accuracy and computational cost. This feedback can also guide the generation of new problems that probe the current program's weaknesses. We provide a theoretical analysis of evaluation reliability and guided development. Experiments on Navier-Stokes and Vlasov-Poisson-type equations across different data sources and regimes demonstrate the effectiveness of GAV. In particular, on the numerical Navier-Stokes task, GAV reduces the mean test error of three existing PDE agents by more than an order of magnitude relative to their original setups. Code is available at https://github.com/PotatoJnny/PDE-GAV.
papers.summary: Coding agents that write solvers for partial differential equations (PDEs) need reliable feedback, but checking a program on a new problem usually requires an expensive reference computation. `Generator-Agent-Verifier` (`GAV`) is an experimentation environment in which a generator learns a distribution of reference solutions from simulation or measurement data. It then uses the method of manufactured solutions to build PDE problems whose answers are known by construction. The agent iterates on its program while a verifier scores accuracy and compute cost, and that feedback can steer generation toward problems that expose the program's weaknesses. On a numerical `Navier-Stokes` task, `GAV` **cuts the mean test error of three existing PDE agents by more than an order of magnitude**, and the approach is also tested on `Vlasov-Poisson`-type equations.

papers.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
papers.abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.69 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.
papers.summary: `EgoHand` is a model that reconstructs 3D hands from monocular egocentric video. It is trained on a curated corpus of 14 million images that mixes synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture. It uses `SOMA-Hand` as its parametric hand model and runs a transformer encoder over 2D hand crops, with camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve alignment with the image. In zero-shot tests on `HOT3D`, `ARCTIC`, and `H2O`, it has lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than baselines at **about 9.69 ms inference latency**. In a blinded user study, participants preferred its poses to those from `Apple EgoDex` and `Ropedia Xperience-10M`, and the model is released under a license that permits commercial use.

papers.title: Measuring Research Progress and Linguistic Inclusion in Low-Resource Languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated research on low-resource and multilingual NLP, but their effectiveness in creating an equitable landscape remains unmapped. We analyze 1,158 peer-reviewed open-access papers published between 2020 and 2025, examining research attention to low-resource languages (LRLs) and representation across language and speaker populations. To assess linguistic inclusion beyond publication counts, we introduce the Linguistic Inclusion Framework (LIF), a multidimensional framework that measures linguistic inclusion in four dimensions: research growth, representation expansion, representation continuity, and distributional equity. While annual publications grew from 52 to 415, a 5.4X increase in their ACL Anthology publication share, this growth largely concentrated on represented languages rather than expanding coverage of underrepresented languages. Further analysis shows that languages spoken in Asia account for 64.1% of speakers across LRLs we analyze but receive only 46.7% of the language representation share (0.7X their proportional share), while European languages receive 5.3X their proportional share. At the country level, linguistically diverse regions such as sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia show the lowest language coverage ratios. Applying the framework at the continental level, we find that no region scores well on all four dimensions, showing that research growth alone is not a reliable metric of progress toward equitable and inclusive language technology\footnote{We will release all collected and annotated data for research purposes}.
papers.summary: The authors analyze 1,158 open-access papers from 2020 to 2025 to see whether the large-language-model era has made research on low-resource languages (LRLs) more equitable. They introduce the `Linguistic Inclusion Framework` (`LIF`), which scores inclusion on four dimensions: research growth, representation expansion, representation continuity, and distributional equity. Annual LRL publications grew from 52 to 415, but most of that growth went to languages already studied rather than to new ones. Asian languages account for 64.1% of the LRL speakers analyzed yet receive only 46.7% of representation share, while **European languages receive 5.3 times their proportional share**, and no continent scores well on all four dimensions.

papers.title: Gender, Sexual Orientation, and the One-Year Refugee Bar: A Computational Study of Bill C-12 and Canadian Refugee Adjudication
papers.abstract:
In March 2026, Bill C-12 amended the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to make refugee claims ineligible for referral to the Refugee Protection Division where they are made more than one year after the claimant's first entry to Canada. Affected claimants are diverted to a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA), which is typically decided by an immigration officer on a paper record, with no guaranteed oral hearing, no appeal on the merits, and no automatic stay of removal pending judicial review. The government defended the bar partly on the premise that genuine refugees claim promptly. Critics countered that late claims are concentrated among vulnerable groups, particularly people fleeing persecution based on gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (SOGIE).
  This article tests those competing premises. Using artificial intelligence tools, checked through human review, it examines nearly 29,000 published decisions of the Refugee Protection Division, the Refugee Appeal Division, and the Federal Court from 2006 to 2025. The results of this study demonstrate that, first, while most claimants claim within a year, roughly one in nine in the published record does not, and gender and SOGIE claims are significantly overrepresented among these late claims. Second, among late claims, refusals of gender and SOGIE claims are more likely than refusals of other claims to be overturned on appeal or judicial review. Late claims on other grounds, by contrast, fare somewhat worse on review than timely claims. The one-year bar therefore removes the hearing, the appeal, and the stay from the late claimants for whom those safeguards have been doing the most work. The article recommends repealing the bar or, failing that, adopting exemptions, procedural protections, and greater transparency in PRRA decision making.
papers.summary: Canada's Bill C-12 bars refugee claims made more than one year after entry from a full hearing and routes them to a paper-based Pre-Removal Risk Assessment with no guaranteed hearing, no merits appeal, and no automatic stay of removal. Using AI tools checked by human review, the author examines nearly 29,000 published refugee and Federal Court decisions from 2006 to 2025 to test the government's premise that genuine refugees claim promptly. About one in nine claims in the published record is late, and claims based on gender or on sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (SOGIE) are significantly overrepresented among them. Among late claims, **refusals of gender and SOGIE claims are more likely than other refusals to be overturned on appeal or judicial review**, which suggests the bar removes safeguards from the claimants who rely on them most.

papers.title: SciFusion: Physics-Guided Compositional Diffusion for Multimodal 3D Scientific Image Generation
papers.abstract: Existing 3D generative approaches are typically developed for individual imaging modalities, requiring substantial modality-specific data and limiting their ability to exploit shared structure across scientific imaging domains. We present SciFusion, a multimodal framework for unified 3D scientific image generation built on a latent diffusion backbone, with two key contributions. First, we introduce a compositional conditioning scheme that factorizes each modality into domain, object, and contrast representations. Sharing these factors across related modalities enables knowledge transfer across heterogeneous imaging domains and allows the factors to be recombined at inference time to synthesize unseen domain-object-contrast compositions in a zero-shot manner. Second, we incorporate domain-specific physics-informed objectives: Fourier spectral consistency for MRI, Radon projection consistency for CT, and multislice diffraction consistency for electron microscopy, to encourage generated samples to respect modality-dependent image formation processes. Extensive experiments across 15 medical and scientific imaging modalities demonstrate that SciFusion improves generation fidelity and cross-domain generalization over modality-specific and flattened multimodal conditioning strategies, while enabling zero-shot synthesis of unseen compositions without training on those target compositions. These results demonstrate that compositional, physics-guided conditioning provides a scalable framework for unified 3D scientific image generation, particularly for emerging modalities where large-scale training data are difficult to obtain.
papers.summary: 3D generative models for scientific imaging are usually built for a single modality and need large amounts of modality-specific data. `SciFusion` is a latent diffusion framework that breaks each modality into domain, object, and contrast factors and shares those factors across related modalities. Recombining the factors at inference time lets it synthesize combinations it never saw in training, zero-shot. Physics-informed losses keep outputs consistent with how each modality forms images: Fourier spectral consistency for MRI, Radon projection consistency for CT, and multislice diffraction consistency for electron microscopy. Across **15 medical and scientific imaging modalities**, it improves fidelity and cross-domain generalization over modality-specific and flat multimodal conditioning.

papers.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.
papers.summary: End-to-end autonomous driving is expensive to train, whether by imitating fleet-scale driving logs or by running reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator. `TerraTransfer++` first trains a policy by self-play in a fast vectorized simulator, then distills its rollouts into a `flow-matching` trajectory teacher that can also plan. Lightweight adapters on a frozen vision backbone are trained to reproduce the teachers' latent spaces, so the only data needed is paired image and scene-state frames, with no expert demonstrations. The resulting closed-loop policy beats all published imitation-based end-to-end methods on `HUGSim`, and the planner reaches **59.4 EPDMS on `NAVSIM` navhard, above every published method**, plus 95.5 PDMS on navtest, all without human demonstrations.

papers.title: MPBRS: Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Unified Reward Configuration in Humanoid Locomotion
papers.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.
papers.summary: Reward functions for humanoid locomotion with reinforcement learning (RL) are hard to tune: shaping terms can conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to one robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. The authors study `Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping` (`MPBRS`), which shapes rewards through differences of several potential functions so that the optimal policy stays the same. They propose a single reward configuration and apply **the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots**, needing only robot metadata such as joint mappings and default poses. Compared with standard shaping, `MPBRS` scales more consistently across robots and is less sensitive to tuning.

papers.title: Spike-Aware Gradient-Based Mixed-Precision Quantization of Spiking Neural Networks for Vision Applications
papers.abstract: In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have gained massive attention as an energy-efficient neural computing paradigm due to their event-driven and sparse computing capability. However, maintaining accuracy under low-precision constraints, necessary for practical deployment, has been largely unexplored for SNN models. In addition, existing Hessian-based approaches for quantization, such as HAWQ-V2, incur significant memory and computational overhead due to temporal unrolling across multiple SNN timesteps. We propose a spike-aware gradient-based mixed-precision quantization framework for SNNs that adaptively assigns bit-widths using first-order gradient information, avoiding costly second-order Hessian computations. We evaluate our method across various SNN-based architectures, including VGG, ResNet, and Vision Transformer models obtained from both ANN-to-SNN conversion and direct training frameworks, on CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR-10 datasets. Notably, on ResNet-34 evaluated on ImageNet, our method achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78$\times$ compression, which is comparable to that provided by HAWQ-V2, while reducing memory consumption by 2.31$\times$ and bit-allocation runtime by 100$\times$. We also present an energy analysis for mixed-precision SNNs showing that the proposed quantization strategy enables energy-efficient deployment without compromising performance.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are energy-efficient, but keeping them accurate at low numerical precision is little explored, and Hessian-based mixed-precision methods such as `HAWQ-V2` become expensive when the network is unrolled over many timesteps. The proposed method assigns bit-widths per layer using only first-order gradient information, which takes spike behavior into account and avoids second-order Hessian computations. It is evaluated on `VGG`, `ResNet`, and `Vision Transformer` SNNs on `CIFAR10/100`, `ImageNet`, and `DVS-CIFAR-10`. On `ResNet-34` on `ImageNet`, it reaches 73.30% accuracy at 4.78x compression, comparable to `HAWQ-V2`, while **using 2.31x less memory and running bit allocation 100x faster**.

papers.title: AQL-Lite: Enabling Efficient Knowledge Acquisition for Arabic LLMs via Data-Centric Continual Pretraining
papers.abstract: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.
papers.summary: Adapting large language models to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) is held back by noisy web data, dialect variation, and the cost of continual pretraining (CPT). `AQL-Lite` pairs a quality-first data-curation pipeline with partial-parameter CPT. The CPT recipe trains `RS-LoRA` adapters across the network along with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix. At a 1B-token budget, curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic average by 3.51 points, whereas raw web text gives no gain over the base model. In a 5B-token comparison, **`AQL-Lite` recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT in 52% of the wall-clock time**, and a 12B model scaled up with this recipe scores 75.3 on `OALL v2`.

papers.title: On the Adversarial Vulnerability of Neural Receivers with Unrolled LDPC Decoders
papers.abstract: Neural receivers for 5G New Radio (NR) match classical model-based receivers in link-level performance, but their robustness to adversarial perturbations at the receiver input remains underexplored. We show that standard gradient-based attacks applied end-to-end through an unrolled low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoder fail to significantly outperform a matched-power Gaussian perturbation. We identify the failure as gradient masking caused by tanh saturation in the boxplus operation of the belief-propagation (BP) check-node update, with a per-iteration gradient norm decay of more than four orders of magnitude across ten unrolled BP iterations. Based on this finding, we propose two structurally independent loss functions that restore attack efficacy. L_BP routes the gradient through the unsaturated early iterations via per-iteration supervision, while L_LLR is a margin loss on pre-decoder log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) whose gradient bypasses the LDPC decoder entirely. Both loss functions increase the block-error rate (BLER) by one to four orders of magnitude at matched perturbation power, with the results reproduced on both the Sionna NeuralReceiver and DeepRx. At low PSR, L_LLR-optimized perturbations achieve up to three orders of magnitude higher BLER on unseen channel realizations than LBP-optimized perturbations.
papers.summary: Neural receivers for 5G New Radio match classical receivers in link performance, but their robustness to adversarial input perturbations has received little study. The authors find that standard gradient attacks run end-to-end through an unrolled low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoder do no better than Gaussian noise of the same power. They trace this to gradient masking: tanh saturation in the belief-propagation check-node update shrinks the gradient by more than four orders of magnitude over ten iterations. Two new losses fix this, one supervising the early unsaturated iterations and one a margin loss on the log-likelihood ratios before the decoder. Together they **raise the block-error rate by one to four orders of magnitude** on both the `Sionna NeuralReceiver` and `DeepRx`.

papers.title: Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly consulted for moral judgment. We aim to improve performance on such tasks by rewarding good arguments, on the premise that arguing well increases the likelihood of judging well. We train a reinforcement learning policy initialized from a state-of-the-art language model in a self-judged tournament with masked thinking: the generated arguments are judged pairwise on argument quality by the policy itself. As an empirical basis, we extract authentic dilemmas from classic novels, using a logic solver to verify that each constitutes a conflict. We show that our judge rates argument quality like human annotators, and the policy then adopts the language register that it rewards. Testing on the external benchmarks MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and MORABLES, we find that the policy becomes more decisive and invariant to the order in which options are presented, but sycophancy and reframing remain a challenge to validity. Two ablation studies with synthetic dilemmas and unmasked thinking match the reordering gains, but show a weaker register shift and higher sycophancy. We conclude that consistency is not validity: consistency under reordering can be optimized without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal.
papers.summary: The authors try to improve language models' moral judgments by rewarding good arguments. They train a reinforcement learning policy, starting from a strong language model, in a tournament where the policy itself judges pairs of arguments while its reasoning is masked. The training dilemmas are taken from classic novels, and a logic solver checks that each one is a genuine conflict. On `MoralChoice`, `ELEPHANT`, and `MORABLES`, the policy becomes more decisive and no longer depends on the order in which options are presented, but sycophancy and sensitivity to reframing remain. The authors conclude that **consistency under reordering can be optimized without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal**.

papers.title: Route-and-Generate: KL-Regularized Router Improvement for Reasoning Routing in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models often apply complex reasoning indiscriminately, leading to overthinking on simple tasks and underthinking on harder ones. We present Route-and-Generate (Rouge), a hierarchical training framework that enables LLMs to adaptively decide when and how much reasoning is required for each input. Our approach decouples reasoning effort allocation from answer generation by introducing a routing policy that allocates a fixed sampling budget across multiple reasoning formats, while the base model is optimized with GRPO using per-sample rewards. To promote efficient reasoning, we employ a rank-based reward that favors shorter correct solutions, and update the routing policy via a closed-form KL-regularized policy improvement step distilled into a neural router. This design encourages concise answers on easy problems while reserving longer reasoning for harder ones, achieving improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
papers.summary: Large language models often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. `Route-and-Generate` (`Rouge`) separates the decision about how much to reason from the generation of the answer. A routing policy splits a fixed sampling budget across several reasoning formats, while the base model is trained with `GRPO` using a rank-based reward that favors shorter correct solutions. The router is updated with a closed-form KL-regularized policy improvement step and distilled into a neural router, so the model **gives concise answers on easy problems and reserves long reasoning for hard ones**. The authors report better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across several reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: CiteAnchor: Source-Aware Grounding for Hallucinated Citation Detection and Resolution
papers.abstract: Hallucinated citations make it harder to trace sources and verify the evidence behind scientific claims. Detecting them is difficult because bibliographic records can be incomplete or differ across source types and publication versions. A plausible match alone neither validates the citation nor establishes its underlying source. We introduce CiteResolve, a benchmark of 423 real-world hallucinated citations annotated for source recoverability. We further propose CiteAnchor, a source-aware grounding framework that adapts retrieval and field-level verification to each source type and separately determines citation validity and whether a unique source can be recovered. On an existing detection benchmark, CiteAnchor achieves 0.841 F1 with GPT-5.6 Luna and 0.784 with an open-weight backbone, outperforming the baseline with the same backbones by 7.9 and 36.8 points. On CiteResolve, it achieves 74.7% and 70.7% end-to-end task success, outperforming the corresponding web search baselines by 16.3 and 65.3 percentage points. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/oldwizard7/CiteANCHOR_code.
papers.summary: Hallucinated citations are hard to detect because real bibliographic records are often incomplete or differ across source types and publication versions, so a plausible-looking match proves little. The authors release `CiteResolve`, a benchmark of 423 real-world hallucinated citations annotated for whether the intended source can be recovered. They also propose `CiteAnchor`, which adapts retrieval and field-level checks to each source type and decides separately whether a citation is valid and whether a unique source can be found. On an existing detection benchmark, it reaches 0.841 F1 with `GPT-5.6 Luna` and 0.784 with an open-weight model. On `CiteResolve`, its end-to-end success is **up to 65.3 percentage points above web-search baselines**.

papers.title: CTRL-FM: Inference-Time Structural Control for Flow-Based Virtual Sensing under Long-Horizon Node Outages
papers.abstract: Long-horizon node outages are harder than conventional missing-value imputation because complete sensor trajectories remain unobserved for extended periods, while the usefulness of spatial and temporal dependencies varies across outage locations and operating regimes. Existing graph, diffusion, and flow-based methods typically impose a fixed structural bias, which can oversmooth abrupt changes or propagate errors from unreliable neighbors. We introduce CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time decision. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns a conditional velocity field while keeping observed measurements exactly fixed. For each realized outage, CTRL-FM constructs self-supervised proxy outages from surviving measurements and uses their known values to select among uncontrolled, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and balanced control policies. The selected policy is locally modulated by graph and temporal reliability estimated exclusively from surviving observations, while boundary-anchored trends provide structural guidance. Control is applied only to missing entries and is rejected when proxy evidence does not sufficiently improve over uncontrolled sampling. Across PeMS08, METR-LA, Air-36, and AQI, CTRL-FM achieves the strongest overall performance under 30% and 60% node outages. Stress tests with up to 75% sensor loss further show graceful degradation and consistent gains over training-time and fixed structural control. These results demonstrate that validating, selecting, and locally adapting structural guidance for each realized outage is more effective than imposing a single global structural prior.
papers.summary: When a sensor goes offline for a long time, its whole trajectory is missing, and how useful spatial or temporal neighbors are for filling it in depends on where and when the outage happens. `CTRL-FM` is a `flow-matching` imputation model that keeps observed values fixed and chooses its structural guidance at inference time, separately for each outage. It builds proxy outages from the surviving measurements and uses their known values to choose among uncontrolled, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and balanced control policies. If the proxy evidence shows no improvement, it falls back to uncontrolled sampling. It **achieves the strongest overall performance under 30% and 60% node outages** on `PeMS08`, `METR-LA`, `Air-36`, and `AQI`, and degrades gracefully with up to 75% sensor loss.

papers.title: Probing and Steering for Safety-Relevant Behaviours in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Activation probes are computed directions in a language model's residual stream, used both to detect safety-relevant behaviours and, by adding their direction back into the stream, to steer them. We explore how the main design choices behind such probes interact, within one pipeline, on one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and across three behaviours: deception, high-stakes awareness and sycophancy. The pipeline crosses two estimators (difference-of-means and logistic regression) with three token-pooling schemes (last, mean and learned attention), selects appropriate layers to detect or steer a behaviour, and evaluates every direction twice: as a detector of the behaviour, and as a steering vector to push outputs towards the behaviour. Prior work read together suggests a read/write dissociation, in which logistic regression reads (detects) best but difference-of-means directions write (steer) best. We find that it holds for deception and high-stakes but not for sycophancy, where the pattern reverses. The reversal appears to follow partially from the data rather than from the estimators. The best pooling technique and the layer choice depend on the behaviour and data, and the layer that steers best can sit well before the layer that detects best. The right steering metric to use between changing a model's perception and eliciting behaviour depends on the task - and the two can disagree outright. The exported probes and directions power an interactive interface through which a user can score and steer text directly.
papers.summary: Activation probes are directions in a language model's internal activations that can detect a behavior and, when added back into the activations, steer it. Using `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, the authors systematically compare probe designs for three behaviors: deception, awareness of high stakes, and sycophancy. They cross two estimators, `difference-of-means` and `logistic regression`, with three token-pooling schemes and evaluate every direction both as a detector and as a steering vector. Prior work suggests logistic regression detects best while difference-of-means steers best; this holds for deception and high-stakes awareness but **reverses for sycophancy**, apparently partly because of the data. The best layer for steering can also sit well before the best layer for detection.

papers.title: Climbing the Ladder: Automating Data Pipelines and Reproducing Baselines in Low-Resource Settings
papers.abstract: The massively multilingual translation systems that now include Sicilian learned it from noisy, non-standardised web text. To obtain better translation quality, we redevelop the small neural machine translation (NMT) system that Wdowiak customized for Sicilian. We rebuild on maintained software the extraction of the parallel text from the PDFs of the bilingual journal Arba Sicula, whose sentences are aligned by a language-agnostic sentence encoder with thresholds tuned against an existing hand alignment and then filtered for the typical errors of automatic alignment. Furthermore, the tokenization and the desinence-biased subword segmentation of the original system are ported to a Perl-free implementation, and all the results are measured on a frozen test set drawn from the journal. We compare small Transformers trained from scratch with the pretrained NLLB model adapted by low-rank fine-tuning, in both directions and with Italian as a closely related bridge language, and we adapt to the pretrained model the reverse-training recipe of the original system, i.e., a stage on forward-scored back-translations of the web Sicilian followed by a stage on the curated literary text. The pretrained model is by far the better of the two, and the staged training improves the translation into Sicilian more than the translation from it. On the test set of the original system, and in the tokenized space in which it was scored, the staged model with a larger adapter and more back-translations is above the reverse-training recipe in the directions that involve English and below it between Sicilian and Italian. Yet, a multilingual adapter degrades the directions on which it was not trained, which limits its use as a general multilingual model.
papers.summary: Multilingual translation systems that cover Sicilian learned it mostly from noisy, non-standardized web text. The authors rebuild an earlier small Sicilian neural machine translation system on maintained software, re-extracting aligned sentence pairs from the bilingual journal Arba Sicula and porting its tokenization and subword segmentation. They compare small Transformers trained from scratch with the pretrained `NLLB` model adapted by low-rank fine-tuning, including staged training on back-translated web Sicilian followed by curated literary text. **The pretrained model is by far the better of the two**, and staged training helps translation into Sicilian more than translation out of it. However, a multilingual adapter degrades the translation directions it was not trained on.

papers.title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
papers.abstract: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.
papers.summary: Large language model agents used as long-horizon planners are costly and prone to invalid actions, so `MemPlan` instead uses the model as a bridge between language and a symbolic `PDDL` planner in partially observable text environments. The PDDL domain stays fixed, and at each step the PDDL problem is rebuilt from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns lower action costs to plausible hypotheses, while negative memory turns assumptions already refuted by execution into exclusion constraints. A language-to-symbol interface trained offline with supervised fine-tuning parses observations and grounds actions as commands. On `TextWorld`, `ALFWorld`, and `Robotouille`, `MemPlan` improves task completion and step efficiency while **substantially reducing online token cost compared with `ReAct`**.

papers.title: Bayesian Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification with Abstention
papers.abstract: We study the Bayesian fixed-confidence best-arm identification problem in which a learner can abstain from making a terminal recommendation. Subject to a target error probability $\delta$ and an abstention budget $\alpha$, we propose Screen-and-Confirm (S&C) and analyze its expected stopping time. We further derive the minimum expected stopping time for any algorithm that satisfies these constraints. For Gaussian priors and rewards, as $(\delta,\alpha)\downarrow(0,0)$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants, with rate $\kappa_\nu^2[1+\log((\alpha+\delta)/\delta)]/(\alpha+\delta)$, where $\kappa_\nu$ is the prior density of the top-two gap at zero, highlighting that nearly tied instances govern the sampling cost. When abstention is disallowed ($\alpha=0$), S&C yields the optimal $\Theta(1/\delta)$ dependence for fixed model parameters, removing the additional $\log(1/\delta)$ factor in the upper bound of Jang et al. (2024) under our Gaussian assumptions. We further characterize the exact multiplicative constant of the minimum expected stopping time for practical regimes including (i) fixed $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and (ii) $\alpha/\delta\to\infty$, which are also achieved by S&C.
papers.summary: The authors study Bayesian best-arm identification at a fixed confidence level when the learner may abstain from recommending an arm, under a target error probability and an abstention budget. They propose `Screen-and-Confirm` (`S&C`) and prove upper and lower bounds on its expected stopping time that match up to constant factors for Gaussian priors and rewards. The bounds show that nearly tied top arms drive the sampling cost. Without abstention, `S&C` **achieves the optimal 1/δ dependence on the error probability δ, removing an extra log(1/δ) factor** from prior upper bounds. The authors also give exact constants for several practical regimes.

papers.title: Text-Only LLM Correctors Break Correct Transcripts: A Repair-Damage Analysis of Audio Grounding in ASR Error Correction
papers.abstract: LLM correctors of ASR output are judged by aggregate WER, which hides what they fix and what they break. We decompose every WER change exactly into repaired tokens, damaged tokens and insertions, and use this to ask what the source audio adds to a corrector. We compare correction with and without the audio, for the model's own draft and for the output of an independent recogniser, on three corpora. With Gemini 2.5 Flash, text-only correction of its own draft breaks 13-32% of already-correct transcripts; with the audio, 1-3%. Damage falls in both settings. Repair falls against the own draft and rises against the recogniser. On medical dictation, kept insertions cancel the gain in net WER. The open-weight Voxtral, which rarely edits, does not show this pattern. Prompts differ between the two arms, so the contrasts bound the effect of the audio and do not isolate it.
papers.summary: Large language models used to correct automatic speech recognition (ASR) output are usually judged by overall word error rate (WER), which hides what they fix and what they break. The authors decompose every WER change exactly into repaired tokens, damaged tokens, and insertions, and compare correction with and without access to the audio on three corpora. With `Gemini 2.5 Flash`, **text-only correction of its own draft breaks 13-32% of already-correct transcripts, versus 1-3% with the audio**, and on medical dictation, insertions cancel the net WER gain. The open-weight `Voxtral` rarely edits and does not show this pattern. Because the prompts differ between the two setups, the comparison bounds the effect of the audio rather than isolating it.

papers.title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
papers.abstract: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.
papers.summary: Multi-agent path planning with fixed start and end configurations can be posed as a high-dimensional optimal control problem. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become intractable as the number of agents grows. `OCFormer` is a transformer that learns a coordinate transformation from a simple latent space, where agents move independently, to the physical space where they interact and must avoid collisions. It is trained with a physics-informed loss built from the PMP Hamiltonian equations plus a boundary-matching term, needs no precomputed trajectories, and its self-attention makes it permutation-equivariant over agents. Trained across many boundary conditions, it produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen configurations in **a single forward pass of about 220ms**, scales to 128 agents in 2D and 3D, and can be adapted to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds by fine-tuning with `L-BFGS`.

papers.title: Soft Ontology Priors over Latent Concept Posteriors for Weakly Supervised Neuro-Symbolic Learning
papers.abstract: Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) predictors that supervise only the task label suffer from reasoning shortcuts: distinct concept mappings achieve the same maximum likelihood, leaving the recovered concepts unidentifiable and unsafe for downstream reuse. We attack this failure by injecting a soft ontology prior over the latent concepts into the training objective and compiling it together with the task constraint into a smooth, decomposable probabilistic circuit. Under independent Bernoulli perception, the normalisers of the resulting structured concept posterior reduce to weighted model counts that are linear in the compiled circuit size, because the neural leaf weights fold into the circuit before evaluation. The soft compilation strategy places expert axioms in the circuit's weights rather than its support (task-structural axioms guaranteed by the data-generating process stay hard), so noisy expert axioms only redistribute prior mass and cannot empty the support. We characterise how the prior reweights label-restricted shortcut mass through differences in ontology violation energy, show that soft priors incur bounded log-density perturbations under bounded axiom noise, and prove that the hard-support counterpart can be made degenerate by a single corrupted axiom. We validate these predictions on an audited six-concept view of the real-world BDD-OIA driving benchmark and on controlled NeSy tasks.
papers.summary: Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) models supervised only on task labels suffer from reasoning shortcuts: several different concept mappings fit the labels equally well, so the learned concepts cannot be identified or safely reused. The authors add a soft ontology prior over the latent concepts and compile it, together with the task constraint, into a smooth, decomposable probabilistic circuit whose normalizers are weighted model counts, linear in circuit size. Expert axioms are encoded in the circuit's weights rather than its support, so noisy axioms only shift prior mass. The theory shows soft priors cause bounded log-density perturbations under bounded axiom noise, while **a single corrupted axiom can make the hard-constraint version degenerate**. Experiments use an audited six-concept view of the `BDD-OIA` driving benchmark and controlled NeSy tasks.

papers.title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.
papers.summary: Classifiers that predict which ion channel (calcium, potassium or sodium) a venom compound targets report 80–90% accuracy. Those numbers rely on random splits that leak phylogenetic information and do not reflect performance on unseen taxa. On a benchmark of 1,373 `ColabFold`-predicted venom structures from five taxa, the authors fuse `ESM-2` sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network and compare five structural inductive biases under leave-one-taxon-out evaluation. All models score 81–86% on random splits. Under taxonomic shift, a sequence-only baseline drops to about 30% and the other geometric priors reach 54–55%, while the persistent-homology model `PH-GNN` reaches **63.4%, more than 8 points ahead of the next-best method**.

papers.title: AcoustiPrint: Physics-Guided Neural Design of Manufacturable Acoustic Structures
papers.abstract: Recent work in additive manufacturing and neural inverse design enables the creation of complex three-dimensional structures to manipulate physical fields, yet these designs must also adhere to discrete, non-differentiable fabrication constraints. Current methods limit the design space by imposing differentiable soft manufacturability loss penalties, or by fixing structures through post-processing, causing a discrepancy between the geometry optimized by the physics model and the final fabricated result. Thus, we present AcoustiPrint, a physics-informed neural architecture for constrained inverse design that represents three-dimensional geometries with an implicit neural representation (INR) and passes each candidate through a printability operator before evaluating its final response. The printability operator executes layer-wise self-support, discrete material selection, and whole-body connectivity, assuring fabrication feasibility. To allow for backpropagation through the discrete non-differentiable operations, we use surrogate gradients for the backward pass and a self-supervised printability objective that progressively drives the INR toward a valid design domain. We demonstrate AcoustiPrint for personalized transcranial focused ultrasound, where inter-patient differences in acoustic properties and head geometry deform wave propagation and requires patient-specific acoustic focusing. AcoustiPrint jointly optimizes three-dimensional geometry and material composition through differentiable wave physics while ensuring manufacturability. Experiments show manufacturable acoustic structures with enhanced focal accuracy and over density-based and phase-based baselines, demonstrating a generalized methodology for neural design through non-differentiable manufacturing constraints and differentiable physics.
papers.summary: Neural inverse design of 3D-printed structures has to respect discrete, non-differentiable fabrication constraints, and existing methods either rely on soft penalties or fix designs in post-processing, so the optimized and fabricated geometries diverge. `AcoustiPrint` represents geometry with an implicit neural representation (INR) and passes every candidate through a printability operator that enforces layer-wise self-support, discrete material choice and whole-body connectivity before its physical response is simulated. Surrogate gradients and a self-supervised printability objective allow backpropagation through these discrete steps. Applied to patient-specific transcranial focused ultrasound, it jointly optimizes geometry and material through differentiable wave physics and yields **manufacturable structures with better focal accuracy** than density-based and phase-based baselines.

papers.title: SIM-UT: A User Simulation based Evaluation Framework for Medical Triage Chatbots
papers.abstract: LLM-based chat agents are increasingly used for complex, multi-turn, multilingual medical triage in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet evaluation methods focus on single-turn, English-only benchmarks that primarily test the chatbots' knowledge. In practice, users are often confused, overwhelmed, or emotionally vulnerable, giving unclear, misspelled single-word answers or long messages in regional dialects, and the context of a conversation can shift rapidly. We propose SIM-UT (Simulation of User Behaviour for Triage), a multi-turn, simulation-based evaluation method that identifies ecologically valid, contextually relevant failure modes of LLM-based triage chat agents. Using SIM-UT, we evaluated three real-world WhatsApp-based health chatbots: a respiratory screening programme in India, a hearing health support programme in South Africa, and a diabetes and lifestyle coaching agent in Kenya. We compared a medically fine-tuned open model (MedGemma) against general-purpose frontier models (ChatGPT and Claude) across 5,000+ multilingual simulated conversation turns grounded in the personas, constraints, and communication patterns of the real user populations, over 2-4 iterative rounds. A key failure mode emerged in both model families: de-escalation risk. The agents initially identified medical emergencies correctly, but when the user minimised the symptoms without introducing new clinical information, they de-escalated, exhibiting clinically dangerous sycophancy, for example agreeing that vaginal bleeding in pregnancy was "not a problem" or that decreased fetal movements at 32 weeks "can be normal". We recommend user simulation-based behavioural evaluation, grounded in real user context and covering adversarial and edge cases, as standard practice for triage chatbots in production, so that safeguards can be added before deployment or in subsequent iterations.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) triage chatbots are deployed in low- and middle-income countries, but they are mostly evaluated on single-turn, English-only knowledge benchmarks that ignore confused, terse or dialect-heavy users. `SIM-UT` (Simulation of User Behaviour for Triage) is a multi-turn evaluation method that simulates users grounded in the personas, constraints and communication patterns of real user populations. It was applied to three WhatsApp health chatbots in India, South Africa and Kenya, comparing `MedGemma` with `ChatGPT` and `Claude` across more than 5,000 multilingual simulated turns. Both model families showed **de-escalation risk**: after correctly flagging an emergency, they backed down once the user downplayed the symptoms, for example agreeing that vaginal bleeding in pregnancy was "not a problem".

papers.title: X-pressing Intimacy: Mental Health Disclosure After Twitter Acquisition
papers.abstract: Social media platforms provide spaces for individuals to disclose mental health experiences and seek support, yet how these disclosures evolve during major shifts in platform governance remains unclear. We examine mental health self-disclosure surrounding Elon Musk's October 2022 acquisition of Twitter, analyzing approximately 824K tweets across anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder (BD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and suicidal ideation (SI) or related experiences, alongside 266K comparison tweets. Using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) and an LLM-based intimacy classifier, we characterize changes in psycholinguistic expression and disclosure intimacy. Following the acquisition, we observe declines in affective and social language, alongside increases in first-person singular pronouns and future-focused expressions. Intimacy patterns vary by condition: anxiety, depression, and BPD show increases in low-intimacy and decreases in moderate-intimacy disclosures, whereas suicide-related posts show more high-intimacy disclosures. However, compared with broader Twitter discourse, only the relative decline in moderate- versus low-intimacy disclosure for BPD remains statistically significant. Our findings underscore the importance of considering both language and intimacy when studying platform transitions, informing the design of online environments that support sensitive self-disclosure.
papers.summary: The study asks how mental health self-disclosure on Twitter changed after Elon Musk's October 2022 acquisition. It analyzes about 824K tweets on anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder (BPD) and suicidal ideation, plus 266K comparison tweets, using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (`LIWC`) and an LLM-based intimacy classifier. After the acquisition, affective and social language declined while first-person singular and future-focused language rose, and intimacy patterns shifted in different directions depending on the condition. Compared against broader Twitter discourse, however, **only the relative decline in moderate- versus low-intimacy disclosure for BPD remained statistically significant**.

papers.title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses.
