Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.
papers.summary: LLM agents that read several accessible documents can combine them and disclose a sensitive conclusion that no single document reveals, known as the mosaic effect. Using 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical and military scenarios, the authors collect 10,800 answers from three agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents running in two open-source harnesses. Even for benign queries answerable from one document, the best model, `GPT-5.6-Sol`, disclosed forbidden composite conclusions in 7.08% of simulated answers, and live harnesses did worse. Visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules lowered disclosure rates, but **unsafe disclosures persisted in 32.37% of simulated answers across all query intents**, and refusals often revealed the prohibited conclusion anyway.

papers.title: High-Value Training Data from Noisy, Diverse Sources
papers.abstract: Training state-of-the-art models increasingly requires learning from large, heterogeneous datasets whose examples vary in quality, domain relevance, and source of supervision. Dataweighting---assigning different weights to training examples---offers a general way to control how such data influences training, but learning effective weights at scale remains challenging. We develop a scalable approach to learning dataweights: given a small, high-quality target dataset, we use metagradients through the training process to efficiently optimize training-example weights directly for performance on the target domain. To scale beyond a fixed dataset and model, we learn parametric weighting rules that generalize to new and streaming examples and transfer from smaller models to substantially larger ones. We study reward modeling as a prototypical application, where preference data may be noisy, adversarial, synthetic, or mismatched with the target domain. Learned dataweights improve held-out performance, automatically adapt reward models to specialized domains, and allow mixtures of human and synthetic supervision to outperform either source alone.
papers.summary: Training on large, heterogeneous datasets of mixed quality raises the question of how much weight each example should get. The method uses metagradients taken through the training process to optimize per-example weights against performance on a small, high-quality target dataset. It also learns parametric weighting rules that generalize to new and streaming examples and transfer from small models to much larger ones. In reward modeling with noisy, adversarial, synthetic or mismatched preference data, the learned weights improve held-out performance and adapt reward models to specialized domains. They also **let mixtures of human and synthetic supervision outperform either source alone**.

papers.title: Memory-Augmented Online Test-Time Adaptation for EEG Motor Imagery via Perturbation Consistency and Confidence Calibration
papers.abstract: Recently, electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have gained traction as portable neural measurement systems. However, the practical deployment of these instruments is often hindered by nonstationarity and cross-subject distribution shifts, which lead to significant intersubject inconsistency. Existing adaptation methods remain impractical for real-time measurement scenarios, as they typically require offline access to source or aggregated target data. To address these challenges, this article proposes memory-augmented online test-time adaptation (OTTA) with perturbation consistency and confidence calibration (MOPC), a source-free framework designed to enhance the reliability of BCI instrumentation. MOPC enables the measurement system to update its decoding parameters on the fly during the inference stage, facilitating single-pass adaptation without accessing sensitive source data. We introduce random-mask perturbations to enforce prediction consistency against inherent EEG signal noise and acquisition artifacts. Furthermore, a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss is designed to integrate feature-space similarity, effectively mitigating unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance during continuous signal acquisition. To ensure system stability and prevent the catastrophic forgetting of established neural patterns, a lightweight memory module is incorporated to regularize parameter updates within a tight latency budget. Evaluated on the BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI datasets, MOPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods by 2.22~\% and 3.67~\%, respectively, while keeping the per-trial adaptation latency to approximately 40--60 ms. This study provides a robust, recalibration-free solution for real-time EEG decoding, marking a significant advancement in the precision and usability of practical BCI measurement instruments.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) brain–computer interfaces suffer from nonstationary signals and differences between subjects, and most adaptation methods need offline access to source or aggregated target data. `MOPC` is a source-free online test-time adaptation framework that updates the decoder during inference, one trial at a time. It enforces prediction consistency under random-mask perturbations, uses a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss to handle unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance, and adds a lightweight memory module to prevent catastrophic forgetting. On `BCI IV IIb` and `OpenBMI` it beats prior methods by 2.22 and 3.67 points while keeping **per-trial adaptation latency around 40–60 ms**.

papers.title: RoleFlow: Self-Evolving Multi-Role Agentic Collaboration via Structural Adaptation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their adaptability to evolving task requirements. Although recent approaches enable dynamic orchestration, trajectory-level rewards they apply assign one outcome to each decision, ofen struggling to identify the contributions of individual structural changes. We propose RoleFlow, a self-evolving multi-role agentic system that refines collaboration structures through feedback-driven atomic edits and on-demand role synthesis. To make structural adaptation learnable, we introduce Single-Edit Counterfactual Policy Optimization (SECPO), which evaluates each edit against its no-edit counterpart at the same chain state and assigns targeted credit to edit-specific tokens. Across seven benchmarks spanning four domains, RoleFlow achieves the optimal average performance, surpassing the strongest competitor by 4.7 points. It leads on all three multi-hop QA benchmarks by 3.2-7.5 F1 points and also shows supremacy on mathematical reasoning, web interaction, and code generation. Further analyses demonstrate cross-benchmark transferability, training-data efficiency, and cross-executor generalization.
papers.summary: LLM multi-agent systems usually use fixed collaboration structures, and dynamic orchestration methods trained on trajectory-level rewards struggle to credit individual structural changes. `RoleFlow` refines the collaboration structure through feedback-driven atomic edits and synthesizes new roles on demand. Its training method, Single-Edit Counterfactual Policy Optimization (`SECPO`), scores each edit against a no-edit counterpart at the same chain state and assigns credit to the edit-specific tokens. Across seven benchmarks in four domains, RoleFlow **beats the strongest competitor by 4.7 points on average**, leads all three multi-hop QA benchmarks by 3.2–7.5 F1, and also performs best on math, web interaction and code generation.

papers.title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.
papers.summary: LLM search agents often lack search-state awareness, meaning they cannot tell what information they have gathered and what is still missing, which leads to hallucinated reasoning and searches that stop too early. Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (`SARL`) teaches models to assess their own search state during training and needs no extra assessment step at test time. A dual reward credits the corrective effect of each self-assessment and penalizes relying on it too much. SARL reports a **24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline**, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks, and it stays stable over longer search horizons where existing methods degrade.

papers.title: Secure Agentic AI and Multimodal Intelligence in 6G Communication Systems
papers.abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) communication systems are expected to support immersive, intent-driven, and latency-critical services through tight integration of multimodal intelligence, edge computing, and autonomous network control. In this setting, agentic AI systems can reason over heterogeneous inputs, use tools and network functions, coordinate across distributed entities, and adapt to dynamic environments. These capabilities make agentic multimodal intelligence promising for 6G applications such as semantic communications, digital twins, and zero-touch network management, but they also introduce security and privacy risks that extend beyond conventional AI and network security models. Vulnerabilities can propagate across multimodal data pipelines, memory, tools, communication interfaces, and inter-agent coordination loops. We survey multimodal intelligence and agentic AI for 6G cross-layered communication systems from the perspectives of privacy and security. We present a 6G-oriented system view spanning perception, memory, tool use, and multi-agent orchestration; analyze threat models and attack surfaces across sensing, cognition, action, memory, and communication layers; organize existing attacks into a structured taxonomy; and review mitigation strategies including prompt and memory defenses, inter-agent trust mechanisms, secure orchestration, and privacy-preserving learning. We conclude by outlining open research directions for trustworthy multimodal multi-agent 6G systems.
papers.summary: Sixth-generation (6G) networks are expected to rely on agentic AI that reasons over multimodal inputs, calls tools and network functions, and coordinates across distributed entities, which opens new security and privacy risks. This survey sets out a 6G-oriented system view covering perception, memory, tool use and multi-agent orchestration. It analyzes threat models and attack surfaces across the sensing, cognition, action, memory and communication layers and arranges existing attacks into a **structured taxonomy**. It then reviews defenses, including prompt and memory protections, trust mechanisms between agents, secure orchestration and privacy-preserving learning, and closes with open research directions.

papers.title: Towards Faithful Data Selection: Statistical Limits and Scalable Algorithms
papers.abstract: What does it mean to have an optimal data selection algorithm? Optimality is conventionally framed as finding a subset that minimizes the population error of the classifier trained only on that subset. Our starting point in this work is first to show that this goal is information-theoretically impossible unless the data selection algorithm has access to a validation set order-wise larger than the training set. This impossibility result motivates shifting from unverifiable population risk minimization to a one-sided guarantee that we refer to as faithfulness: for any candidate subset, we provide an estimable proxy that upper-bounds the difference between training on the full training data and on only the subset. We model training with the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm and bound the Kullback--Leibler divergence between subset-trained and full-data-trained parameter distributions by the trajectory-accumulated gradient discrepancy. Minimizing this discrepancy gives a principled way to select a subset. Even though the resulting problem is NP-hard, we propose a swap-based local search that decreases the bound at every accepted step. It can therefore refine the output of any selector without worsening its bound. Finally, we provide experimental results on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 showing that it matches existing data selection baselines. Implementation of our algorithm and the code for reproducing the results are available at: https://github.com/Mehdi-Inane/data_selection_swap.
papers.summary: The usual goal for data selection is to pick a subset that minimizes the population error of a model trained on it. The authors first show that goal is **information-theoretically impossible unless the validation set is order-wise larger than the training set**. They replace it with a one-sided guarantee they call faithfulness: an estimable bound on how far subset training can diverge from full-data training. Modeling training as the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm, they bound the Kullback–Leibler divergence by the gradient discrepancy accumulated along the training trajectory. Minimizing that bound is NP-hard, so they propose a swap-based local search that can refine any selector's output without worsening the bound, and it matches existing baselines on `CIFAR10` and `CIFAR100`.

papers.title: SpecMAGIC: Specification-Guided Multi-Task Generalization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-task generalization is an important yet underexplored problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Many real-world applications require multi-agent systems to generalize across complex, temporally extended tasks with diverse inter-agent coordination requirements. We introduce a specification language that combines temporal-logic task specifications with operators for expressing such requirements. We propose SpecMAGIC, a hierarchical framework that leverages the automaton structure of task specifications for subtask decomposition. A centralized high-level planner identifies and allocates compatible subtask sequences across agents, while decentralized low-level policies execute individual subtasks. This enables zero-shot generalization to new tasks by composing reusable subtask policies according to new specifications, without retraining. We establish soundness and probabilistic completeness of the high-level planner. Experiments on multi-agent navigation tasks show that SpecMAGIC substantially outperforms existing approaches on unseen task specifications and maintains strong performance as the number of agents increases.
papers.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies rarely generalize to new, temporally extended tasks that need different kinds of coordination between agents. The authors define a specification language that combines temporal logic with operators for coordination requirements. `SpecMAGIC` uses the automaton structure of a specification to decompose it into subtasks: a centralized planner allocates compatible subtask sequences to agents, and decentralized low-level policies carry them out. This allows **zero-shot generalization to new task specifications by composing reusable subtask policies without retraining**. The planner is proven sound and probabilistically complete, and on multi-agent navigation the method beats existing approaches on unseen specifications and holds up as the number of agents grows.

papers.title: Stability Analysis of Signed Graphs under Structural Perturbations
papers.abstract: Signed graph learning has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling networks with both positive and negative interactions. While graph-filter-based methods have achieved promising empirical performance on signed networks, their stability under edge perturbations remains less well understood. Existing stability analyses primarily focus on unsigned graphs and do not account for sign-flip perturbations. In this paper, we study the stability of signed graph filters under edge additions, deletions, and sign flips. Our theoretical analysis reveals how signed edge perturbations and node feature correlations jointly determine the learned representation stability. Based on this analysis, we propose a theory-guided perturbation strategy that selects structurally influential signed-edge modifications. Experiments on synthetic and real signed graphs show that the proposed method consistently induces larger embedding drift, polarity change, and downstream link prediction degradation than baselines. These results highlight the importance of \textit{sign-aware} and \textit{distribution-aware} stability analysis for signed graph learning.
papers.summary: Signed graphs model networks that have both positive and negative interactions, but stability analyses of graph filters have mostly addressed unsigned graphs and ignored sign flips. This work analyzes how signed graph filters respond to edge additions, deletions and sign flips, and shows that **signed edge perturbations and node feature correlations jointly determine how stable the learned representations are**. Building on the analysis, the authors propose a theory-guided strategy for choosing influential signed-edge modifications. On synthetic and real signed graphs it causes more embedding drift, polarity change and link-prediction degradation than baseline perturbation methods.

papers.title: A Three-Pillar Governance Framework for Safe and Trustworthy AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents capable of autonomous decision-making introduce significant challenges related to safety, alignment, accountability, and human oversight. Existing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and responsible AI approaches provide important foundations, but many remain fragmented across system design, governance, and operational deployment. This paper presents a Three-Pillar (3P) model and framework for developing safe and trustworthy AI agents through transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness. The framework defines an evolutionary path in which increasing agent autonomy is introduced through progressive validation, structured human oversight, and auditable operational controls. We further describe how the model supports agent lifecycle monitoring, decision traceability, escalation management, and human-agent collaboration within enterprise agentic environments. By integrating oversight principles with operational mechanisms, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for deploying AI agents that remain aligned with human intent while enabling controlled progression toward higher autonomy.
papers.summary: Existing human-in-the-loop (HITL) and responsible-AI approaches to governing autonomous AI agents tend to be fragmented across system design, governance and operational deployment. The proposed Three-Pillar (`3P`) framework organizes agent development around transparency, accountability and trustworthiness. It lays out **a path in which agent autonomy grows only through progressive validation, structured human oversight and auditable operational controls**. The paper describes how the framework supports lifecycle monitoring, decision traceability, escalation management and human-agent collaboration in enterprise agent deployments.

papers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.
papers.summary: Reasoning LLMs often keep reasoning after reaching a correct answer, which wastes tokens and sometimes replaces the right answer with a wrong one. Stopping controllers trained directly at a fixed token price need retraining for each new price. `BELT` (BELief-based Termination) instead learns price-independent beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen model's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on CPU for any accuracy-cost trade-off. Across five out-of-distribution math benchmarks it **cuts generated tokens by 41% on `Qwen3-1.7B` and 51% on `OLMo-3-7B-Think` without losing accuracy**. The math-trained probe transfers to coding and agentic tasks, and it needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than the five price-specific checkpoints of the `OS-Pruner` baseline.

papers.title: aggmetrics: Aggregating Classification Performance Measures for Machine Learning
papers.abstract: aggmetrics is a Python package that extends any binary performance measure expressed in the four confusion-matrix counts to multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, cost-sensitive, soft-label and cross-validation settings, by substituting one of four aggregation operators for what libraries usually expose as an average switch. The package also stores, for every measure, the structural properties that decide which identities apply to it, can infer those properties from a user-supplied formula, and uses them to warn when a measure is used where it does not behave as commonly assumed. Its test suite encodes the results of the companion theory as executable tests. The package is BSD-3 licensed, depends only on NumPy, and is available at https://github.com/rcprati/aggmetrics; documentation at https://aggmetrics.readthedocs.io.
papers.summary: `aggmetrics` is a Python package that extends any binary performance measure defined from the four confusion-matrix counts to multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, cost-sensitive, soft-label and cross-validation settings. It does this by replacing the usual "average" switch with one of four aggregation operators. For each measure, the package records the structural properties that determine which identities hold and can infer them from a user-supplied formula. It uses those properties to **warn when a measure is used where it does not behave as commonly assumed**. The package depends only on `NumPy`, is BSD-3 licensed, and its test suite encodes the results of a companion theory paper as executable tests.

papers.title: Short-to-Long: Detached Features for Long-Horizon Value Learning
papers.abstract: Learning useful representations from continually changing value targets remains a challenge in deep reinforcement learning. We study the temporal horizon of this supervision: smaller discounts make these targets less sensitive to distant bootstrap changes, but using them for behavior changes the control objective. We introduce Short-to-Long (S2L), which supplies a long-horizon behavior learner with features trained by smaller-discount source networks. Detached connections prevent the behavior value loss from updating the sources, allowing each source to follow its own value objective while the behavior discount remains unchanged. Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, the approach yields aggregate performance gains, improving the paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games. Matched Atari ablations support the roles of feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation. Fixed-trajectory measurements further show reduced drift in source value targets with mixed discounts.
papers.summary: Deep reinforcement learning has to learn representations from value targets that keep shifting, and long discount horizons make those targets especially sensitive to distant bootstrap changes. `Short-to-Long` (`S2L`) gives a long-horizon behavior learner features from source networks trained with smaller discounts. Detached connections stop the behavior loss from updating those sources, so the control objective stays unchanged. Across Atari, online continuous control and offline continuous control the approach yields aggregate gains, **improving the paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games**. Ablations support the roles of feature transfer, smaller source discounts and gradient isolation.

papers.title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
papers.abstract: Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.
papers.summary: Kernelized views of self-attention typically use fixed or stationary kernels, which limits how well the similarity structure can adapt to complex token interactions. Flow-based spectral kernel attention (`FSKA`) learns nonstationary attention kernels by modeling their bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows, while staying compatible with linear-attention computation. The authors show that expressive kernels allow removing the query and key projections and fixing the value projections as orthogonal. FSKA is competitive with or better than existing attention mechanisms in classification experiments while **reducing projection-related trainable parameters by about 40–47%** and keeping linear memory scaling.

papers.title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
papers.abstract: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR-targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store are available on the project page.
papers.summary: `SplatLab` is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (`3DGS`). It reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates it on `Mip-NeRF 360` and `LLFF`, and writes the manuscript, with every reported number tied to a logged training run. Candidate extensions are plugin mutations on a verified reproduction. They are ranked by an Elo tournament across eight islands using measured PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio), and a standing falsifier deducts Elo when a candidate fails stress tests. The generated manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by **+0.18 to +3.78 dB PSNR**, including a nebula-rendering task with no prior 3DGS method, and the authors report that a research cycle shrinks from months to days.

papers.title: Learning to Incentivise: Using Reinforcement Learning for Sustainable Urban Mobility
papers.abstract: Traffic management has traditionally focused on toll-based and road pricing solutions. However, road pricing often raises concerns about accessibility and public dissatisfaction, leading to its prohibition in some places, such as Finland. This study optimises the dynamic allocation of incentives to drivers, encouraging them to reroute onto alternative (potentially longer) paths to achieve greater societal benefit, reduced total travel time (TTT) and total emissions in the transportation network, contributing to sustainable urban mobility. We employ a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach to dynamically assign incentives to drivers to reduce both TTT and emissions, with travel times estimated using traffic simulation software. We demonstrate that, with an unlimited budget and an objective of minimising travel time, the incentive scheme reduces TTT by 16%, compared to the dynamic User-Equilibrium (UE) with a budget equivalent to about 11% of the UE total time. When the goal is to minimise emissions, a 9% reduction in CO2 emissions is observed under an unlimited budget. We demonstrate a critical trade-off: minimising TTT leads to an increase in emissions, while prioritising emission reductions raises TTT. However, with the right combination of weights in the multi-objective function, both TTT and total emissions are improved beyond the baseline.
papers.summary: Road pricing is unpopular and banned in some places, such as Finland, so the authors instead pay drivers incentives to take alternative, sometimes longer, routes. A multi-agent reinforcement learning approach assigns these incentives dynamically, with travel times estimated by traffic simulation software. With an unlimited budget, minimizing time cuts total travel time (TTT) by **16% compared with the dynamic User-Equilibrium**, and minimizing emissions cuts CO2 by 9%. Optimizing one objective worsens the other, but well-chosen weights in a multi-objective function improve both over the baseline.

papers.title: DiffLTM: Continuous Diffusions Large Tabular Models for Conditional Generation
papers.abstract:
Conditional generation is a key capability to be supported by Large Tabular Models, enabling a number of applications. Accurate conditional generation has to contend with two key challenges: $(i)$ Data comprise a mixture of numerical and categorical entries, the latter often with high cardinality and heavily unbalanced proportions; $(ii)$ Conditional generation becomes increasingly difficult for rare sub-populations. The best models in this class use a hybrid of continuous and discrete diffusions. In this paper, we design a continuous diffusion model with strong generation quality. An important element is the use of cross-entropy loss for categoricals, for which we provide a first theoretical justification. We introduce metrics that focus on rare subpopulations. Further, we generalize conditional generation techniques to enable new types of conditioning. Finally, we show that our model (trained on labor data) can capture classical insights from econometrics.
  Code is available at https://github.com/granica-ai/DiffLTM
papers.summary: Large Tabular Models struggle with conditional generation because tables mix numerical and categorical columns, often with high-cardinality and imbalanced categories, and rare sub-populations are hard to model. `DiffLTM` is a purely continuous diffusion model, whereas the strongest prior models combine continuous and discrete diffusion. It uses a cross-entropy loss for categorical columns, for which the authors give **the first theoretical justification**. The work also introduces metrics focused on rare sub-populations and new types of conditioning, and shows that a model trained on labor data reproduces classical findings from econometrics.

papers.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are judged by a loose collection of metrics such as sparsity, dead features, and reconstruction, with no single objective explaining why those metrics matter. The authors propose that SAE features should form an "atomic interpretable unit basis", meaning a coordinate system suited to semantically meaningful explanation. They organize existing and new metrics, including `DAME` (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation), into a benchmark and apply it to hundreds of SAEs. They find that some SAEs look monosemantic under standard metrics but are functionally polysemantic: **the features that contribute most to model computation are systematically less interpretable and more redundant**.

papers.title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
papers.summary: In a pre-registered study, the authors test whether an embodied agent's experience should be distilled into its policy weights or stored externally and retrieved at inference. A vision-language model (VLM) teacher that retrieves lessons from its own past attempts generates trajectories on a reach task, and `LoRA` student policies are distilled from those trajectories. Distilling memory into weights gave only a non-significant +1 point gain, while **attaching the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to fixed student weights added +34 percentage points**, matching the teacher. Once the buffer was attached, the adapter added nothing detectable, and on a second, harder task the retrieval advantage pointed the same way but was not significant.

papers.title: FIGFLEX: A Mixed-Precision FP-INT GEMM Accelerator Co-Designed with Low-Bit LLM Quantization
papers.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps LLM activations in floating point and stores weights as low-bit integers, turning the dominant workload into floating-point-integer (FP-INT) general matrix multiplication. Recent quantizers reach a 2-3-bit average with mixed precision, but hardware has not kept pace: GPUs dequantize weights to FP16 before the tensor-core multiply-accumulate, and bit-parallel FP-INT accelerators run at a single weight precision, so fewer bits save memory but not computation. In this paper, we present FIGFLEX, an algorithm-hardware co-designed mixed-precision accelerator whose bit-parallel datapath scales throughput as precision falls. FIGFLEX contributes (1) a shift-add, radix-4 reformulation of FP-INT multiplication that fuses the multiply-accumulate into a unified, precision-flexible partial-product reduction and roughly halves the partial products, together with a novel INT3 optimization that reclaims the idle datapath radix-4 leaves at that precision; and (2) a mixed-precision quantizer that assigns each channel group its bit-width according to the error GPTQ cannot compensate, with a per-input-channel column scaling whose power-of-two normalization keeps the scaled activations out of the FP16 subnormal range, so that the quantized model maps directly onto FIGFLEX's datapath with the same accuracy as on a GPU. On LLaMA-2-7B, FIGFLEX attains 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision, lower than GPTQ, AWQ, SliM-LLM, AMQ, and QuIP# (without fine-tuning), while delivering 1.56x and 1.42x higher whole-chip throughput per area on the linear GEMMs of a 3-bit mixed-precision model than AxCore and FIGLUT, respectively.
papers.summary: Weight-only quantization makes floating-point-by-integer (FP-INT) matrix multiplication the main LLM workload, but GPUs and existing accelerators gain no compute savings from fewer weight bits. `FIGFLEX` is a co-designed accelerator and quantizer. Its shift-add, radix-4 datapath scales throughput as bit-width falls, and its mixed-precision quantizer assigns each channel group the bit-width needed to cover the error that `GPTQ` cannot compensate. On `LLaMA-2-7B` it reaches 5.85 and 8.77 `WikiText-2` perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision, beating `GPTQ`, `AWQ`, and `QuIP#`, with **1.56x and 1.42x higher throughput per area** than the `AxCore` and `FIGLUT` accelerators.

papers.title: Why Bother Me Again? Benchmarking Personal Agent Memory for Interaction Preferences
papers.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.
papers.summary: Personal agents can burden users with repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach, yet memory benchmarks mostly test factual recall. `MemPABench` is an interactive environment in which four simulated users, holding 14 interaction preferences, give feedback over 99 sessions spanning four months, with planned preference changes along the way. Agents must decide when to clarify, confirm, or act on their own. Across four memory systems and four LLM backbones, **retrieval-based memory (`Mem0`, `MemOS`, simple RAG) did not outperform having no memory**. File-based memory improved accuracy but applied preferences outside their relevant contexts, and agents often fell back on default habits even when the correct preference was available.

papers.title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
papers.abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.
papers.summary: The authors define "event worlds": systems with multiple independent actors that keep changing without the agent's input and are observed only through event logs. They ask whether LLMs can serve as world models for such systems, using benchmarks built from human `Diplomacy` games and real `Polymarket` trades. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when every actor's actions are given. When only the agent's own action is known, **models struggle wherever other actors strongly shape the outcome, and larger models or longer histories help little**. This gap also hurts multi-step rollouts and leads models to overestimate how likely plans are to succeed, though imagined experience from these world models still improves policy learning.

papers.title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, and they may not fully capture what the trace shows. We study this in a tool-use setting built on GSM8K, where agents call a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, giving clear ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported. We audit three trace-level detectors across six production models and 30 problems per model. Final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation can disagree in systematic ways. A key failure mode is silent tool-output override: the calculator returns a corrupted value, but the model later uses a different, often correct, value without calling the tool again, so the bad value stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review of 90 traces agrees perfectly with the automated labels for final correctness (67/67), fault impact (19/19), and fault relevance (18/18), but only 67/81 for verification; all 14 disagreements fall into four recurring patterns. Execution limits also change the reported result: in an ablation across two models, one ranges from 21/30 to 27/30 correct as step and token budgets change, while the other stays between 27/30 and 29/30. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should come with the trace evidence behind it, whether the question the detector asks applied to that trace, whether the run was cut off by an execution limit, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.
papers.summary: Agent evaluations reduce execution traces to labels such as answer correctness, tool re-verification, and fault propagation, and the authors audit whether those labels match what the traces actually show. In a `GSM8K` setting where a calculator tool sometimes returns corrupted outputs, they examine three detectors across six production models. A common failure is **silent tool-output override**: the model discards the corrupted value without calling the tool again, so the error stops spreading but the verification detector records no re-check. Human review agreed with every correctness and fault label but with only 67 of 81 verification labels, and one model's score ranged from 21/30 to 27/30 depending on step and token budgets.

papers.title: Optimal Multitask Representations Under a Rate Constraint: An Information Bottleneck Analysis
papers.abstract: Which pretraining objective yields the best representation for downstream tasks under an information budget? We formalize this problem as a multitask information bottleneck, using a mutual information constraint to model incomplete information retention. For Gaussian inputs and tasks, we characterize optimal representations and show that a weakly task-aligned specialist can outperform a reconstruction generalist at low rates but lose at high rates. We also construct task families for which every fixed Gaussian prediction objective incurs arbitrarily large relative regret, driven by reversals in optimal allocation priorities. Conversely, the average task information matrix defines an objective with a uniform relative-regret bound controlled by maximum task SNR. CelebA and dSprites experiments illustrate that compression can change which pretraining objective performs best, and even task-aware training can reverse which downstream task is better preserved as rate increases.
papers.summary: The question is which pretraining objective gives the best representation for downstream tasks when the information the representation can retain is capped. The authors formalize this as a multitask information bottleneck. For Gaussian inputs and tasks, they show that a weakly task-aligned specialist can beat a reconstruction generalist at low rates but loses at high rates, and **any fixed prediction objective can suffer arbitrarily large relative regret** on some task families. An objective built from the average task information matrix has a uniform regret bound, and experiments on `CelebA` and `dSprites` show that compression can change which objective works best.

papers.title: From Prose to Properties: Testing Research Claims with ARATest for Agent-Native Science
papers.abstract:
AI agents now run experiments and report findings, so research produces claims faster than researchers can check them. Each empirical claim implies a property that must hold over its cases, but it states that property only in prose. Without an explicit property, no test can decide which evidence would falsify a claim, so validation cannot keep pace with the claims agents produce. To make claims testable, we approximate a claim's semantics by abstracting its property skeleton, a parameterized relation that recurs across claims. We present ARATest, a property-based testing library that checks these skeletons as executable tests. A typed declaration binds a claim to a skeleton and fixes the claim's compared quantities, cases, scope, and numerical policy. A shared case type makes every generator supply cases in the claim's statistical unit. A three-valued semantics assigns each property one of three verdicts: holds, violated, or inconclusive. Every violation carries a replayable witness. A default generator reads the evidence that agent-native research artifacts (ARA) link to each claim, and auto-research generators dispatch an agent to run released code for fresh cases. Our DissClaimer plugin supplies that agent and runs these generators as continuous testing.
  Of 243 claims in 33 ARA artifacts, 54 received faithful declarations bound to evidence: 32 held, eight were violated, and 14 remained inconclusive. Two violations exposed errors in published papers that their authors confirmed. ARATest detected all 553 seeded faults without a false alarm on 19 valid controls, outperforming two LLM judges. Fresh runs exposed behaviors that reported evidence could not show. These results suggest that one fixed test can check explicit claim properties against both reported and fresh evidence.
papers.summary: AI agents now produce research claims faster than people can check them, and those claims are stated in prose rather than as testable properties. `ARATest` is a property-based testing library that maps each claim onto a reusable property skeleton and checks it against linked evidence or against fresh runs of released code performed by an agent, the `DissClaimer` plugin. Each property gets a verdict of holds, violated, or inconclusive, and every violation comes with a replayable witness. Of 54 claims with faithful declarations, 32 held, 8 were violated, and 14 were inconclusive; **two violations exposed errors in published papers that their authors confirmed**, and the tool caught all 553 seeded faults with no false alarms.

papers.title: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3
papers.abstract: A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.
papers.summary: A harness is the program that orchestrates an LLM's perception, memory, tool use, and recovery; the authors test whether frontier models can build and improve their own harness on `ARC-AGI-3`, an interactive benchmark of unfamiliar games. Each model builds a harness through a fixed coding bootstrap, plays five development games, and revises its whole codebase twice. Every version is scored on twenty held-out games using Relative Human Action Efficiency (`RHAE`), a measure of level completion and action efficiency against human baselines. Across 27 lineages, harness scores ranged from zero to near ceiling, but **two revisions raised mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points**, with a confidence interval that includes zero. Gains on the development games overstated held-out improvement, and cutting inference cost sometimes cost task performance.

papers.title: PhysibleMDM: Enforcing Inference-Time Physical Feasibility Constraints on Motion Diffusion Models via Noise Optimization
papers.abstract: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.
papers.summary: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate varied human motion that often breaks physics, which limits its use in simulation and control. `PhysibleMDM` optimizes the diffusion noise at inference time, without retraining, against surrogate feasibility constraints. These combine kinematic checks (ground penetration, foot slip, self-collision) with an inverse-dynamics feasibility test, and the noise is optimized with the gradient-free `Sep-CMA-ES` evolution strategy. On an `SMPL` humanoid across 100 motion styles, it **cuts ground penetration, self-collision, and foot slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%**, and it also improves dynamic feasibility on a custom bipedal robot.

papers.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of LLM Fact-Checkers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer factual questions, but their answers can contain errors and must be fact-checked claim by claim. Yet the resulting score depends on three design decisions: which questions the claims answer, under what conditions each claim is judged, and which sources count as evidence. No existing benchmark specifies all three. We introduce JSFactCheckBench, a Japanese benchmark that specifies all three, with 1,913 claims from LLM answers to questions about misleading information that circulated on Japanese social media, each annotated for factuality at a reference time and for importance to the question, using evidence from preselected Web sources. Across six LLMs, all verify claims directly answering the question less accurately than supplementary claims, a gap that aggregate scores obscure. Scores also drop when models must locate the relevant content in longer or multiple sources and, for all four open models, when the surrounding question and response are added. These weaknesses are visible only because the benchmark records the conditions behind each label. A benchmark that leaves them implicit cannot reveal them.
papers.summary: Scores for claim-level fact-checking of LLM answers depend on three choices that existing benchmarks leave unspecified: which question each claim answers, the conditions under which it is judged, and which sources count as evidence. `JSFactCheckBench` is a Japanese benchmark that fixes all three. It contains 1,913 claims from LLM answers about misleading information that circulated on Japanese social media, each labeled for factuality at a reference time and for importance to the question. Across six LLMs, **all models verify claims that directly answer the question less accurately than supplementary claims**, a gap that aggregate scores hide. Accuracy also drops with longer or multiple sources and, for the open models, when the surrounding question and response are included.

papers.title: Behind Aggregate Scores: What Systematically Varying Arena-Hard's LLM Judge Reveals
papers.abstract: LLM judges are used to determine which of two answers is better. Trusting these verdicts requires knowing how repeatable they are and how much they depend on the judge's instructions. We show that similar aggregate scores can conceal substantial changes in individual verdicts, both when the same setup is repeated and when the instructions change. Using 500 Arena-Hard v2.0 prompts with two models' answers held fixed, we run GPT-4.1 as the judge under all eight combinations of criteria, output format and task framing, and repeat every setup unchanged at temperature zero on a pinned model version. Rerunning the default setup moves the aggregate score by about one point but changes the win/tie/loss outcome on 21.2% of prompts. Instruction changes introduce further sensitivity: in one setup, which asks for the verdict without reasoning and also drops several other instructions, outcomes change on 28.2 percentage points more prompts than the two setups' unchanged reruns do on average, and the aggregate score falls by 4.09 points. In another, where the criteria prioritise accuracy, outcomes change on 6.7 percentage points more prompts by the same comparison, while the aggregate score barely moves. A stable aggregate score therefore does not establish that individual verdicts are repeatable. This distinction matters when those verdicts are used as preference labels or to assess individual responses. Evaluations that rely on individual verdicts should repeat each setup they use and report both aggregate scores and prompt-level agreement.
papers.summary: The authors test how repeatable LLM-judge verdicts are and how much they depend on the judge's instructions. They used `GPT-4.1` as judge on 500 `Arena-Hard v2.0` prompts with fixed answers, across eight instruction variants, each rerun at temperature zero on a pinned model version. Rerunning the default setup unchanged moved the aggregate score by only about one point but **flipped the win/tie/loss outcome on 21.2% of prompts**. Some instruction changes altered far more verdicts while leaving the aggregate nearly unchanged. The authors recommend repeating each judge setup and reporting prompt-level agreement alongside aggregate scores, especially when verdicts are used as preference labels.

papers.title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards a Better Understanding of LLM Steganography via Rolewise Decomposition
papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.
papers.summary: In LLM steganography, an encoder model hides a private message in an ordinary-looking response and a decoder tries to recover it, and success is usually measured only by end-to-end recovery. The authors propose a rolewise decomposition that separately checks what the encoder embedded, what the decoder recovered, and what deterministic verification can confirm. Across 7,200 encoder responses, they find **168 verifiable encodings that decoders missed** and 706 responses that hid messages through word-length or token-initial patterns the encoder was never told to use. They argue that encoding and decoding should be evaluated separately to understand and mitigate the safety risks of LLM steganography.

papers.title: Protegrity-PII Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Protegrity-PII, a new PII decision model for structured and unstructured text. Protegrity-PII achieves a typed recall of 0.915 with a precision of 0.907 on a new benchmark we propose, PII-SCOPE. Our model processes text in 0.49 seconds per million characters at \$0.0005 per million characters on a single RTX 6000 using batched inference. Due in part to the expansive nature of the entity type taxonomy used in training, Protegrity-PII achieves superior out-of-distribution generalization when benchmarked against a selection of state of the art models and datasets.
papers.summary: `Protegrity-PII` is a model for detecting personally identifiable information (PII) in structured and unstructured text, accompanied by a new benchmark, `PII-SCOPE`. On that benchmark it reaches **0.915 typed recall at 0.907 precision**. With batched inference on a single RTX 6000 GPU, it processes a million characters in 0.49 seconds for about $0.0005. The authors attribute its stronger out-of-distribution generalization over state-of-the-art models partly to the broad entity-type taxonomy used in training.

papers.title: NEST: Nested Embedding Representation for Multiscale Clustering
papers.abstract: Real-world data often exhibits cluster structure at multiple resolutions, yet existing methods typically learn a single partition or construct an explicit hierarchy. Inspired by Matryoshka Representation Learning, we introduce NEST, an unsupervised framework that encodes coarse-to-fine structure within a single embedding. NEST jointly optimizes clustering and separation across nested prefix subspaces, enabling progressively finer distinctions as embedding dimensionality increases, with rank and within-cluster regularization that keep the embedding from collapsing. Empirically, distances in the learned embedding follow the hierarchy distance more closely than those of the input, although the hierarchy is never observed during training. On synthetic hierarchies, NEST recovers multiscale structure given only the number of clusters per level. Experiments on vision, text, and single-cell data further demonstrate multiscale organization across real-world representations. By making clustering granularity an intrinsic property of the representation, NEST provides a unified approach to multiscale structure discovery.
papers.summary: Real-world data often has cluster structure at several resolutions, but most methods learn a single partition or build an explicit hierarchy. Inspired by `Matryoshka Representation Learning`, `NEST` learns one unsupervised embedding whose nested prefix subspaces capture progressively finer clusterings, with regularization that prevents collapse. Although the hierarchy is never seen during training, **distances in the learned embedding track hierarchy distance more closely than distances in the input**. On synthetic hierarchies it recovers the multiscale structure given only the number of clusters per level, and it shows similar multiscale organization on vision, text, and single-cell data.

papers.title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
papers.abstract: Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates give state-space guarantees of stability and safety, but synthesizing and verifying them---especially for nonlinear, high-dimensional systems---remains an open challenge. Existing pipelines verify candidates with numerical solvers (sum-of-squares programs), interval methods, or satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) solvers, which often require relaxations, are conservative, or scale poorly with model dimension and nonlinearity. These limitations have also shaped benchmark design: standard test suites are dominated by low-dimensional polynomial systems chosen to suit what solvers can handle rather than what engineering applications require. We address both sides of this challenge. First, we introduce DynaCertBench, a benchmark of 105 instances: 80 non-redundant systems curated from the literature, extended with high-dimensional and control-constrained variants and new nonlinearly coupled systems, comprehensively spanning stability, region-of-attraction, forward-invariance, and safety tasks. Second, we present LLM2Cert, an LLM-driven framework that synthesizes candidate certificates and verifies them against their proof obligations: each obligation is routed to an SMT solver or directly to the Lean Proof-Repair agent. On DynaCertBench, LLM2Cert verifies 81 of 105 instances ($77.1\%$), a $17.1$ percentage point improvement over one-shot proposal without feedback. On the 81 fixed certificates, LLM2Cert verifies 22 that All-SMT leaves unresolved. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/llm2cert.
papers.summary: Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates prove the stability and safety of dynamical systems, but finding and verifying them for high-dimensional nonlinear systems is hard, and existing benchmarks favor low-dimensional polynomial systems that solvers can handle. The authors introduce `DynaCertBench`, 105 instances spanning stability, region-of-attraction, invariance, and safety tasks, along with `LLM2Cert`, which has an LLM propose certificates and routes each proof obligation either to an SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solver or to a `Lean` proof-repair agent. `LLM2Cert` **verifies 81 of 105 instances (77.1%)**, 17.1 percentage points more than one-shot proposals without feedback, and verifies 22 certificates that SMT solvers alone leave unresolved.

papers.title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.
papers.summary: The authors add lane-change prediction for surrounding vehicles, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, to an autonomous vehicle's decision-making and test it in risky merging scenarios in the `CARLA` simulator. The predictor anticipates lane changes about 3 to 4 seconds before they happen. In the representative scenarios evaluated, reactive driving ends in a collision while both predictive strategies, early braking and an evasive lane change, avoid it. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration falls by 31.5% with braking and **91.0% with the lane change**, and an ISO 2631-1 vibration estimate is used to assess ride comfort.

papers.title: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
papers.abstract: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.
papers.summary: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard file format for exchanging building information in architecture, engineering and construction, are increasingly queried through LLMs in natural language. Free-text answers are expensive to grade, so `IFC-MCQ` generates multiple-choice benchmarks automatically from IFC files. Answer keys come straight from the file, and distractors are built from other file values or predefined rules. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes. Tests of two agent setups, one using tool-based retrieval and one using code-based retrieval, revealed **failure modes specific to each category, with performance changing depending on the source model and the retrieval interface**.

papers.title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
papers.abstract: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. Even the strongest configuration reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, while spending 27M tokens and 63 minutes per task on average, demonstrating the substantial gap between current agents and autonomous physical engineering design.
papers.summary: `PLE` is a benchmark of 85 long-horizon agentic tasks in electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where each task is a realistic, billable deliverable such as a design package a licensed reviewer would approve. Some tasks were written entirely by practising engineers.
