ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented and agent systems usually run separate models for text embedding and text generation. Existing unified models such as `GritLM` share weights between the two but do not let either capability shape the other. `ULME` inserts learnable slots between query and answer in a decoder-only LLM and trains three losses on the shared backbone: a contrastive loss for a semantic embedding, a language-modeling loss for the answer, and a stop-gradient loss that aligns a reasoning embedding with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation shapes what the embedding encodes. Across `Qwen2.5` and `Qwen3` models from 0.5B to 8B parameters, a single checkpoint **improves `MTEB` by 3.3 to 4.1 points** over the strongest open baseline, while matching a generation-only fine-tune on `MMLU`, `GSM8K`, and `HumanEval`.

papers.title: AIRO: A Streaming-Based Machine Learning Framework for Threat Detection and Security in Industrial Internet of Things
papers.abstract: Modern Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) im- plementations now connect edge gateways, cloud dashboards and business applications. This improves visibility and remote monitoring. However it simultaneously exposes industrial traffic to various cyber threats including scanning, web attacks and Structured Query Language (SQL) injection (SQLi), phishing- driven credential theft, and command-and-control (C2) activity. Although rule-based tools remain useful for detecting known signatures, their efficacy decreases with minimally altered attacks or when alerts require manual investigation. This paper presents AIRO (Autonomous Intelligence-Driven Cybersecurity Risk Re- duction System), an efficient framework for IIoT monitoring and response. AIRO combines Apache Kafka streaming, attack- specific feature extraction, machine learning (ML) inference, confidence-based decision logic and risk reduction measures such as Internet Protocol (IP) blocking, account suspension and traffic limiting. We developed four specialized datasets for C2 beaconing, reconnaissance, SQLi, and phishing to evaluate AIRO. These datasets include noisy and overlapping characteristic distribu- tions to minimize label leakage. The best-performing models, primarily Gradient Boosting and LightGBM, achieve F1-scores up to 0.9229 while ensuring low-latency from event input to mitigation
papers.summary: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) systems expose traffic to scanning, web attacks, SQL injection, phishing, and command-and-control (C2) beaconing, threats that signature-based tools miss once attacks are slightly altered. `AIRO` combines `Apache Kafka` streaming, attack-specific feature extraction, machine learning inference, and confidence-based decisions that trigger IP blocking, account suspension, or rate limiting. The authors built four deliberately noisy datasets covering C2 beaconing, reconnaissance, SQL injection, and phishing, on which `Gradient Boosting` and `LightGBM` models **reach F1-scores up to 0.9229** with low end-to-end latency from event to mitigation.

papers.title: Meaning Contracts: Local Semantic Geometry in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within-concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross-lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same-factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out-of-domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity-bearing semantic narrowing from high-probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization-specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence-level and token-local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token-local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.
papers.summary: Representation analyses typically ask whether two meanings are close in embedding space. This study instead characterizes the local geometry within a single concept: what stays constant across different phrasings and what shifts when a meaning is made more specific. Two controlled probes, one using translation as a perturbation and one using semantic refinement, are applied to `Gemma 4`, `Llama 3.2`, `Qwen 2.5`, and `Pythia` and validated with blind human judgments. In all four models, sentence pairs order cleanly by semantic relatedness over a band of layers once dominant variance directions are removed, and **refinement moves representations into tighter neighborhoods**, consistent with meaning being organized as local anisotropic regions around an invariant core.

papers.title: Solvable models of learning to pursue a moving target
papers.abstract: Agents tasked with intercepting a moving target must learn how to reach it, ideally as efficiently as possible. As observers of animal pursuit behavior have noticed, different strategies are possible: on one extreme, the agent reactively moves toward the target's current location; on the other, the agent predicts the target's future location and moves directly there. Motivated by the desire to understand how such strategies might be learned, we introduce a continuous-time linear-quadratic model of open-loop target pursuit whose optimal control strategies interpolate between these possibilities. Usefully, a small number of interpretable parameters control which type of strategy is optimal, and it is possible to derive closed-form solutions for optimal strategies, policy learning dynamics, and value learning dynamics. Exploiting our model's linear structure, we find that the time scales of learning precisely correspond to the eigenvalues of certain matrices, and that relevant eigenvalue spectra generically have a gap. We show that this gap indicates that agents tend to learn how to reach their target before optimizing their movement. Our results provide a detailed mathematical characterization of pursuit behavior and its learning dynamics, which can both serve as a benchmark for empirical work, and as a foundation for more elaborate theoretical treatments of pursuit.
papers.summary: Agents chasing a moving target can either move reactively toward where the target is now or predict where it will be and head straight there. The authors introduce a continuous-time linear-quadratic model of open-loop pursuit whose optimal strategies interpolate between these two extremes, controlled by a few interpretable parameters. The model gives closed-form solutions for the optimal strategies, policy learning dynamics, and value learning dynamics. Learning time scales correspond to the eigenvalues of certain matrices, and these spectra generically have a gap, which implies that **agents learn to reach the target before they learn to optimize their movement**.

papers.title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
papers.summary: Masked video pretraining recovers missing content rather than predicting the future, while autoregressive methods have trailed joint-embedding approaches in representation quality. `VANE` is a self-supervised framework in which a causal encoder summarizes past frames and a state predictor infers the representation of the entire next frame in the fixed embedding space of a frozen semantic tokenizer. A lightweight auxiliary decoder reconstructs future-frame patches to keep fine spatial detail, and still images are handled as local-to-global crop sequences so one encoder covers both images and video. The model improves with scale and reaches state of the art among unified encoders on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks, including **a 7.1-point gain in mean-class recall@5 over `V-JEPA 2.1` on `EPIC-KITCHENS-100` action anticipation**.

papers.title: Faithful Latent Harm Monitors Work No Better Than the Models Own Behaviour at a Matched False Alarm Rate
papers.abstract: Large language models have been reported to encode the harmfulness of a request separately from their decision to refuse it, and latent safety monitors such as Latent Guard build on this report by classifying prompts as harmful from the internal activations of the model, with the aim of catching harmful intent even when the model complies. Whether these representations give a signal of harm that survives distribution shift and is independent of model behaviour is unclear. We test this on out-of-distribution prompts made by rewriting existing harmful and benign requests with surface rewording, persuasive framing and jailbreak-style wrappers. Across 15 instruction-tuned LLMs and 38 activation-based readers, we compare harm detection with that of TF-IDF and sentence-embedding classifiers, with independently trained safety classifiers, and with the refusal of each model. Activations are read at the last token of the user instruction, where the model has read the whole request, and at the last chat-template token before the reply, where the planned response can be represented. Because models disagree about which prompts to refuse, we can separate a signal of the harmfulness of the prompt from a signal of the refusal decision of the model. At the end of the instruction, the representation is largely independent of the refusal behaviour of each model but degrades under distribution shift, so that a TF-IDF classifier ranks harm better than the original Latent Guard in every model we test, and linear and MLP probes do about as well as sentence-embedding classifiers trained on the same examples. The representation just before generation detects more, catching 44 percent of harmful prompts at a matched false-alarm rate against 32 percent for the refusal of the model, but that gain follows the refusal decision itself, and part of it comes from refusals that string-matching evaluation misses.
papers.summary: Latent safety monitors such as `Latent Guard` classify prompts as harmful from a model's internal activations, aiming to catch harmful intent even when the model complies. Across 15 instruction-tuned LLMs and 38 activation-based readers, the authors test these monitors on out-of-distribution rewrites of harmful and benign prompts and compare them with `TF-IDF` and sentence-embedding classifiers, standalone safety classifiers, and each model's own refusals. Activations read at the end of the instruction are largely independent of refusal behaviour but degrade under distribution shift, to the point that a `TF-IDF` classifier ranks harm better than the original `Latent Guard` in every model tested. Activations read just before generation catch **44% of harmful prompts versus 32% for the model's own refusals** at a matched false-alarm rate, but that gain follows the refusal decision itself rather than an independent harm signal.

papers.title: Federated Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.
papers.summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (`GraphRAG`) assumes a centralized knowledge graph, but real knowledge is spread across organizations that cannot share their graphs for privacy reasons. `FedGRAG` handles this with a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism, which uses lightweight knowledge indices to find relevant clients without exposing their graph structures. It also uses a controlled-disclosure method that turns retrieved evidence subgraphs into evidence abstracts, which the server then reconstructs. Experiments show that **`FedGRAG` consistently outperforms existing baselines on both retrieval and downstream generation**.

papers.title: Width and Depth Limits Commute During Training
papers.abstract: Recent work established that the infinite-width and infinite-depth limits of residual networks commute at initialization when residual branches are scaled by $1/\sqrt{depth}$. In particular, the network output converges to the same limit whether width and depth tend to infinity sequentially or jointly. We extend this commutativity result to training in linear residual networks. Under the same $1/\sqrt{depth}$ residual-branch scaling (Depth-$\mu$P) and the $\mu$P width parameterization, we prove that, for any fixed number of gradient-descent steps with gradient clipping, the network output converges in $L^2$ along every joint width--depth growth path as both width and depth tend to infinity. Consequently, the infinite-width and infinite-depth limits commute throughout any finite training horizon. Without gradient clipping, the corresponding $L^2$ convergence does not hold in general, but we establish the weaker convergence in probability.
papers.summary: Prior work showed that the infinite-width and infinite-depth limits of residual networks commute at initialization when residual branches are scaled by one over the square root of depth. This work extends that result to training in linear residual networks under `Depth-μP` branch scaling and `μP` width parameterization. The authors prove that, **for any fixed number of gradient-descent steps with gradient clipping, the network output converges in L2 along every joint width-depth growth path**, so the two limits commute throughout any finite training horizon. Without clipping, L2 convergence fails in general, but a weaker convergence in probability still holds.

papers.title: AgentTriage: Replayable Security Diagnosis Across Heterogeneous Agent Runtimes
papers.abstract: When tool-use agents write files, execute code, or send data, their final responses do not explain the resulting security events, and heterogeneous runtimes expose the relevant evidence through incompatible interfaces. We present AgentTriage, an executable contract for replayable security diagnosis across heterogeneous runtimes. The contract admits conclusions whose claims cite canonical runtime events and requires abstention when mandatory evidence is missing. Runtime overlays normalize native observations, while a deterministic pipeline joins invocation and result lifecycles, constructs a typed provenance graph, selects a policy-decisive slice, and binds claims to recorded evidence. Given the same normalized trace, overlay version, and pre-run policy oracle, the diagnosis can be recomputed and its claims re-checked without language-model judgment. Across five runtimes, one contract captures all 159 applicable executions, with an audit of native and synthesized identifiers. On 120 adjudicated cases, AgentTriage achieves 0.858 grounded joint diagnosis, 0.966 required-evidence coverage, and a 0.036 unsupported-claim rate, improving joint diagnosis by 0.175 (95% CI [0.092, 0.258]) over the strongest same-schema baseline. These results quantify the precision of replayable diagnosis and the observation boundaries that require abstention. We release an open-source implementation and selected sanitized evidence at https://github.com/AsnGs/agenttriage-open-source.
papers.summary: When tool-use agents write files, run code, or send data, their final responses do not explain the resulting security events, and different agent runtimes expose evidence through incompatible interfaces. `AgentTriage` defines an executable contract for security diagnosis: runtime overlays normalize native observations, and a deterministic pipeline builds a typed provenance graph, selects the policy-relevant slice, and binds every claim to recorded events, abstaining when required evidence is missing. Because the pipeline is deterministic, a diagnosis can be recomputed and re-checked without any language-model judgment. Across five runtimes, one contract captured all 159 applicable executions, and on 120 adjudicated cases it reached **0.858 grounded joint diagnosis with a 0.036 unsupported-claim rate**, 0.175 above the strongest same-schema baseline.

papers.title: UniGuard: Multi-View Guardrail Learning for Cross-Interface Safety Generalization
papers.abstract: Guardrail models are increasingly used as safety layers for LLMs and agentic systems, but most are trained on fixed prompt or response interfaces and become unreliable when the same safety case appears as a conversation, agent trajectory, multi-agent trace, or policy-conditioned input. We propose UniGuard, a training framework that learns interface-invariant safety representations from multiple semantically aligned views of the same safety case. We also construct the UniGuard-FT dataset by transforming 1,000 public safety cases into prompt, response, multi-turn conversation, agent-trace, and multi-agent-trace views, and train UniGuard-0.6B with classification, supervised contrastive learning, and asymmetric confidence calibration losses. Across unseen-interface benchmarks ATBench, PolicyGuardBench, and DynaBench, UniGuard-0.6B improves over its pretrained guardrail by 45.12 F1 points on average and reduces expected calibration error by 35.41 points, while remaining competitive with much larger guardrails such as Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.2 - despite being a 0.6B model and trained only with synthetic data.
papers.summary: Guardrail models are usually trained on fixed prompt or response formats and become unreliable when the same safety case appears as a multi-turn conversation, an agent trajectory, a multi-agent trace, or a policy-conditioned input. `UniGuard` learns interface-invariant safety representations from multiple aligned views of each case, using the `UniGuard-FT` dataset, which rewrites 1,000 public safety cases into five interface formats. `UniGuard-0.6B` is trained with classification, supervised contrastive, and asymmetric confidence calibration losses. On the unseen-interface benchmarks `ATBench`, `PolicyGuardBench`, and `DynaBench`, it **improves over its base guardrail by 45.12 F1 points on average** and stays competitive with much larger models such as `Claude-Sonnet-4.5` and `GPT-5.2`, despite training only on synthetic data.

papers.title: Random Remasking Scales Masked Diffusion Inference
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate sequences by progressively unmasking tokens, but errors introduced during decoding are typically irreversible. Recent work has shown that iterative correction can improve sample quality, yet existing theory fails to explain this given a learned, imperfect denoiser model. We re-formulate MDM inference as a Markov chain on the clean sequence space, defined by a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-introduces masks and then denoises. This helps us analyze the actual denoising trajectory towards the data distribution. The analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R$^2$D) inference, a purely test-time, finetuning-free, reward-free procedure. To further improve performance, we propose Trajectory Correction Training (TCT), a denoiser-training procedure that exposes the model to its own errors along the generation trajectory. On logical tasks, our approach exhibits a striking near-log-linear test-time scaling, achieving over 97% accuracy on hard Sudoku puzzles and over 99% accuracy on 3-SAT. Our approach also applies to pretrained models on actual language tasks, beating iterative correction baselines and the official Q-mode accuracy of LLaDA2.1-mini on HumanEval+.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate text by progressively unmasking tokens, and errors made during decoding are normally irreversible. The authors recast MDM inference as a Markov chain over clean sequences that randomly re-masks and then denoises, which motivates `Random Remask-Denoise` (`R²D`), a test-time procedure that needs no fine-tuning and no reward. They also propose `Trajectory Correction Training` (`TCT`), which trains the denoiser on its own errors along the generation trajectory. On logic tasks the approach shows near-log-linear test-time scaling, **exceeding 97% accuracy on hard Sudoku and 99% on 3-SAT**, and on pretrained models it beats iterative-correction baselines and the official Q-mode accuracy of `LLaDA2.1-mini` on `HumanEval+`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Masked diffusion models normally freeze each token once it is revealed, so errors made during decoding cannot be undone. The authors recast inference as a Markov chain over complete sequences, where each step randomly remasks tokens and then denoises them, and derive a one-step KL bound that motivates a test-time sampler (`R²D`) and a matching training method (`TCT`).

- `R²D` (Random Remask-Denoise) needs no finetuning and no reward model: it remasks tokens uniformly at random at a fixed noise level, repeats until the argmax prediction stops changing, and only then moves to a lower noise level.
- With standard training on 6.8M-parameter models, accuracy scales near-log-linearly with the correction budget, rising from 19.7% to **93.5% on `Sudoku-Hard`** and from 86.0% to 98.5% on `3-SAT`; standard decoding reaches 48.7%, `ReMDM` 54.7% and `ProSeCo` 55.7% on `Sudoku-Hard`.
- `Trajectory Correction Training` trains the model on its own partial decoding trajectories, with a loss at every position, including tokens it already revealed; combined with `R²D`, it reaches **97.5% on `Sudoku-Hard` and 99.3% on `3-SAT`**.
- On `HumanEval+` with the off-the-shelf 16B `LLaDA2.1-mini`, `R²D` scores **85.4%**, beating the model's published Q-mode result (82.9%), `ProSeCo` (81.7%) and `ReMDM` (71.6%), while using about half of `ReMDM`'s forward passes thanks to early exit.
- Limitations: at the largest budget, per-sample latency is about 77× that of standard decoding on `Sudoku-Hard` (49.4 s vs 0.64 s); the scaling depends on uniform rather than low-confidence remasking; and the paper attributes the strongest gains to tasks with sparse, local constraints, with only one language benchmark tested.

papers.title: Wavenumber-Aware Deep Learning for Robust Analysis of Raman Spectra
papers.abstract: Machine-learning models for spectroscopy usually treat a spectrum as a fixed-grid intensity vector, leaving the physical coordinate implicit in the array index. Such models are tied to a single sampling grid, spectral range and resolution, which limits their use when measurement conditions change. Here we represent each spectral point as a pair of intensity and wavenumber and compute Transformer positional encodings from the wavenumber itself. On Raman spectra of three bacterial species and their synthetic mixtures, this representation remained robust to noise, sparser sampling and partial spectral coverage across convolutional, residual and Transformer networks. In controlled comparisons, wavenumber-based encoding outperformed index-based and learned encodings under partial observation and retained its performance on sampling grids never seen during training, where index-based encoding degraded. These findings were reproduced on a public 30-isolate bacterial benchmark. Explicit physical coordinates offer a simple route to robust spectral analysis under variable measurement conditions.
papers.summary: Machine-learning models for spectroscopy usually treat a spectrum as a fixed-grid intensity vector, which ties them to one sampling grid, spectral range, and resolution. The authors instead represent each point as an intensity paired with its wavenumber and compute Transformer positional encodings from the wavenumber itself. On Raman spectra of three bacterial species and their mixtures, this representation stayed robust to noise, sparser sampling, and partial spectral coverage across convolutional, residual, and Transformer networks. **Wavenumber-based encoding kept its performance on sampling grids never seen during training, where index-based encoding degraded**, and the results held on a public 30-isolate bacterial benchmark.

papers.title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis
papers.abstract: Cancer care is a longitudinal, time-sensitive process requiring coordination among diverse healthcare professionals (HCPs), whose collaboration evolves throughout treatment. Prior studies link care team structure to patient outcomes, but the temporal dynamics of collaboration and their relationship to evolving patient risk remain poorly understood. We introduce a visual analytics framework for modeling and interpreting time-varying care team interactions in oncology. We construct dynamic collaboration networks from electronic health record (EHR)-mediated communication data and use a temporal graph neural network (TGNN) to estimate patient outcome risk over time. We then investigate how changes in care team composition and specialist participation relate to shifts in estimated risk across treatment stages. Our multi-view interactive system combines TGNN-based risk modeling with coordinated visualizations of care team networks, feature-level explanations from a surrogate logistic regression model, and exploratory what-if analysis. Without making causal claims, the system helps analysts examine how risk estimates co-evolve with collaboration patterns and identify care team characteristics associated with these changes. We demonstrate its utility through expert-guided analysis scenarios involving 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers, evaluating its ability to reveal clinically meaningful collaboration patterns. This work improves the interpretability of temporal graph-based models in longitudinal, team-based healthcare, with potential applicability to other evolving collaborative settings.
papers.summary: Cancer care depends on coordination among many healthcare professionals, but it is poorly understood how changes in that collaboration over time relate to patient risk. The authors build dynamic collaboration networks from communication data mediated by electronic health records (EHRs) and use a temporal graph neural network (`TGNN`) to estimate patient outcome risk over time. An interactive multi-view system pairs these risk estimates with care-team network visualizations, feature explanations from a surrogate logistic regression model, and what-if analysis. Expert-guided scenarios covering **505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers** show how the system surfaces collaboration patterns associated with shifts in estimated risk, without making causal claims.

papers.title: How Firm Are AI Models' Ethical Boundaries? A Pay-Stub Editing Test of 15 Models
papers.abstract: Can a small change in wording move an AI model from refusing a sensitive request to acting on it? We test 15 models on the same request to increase the income shown on a pay stub. Across 445 observable trials, models issue editing calls in 14.1% of cases when a loan purpose is stated, 33.1% when the purpose is omitted, and 66.2% when the change is described as fixing a printing error. Astra refuses all ten loan-purpose requests but issues calls in all ten purpose-omitted trials. Fable, Opus, and Muse Spark issue none across all three wordings; Sonnet issues some under the latter two. Response excerpts illustrate different ways of refusing, redirecting, or justifying an edit. The file is a marked test document and all tools are simulated. These results probe how boundaries behave in one setting; they do not prove an overall ethics ranking or that a harmful real-world edit succeeded.
papers.summary: To probe how firm AI models' ethical boundaries are, the authors give 15 models the same request to raise the income shown on a pay stub, phrased three ways, using a marked test document and simulated tools. Across 445 observable trials, models issued editing calls in 14.1% of cases when a loan purpose was stated, 33.1% when the purpose was omitted, and **66.2% when the change was framed as fixing a printing error**. `Astra` refused all ten loan-purpose requests but made edits in all ten trials where the purpose was omitted. `Fable`, `Opus`, and `Muse Spark` made no edits under any wording, while `Sonnet` made some under the latter two; the authors caution that the results do not establish an overall ethics ranking.

papers.title: The Delegation Divide: An Open Index of AI-Agent Delegability across Occupations and Countries
papers.abstract: 35.2% of task time in world employment is at least partly delegable to AI agents in 2026, and only 2.5% can be handed over in full. Existing measures score exposure to generative AI, mostly for the United States. We build the Agent Delegability Index (ADI): two language models rate all 18,796 O*NET 30.2 task statements on a frozen, preregistered rubric of delegation levels and barriers; tasks are mapped to 433 ISCO-08 unit groups and weighted by ILOSTAT employment in 146 countries. Four findings. First, delegable employment rises with income, from 22.5% in low-income to 48.7% in high-income countries, a slope of 7.23 percentage points per log point of GDP per capita. This delegation divide is compositional: the physical barrier dominates the jobs poorer countries employ most. Second, at the occupation level ADI tracks exposure closely (r = 0.93 with Eloundou et al. and 0.89 with Felten et al.), above the preregistered bound of 0.80; ADI adds delegation levels and barriers on top of exposure, for the world, not a new ranking of occupations. Third, full delegation is rare and peaks for tasks that take a human about twelve minutes (11.8 minutes). Fourth, the preregistered adoption gap is not supported: across 101 countries, delegability and observed AI usage correlate at r = 0.86, and the gap between them is not wider in middle-income countries (p = 0.27). Model agreement is kappa = 0.77; a blind human rating of 300 tasks agrees with the model consensus at kappa = 0.85, and an agentic panel with web search at kappa = 0.87. We release the index, the atlas, the prompts and an MCP server at https://github.com/Cespial/delegation-divide.
authors: Cristian Espinal Maya (Universidad Nacional de Colombia)
papers.summary: Existing measures of AI's labour-market impact score exposure to generative AI, mostly for the United States. The `Agent Delegability Index` (`ADI`) has two language models rate all 18,796 `O*NET` task statements on a preregistered rubric of delegation levels and barriers, then maps the tasks to occupations and weights them by employment in 146 countries. It estimates that **35.2% of global task time is at least partly delegable to AI agents in 2026, but only 2.5% can be fully handed over**. Delegable employment rises from 22.5% in low-income to 48.7% in high-income countries, mainly because poorer countries employ more people in physically constrained jobs, and model ratings agree with blind human ratings at kappa 0.85.

papers.title: Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed? Naive RAG Is Stronger Than We Thought
papers.abstract: LLM memory is widely used in long-term conversation understanding. Agentic memory systems often use mutation, structural organization, learned retrieval strategies, or other complex operations. Is this complexity always necessary? We study Raw-RAG, a naive RAG baseline using dense retrieval and reranking over raw history to supply evidence to a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench, Raw-RAG ranks first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark-model settings, outperforming the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13-5.53 points. We investigate why raw-history retrieval remains competitive. Evidence analysis shows that its higher coverage of necessary evidence can offset lower utilization. Useful evidence includes both answer values and the relations and dependency paths needed to derive them. Even complete access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw evidence, highlighting the importance of preserving raw information. These findings challenge the necessity of complex agentic memory for the evaluated conversation tasks and establish naive RAG as an essential baseline.
papers.summary: Agentic memory systems for long-term conversation often rely on memory mutation, structured organization, or learned retrieval, and the authors test whether that complexity is needed. Their baseline, `Raw-RAG`, simply applies dense retrieval and reranking over the raw conversation history and passes the evidence to a reader LLM. Across `LoCoMo`, `LongMemEval`, `MEME`, and `MemoryAgentBench`, **`Raw-RAG` ranks first in six of seven benchmark-model settings**, beating the strongest agentic memory system by 0.13 to 5.53 points. Analysis attributes this to higher coverage of necessary evidence, including the relations needed to derive answers, and shows that even full access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw history.
papers.highlight_summary:
Agentic memory systems for long-term conversation add extraction, mutation, graphs and learned retrieval, but it is unclear how much that complexity buys over plain retrieval. The authors test `Raw-RAG`, a deliberately naive baseline that indexes raw chat history without any LLM processing and lets the reader model work out state changes from the retrieved evidence.

- `Raw-RAG` splits timestamped history into 256-token windows with 32-token overlap, retrieves the 128 nearest windows by dense similarity, and keeps the top 15 after cross-encoder reranking; dropping the reranker costs **3.92 points**, while chunk size and moderate top-k values barely matter.
- Across `LoCoMo`, `LongMemEval`, `MEME` and `MemoryAgentBench`, it ranks **first in 6 of 7 benchmark–model settings** against 12 systems including `EverMemOS`, `MemMachine`, `Mem0` and `Memora`, leading the strongest of them by **0.13–5.53 points** (e.g. **93.70** on `LoCoMo` with `GPT-4.1-mini`); the one loss is `MEME` with `DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, where `MemMachine` is ahead by 1.52 and `Full-context` by 19.98.
- An audit of `Mem0` finds that updates and deletes make up only **4.39%** of write decisions on `LoCoMo` and 2.46% on `LongMemEval`, and replacing them with append-only writes raises `LoCoMo` accuracy from **67.36% to 69.42%**; adding memory management on top of `Raw-RAG` also hurts, with atomic-fact extraction costing **19.62 points**, summaries 5.81 and graph expansion 5.78.
- The analysis attributes the advantage to evidence coverage: `Raw-RAG` most often retrieves sufficient evidence (**45.29%** on `MemoryAgentBench`, **76.35%** on `MEME`) and best preserves the dependency paths behind an answer (62.34%), and even with oracle access to a system's full store, transformed memory still falls 7.58–29.38 points short of raw evidence.
- It is also much cheaper, ingesting and searching a `MEME` slice in **306 s**, which is 5.1× faster than the next system and 30.4× faster than `EverMemOS`; the limits are that results cover only offline public conversation benchmarks, rely on a capable reader to reconstruct state, and leave open the storage and privacy costs of keeping raw history.

papers.title: Primal-Dual Representation Learning for Low-Rank Constrained MDPs
papers.abstract: Representation learning has substantially improved the efficiency of unconstrained continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), but its extension to Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) is difficult because the transition representation must be learned while constraint violation is controlled. In this paper, we study representation learning for low-rank CMDPs with continuous state spaces, and propose REP-PD-TEG for the soft cumulative-violation setting. In the feature learning period, the algorithm interacts with the environment using a decaying-$\epsilon$-greedy mixture execution policy, and uses the collected samples to learn transition features by maximum likelihood. Based on the learned features, it constructs uncertainty bonuses and plans with an optimistic Lagrangian objective to obtain the return policy. We prove regret and soft-violation guarantees for the return policies, and quantify the influence of the decaying-$\epsilon$-greedy exploration. In particular, REP-PD-TEG achieves the optimal $\widetilde O(\sqrt K)$ return policy bound, and gives a $\widetilde O(K^{3/4})$ overall sample bound when exploratory actions are charged. For the stricter hard cumulative violation, where feasibility must be verified episode by episode, we propose REP-PD-H-TEG. It plans under a bonus-corrected lower-confidence utility certificate with the learned representation, and performs a stabilized dual search to obtain the return policy, yielding regret and hard-violation bounds. Together, these results give the first theoretically guaranteed representation-learning method for low-rank continuous-state CMDPs with both soft cumulative guarantees and certified hard-violation control.
papers.summary: Representation learning has made continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) more sample-efficient, but extending it to Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) is hard because features must be learned while constraint violations stay controlled. For low-rank CMDPs, `REP-PD-TEG` learns transition features by maximum likelihood under decaying epsilon-greedy exploration, then plans with an optimistic Lagrangian objective using uncertainty bonuses. It achieves **the optimal square-root-of-K regret bound for the returned policy** under soft cumulative-violation constraints. A variant, `REP-PD-H-TEG`, handles hard per-episode violation constraints through a lower-confidence utility certificate and a stabilized dual search, giving what the authors call the first theoretically guaranteed representation-learning method for this setting.

papers.title: Can Loan Processors and Underwriters Spot AI-Edited Statements? An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: AI-assisted editing can produce loan documents that preserve familiar issuer layouts while changing the applicant's identity. We investigated whether experienced underwriters and loan processors identify such forgeries in first-pass, document-only review. Three practitioners recruited through Upwork each received one applicant package drawn from 134 forged PDFs derived from 47 genuine financial documents supplied with full consent. The edits preserved amounts, dates and balances; identifier inconsistencies introduced by the pipeline were knowingly retained before distribution. Reviewers were not told that files had been altered and returned 132 file-level judgements. Checking their explanations against the originals yielded 14 edit-supported concerns (10.6%): 12 Suspicious judgements and two Insufficient information judgements. All supported concerns involved identifier disagreements within or across documents, and no reported visual cue identified an actual edit. Thus, approximately one in ten judgements contained evidence of the forgery, despite known inconsistencies remaining in the files. These observations motivate evaluating consistency checks and independent source verification alongside human review. With three reviewer-package pairs and no genuine-file controls, the findings describe this exploratory setting rather than population-wide detection accuracy.
papers.summary: AI-assisted editing can produce loan documents that keep a familiar issuer layout while changing the applicant's identity. In an exploratory study, three experienced underwriters and loan processors reviewed packages drawn from 134 forged PDFs without being told the files were altered. **Only about one in ten of their 132 judgements (10.6%) contained evidence of the forgery**, even though known identifier inconsistencies were left in the files. Every supported concern came from mismatched identifiers within or across documents, and no reported visual cue pointed to an actual edit, which motivates automated consistency checks and independent source verification alongside human review.

papers.title: AgentDP: Towards Automated Model Deployment for Heterogeneous Embedded AI Applications
papers.abstract: This paper presents AgentDP, which aims to deploy pre-trained AI models on heterogeneous embedded devices by fully automating model optimization and adaptation (O&A) with Large Language Model (LLM) agents. AgentDP not only significantly reduces human effort via automation but also enhances model inference efficacy by integrating LLMs with device-specific domain knowledge. To deliver a robust automation framework, AgentDP develops novel solutions to address three key technical challenges: 1) To help users elicit clear requirements, we propose a user requirement standardization module; 2) To mitigate the execution environment mismatch between AI models and heterogeneous embedded devices, we design an operator-aware model partition paradigm that enables different parts of the model to be efficiently executed on distinct inference engines. 3) To avoid re-searching optimization hyperparameters for new tasks, we propose a configuration reuse module that heuristically retrieves previous hyperparameter configurations for efficient reuse. Extensive experiments demonstrate that by fully automating the entire O&A process, AgentDP reduces entire model adaptation time by up to 80% compared with manual O&A while achieving higher task accuracy (more than 13% on average) than the baselines. Additionally, a comprehensive user study also exhibits the robust generalizability of AgentDP in adapting to different user requirements for heterogeneous embedded devices.
papers.summary: Deploying pre-trained models on heterogeneous embedded devices requires manual model optimization and adaptation that is slow and device-specific. `AgentDP` automates this with LLM agents and three components: a module that standardizes user requirements, an operator-aware partitioning scheme that runs different parts of a model on different inference engines, and a configuration-reuse module that retrieves earlier hyperparameter settings for new tasks. Experiments show that it **reduces total model adaptation time by up to 80% compared with manual work** while achieving more than 13% higher task accuracy on average than baselines, and a user study supports its generalization across requirements and devices.

papers.title: Abstract Priorities, Concrete Rewards: How Stated Preferences Relate to What People Reward in AI Responses
papers.abstract: AI assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are trained on human feedback and increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences. Yet how closely these preferences reflect what people reward in responses remains unclear. We compare stated and revealed preferences in the public PRISM dataset, in which 1,396 participants reported how much seven response attributes mattered to them and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs. Among responses to the same prompt, features the survey never asked about, such as response length, formatting and refusal language, were at least as strongly associated with ratings as text proxies of the surveyed attributes. Whether stated priorities matched ratings depended on how attributes were measured: participants who prioritized an attribute favoured responses from models that others perceived as strong on it, but not responses that scored higher on text proxies for it. Written feedback was more telling: participants who asked for shorter answers, even in earlier conversations, gave length less weight in their ratings, and those asking for longer answers gave it more. Their relative priorities over the surveyed attributes, however, did not predict this weight. Reasons given for choices reflected perceived attributes more than measured features. Participants also differed stably in how much they weighted several concrete features, especially length, but with a median of 6 conversations per participant, these weights were estimated poorly. The largest gain from personal information in predicting held-out choices was 0.13 percentage points, compared with 1.11 for a stronger pooled model. Stated priorities thus track perceived attributes of AI responses but say little about the concrete features that ratings reward, a distinction that matters for preference elicitation and AI personalization.
papers.summary: AI assistants are increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences, but it is unclear whether those preferences match what people actually reward. Using the public `PRISM` dataset, in which 1,396 participants ranked seven response attributes and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs, the authors find that features the survey never asked about, such as length, formatting, and refusal language, were at least as predictive of ratings as the surveyed attributes. Stated priorities tracked perceived model strengths but not measurable text features, while written feedback such as asking for shorter answers did predict how much length mattered. **Personal information improved prediction of held-out choices by at most 0.13 percentage points, versus 1.11 for a stronger pooled model**.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Generative Reward Models
papers.abstract: We study generative reward models (GenRMs) as online preference providers for policy optimization in creative writing. Across Qwen3 reward-model sizes from 0.6B to 14B, Thinking judges trained with GRPO have higher static Gold-label accuracy than Answer-Only judges trained with SFT. This ranking often reverses when the judges train policies through online DPO: Answer-Only rewarders yield higher peak and top-five-average policy Elo in seven of eight matched settings under a fixed, learned 32B Gold evaluator. Intermediate Thinking-judge checkpoints can also outperform later, more statically accurate checkpoints as rewarders. Sweeps over rewarder size, policy size, training duration and DPO regularization show substantial benefits from reward-model capacity, including judges larger than the policy. We analyze trajectories with evaluator-specific Elo arenas, conditional match-resampling intervals and descriptive scaling fits. These results demonstrate an evaluator-rewarder gap in the studied pipelines: fixed-distribution judging accuracy does not determine downstream optimization quality. The comparison changes judge-training objective as well as response format, and the main ranking is conditional on its learned reference rather than a universal human-quality result. A limited follow-up using a different learned judge is inconclusive overall.
papers.summary: Generative reward models (GenRMs) act as judges that supply preferences during policy training. The authors study them for creative writing across `Qwen3` judge sizes from 0.6B to 14B, comparing Thinking judges trained with `GRPO` against Answer-Only judges trained with supervised fine-tuning. Thinking judges score higher on static gold-label accuracy, but **Answer-Only judges produce better policies through online `DPO` in seven of eight matched settings**, and earlier, less accurate Thinking checkpoints can be better rewarders than later ones. Larger judges help substantially, even when they exceed the policy's size, and the results show that static judging accuracy does not determine downstream optimization quality in these pipelines.
papers.highlight_summary:
Generative reward models (GenRMs) that score higher on static preference benchmarks don't necessarily produce better policies when they supply online training signal. The authors test this in creative writing by training `Qwen3` judges as online-DPO rewarders, sweeping judge format, judge size and policy size, and scoring the resulting policies against a fixed learned 32B "Gold" evaluator.

- A `Qwen3-32B` Gold judge is fine-tuned on vote-derived `LitBench` Reddit story preferences, reaching 79% agreement with those labels, and then relabels pairs to train 0.6B–14B proxy judges. The proxies come in two kinds: Answer-Only judges trained with SFT and Thinking judges trained with `GRPO`. Each proxy then labels fresh response pairs for online DPO of 0.6B–8B policies.
- Thinking judges are more accurate statically at every size (the 4B `GRPO` recipe reaches **83.2%** versus 60.0% off the shelf), but the ranking reverses in training: Answer-Only rewarders give higher peak and top-five Gold Elo in **7 of 8 matched settings**, with a mean peak gap of **126 Elo**, and 5 of 8 bootstrap intervals exclude zero.
- Static accuracy can also mislead when choosing a checkpoint: an intermediate 250-step Thinking judge (79.2% accuracy) trains better policies than the later 300-step judge (82.3%), and Thinking-trained runs lose on average 130 Elo from peak to final versus 60 for Answer-Only.
- Judges larger than the policy keep helping: a 14B Answer-Only judge with a 4B policy peaks at **1719 Gold Elo**, a descriptive log-linear fit reaches R² of 95.2% with roughly 136 Elo per judge-size doubling for Answer-Only, and the smallest DPO β tested (0.002) lifts peak Gold Elo from 357 to **1122**.
- All results rest on a learned Gold judge from the same model family and a single seed per configuration, and they mix two changes at once, the training objective (SFT versus GRPO) and the response format; a check with a different judge, `Qwen3-235B`, was inconclusive (52.5%, 42 of 80), and high-Elo outputs collapse into templates, with 94% of one setting's peak outputs sharing the same opening line.

papers.title: Adaptive Deadline- and Energy-Aware Caching Algorithms in Dynamic Multi-UAV Edge Networks
papers.abstract: Content caching via unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) becomes one of the solutions to maintain content delivery when terrestrial infrastructure is unavailable or disrupted. However, existing caching approaches often focus primarily on cache-hit performance or average delivery delay, without jointly addressing spatially heterogeneous and time-varying demand, content-specific deadlines, and uneven communication-energy consumption across UAVs. To address these challenges, we formulate a dynamic deadline- and energy-aware cache placement and replacement problem that jointly considers deadline misses, UAV-side communication energy, and inter-UAV energy imbalance. To achieve this, we first develop deadline- and energy-aware UBAC (DE-UBAC), an interpretable hierarchical rule-based realization that incorporates deadline-aware prioritization, cooperative placement, energy-aware coordination, and cache-update cost. However, predefined priorities and thresholds limit its adaptability under dynamically coupled network conditions. We therefore propose GRU-assisted Deadline- and Energy-aware Proximal Policy Optimization (GRU-DEPPO), which combines local and global GRU-based temporal representations with a centralized PPO actor-critic for adaptive cache placement and replacement. Simulation results show that GRU-DEPPO achieves the lowest deadline-miss rate and total UAV-side communication energy among the considered schemes. Compared with DE-UBAC, GRU-DEPPO reduces the deadline-miss rate by approximately 61% and inter-UAV energy imbalance by approximately 40%.
papers.summary: Drones (unmanned aerial vehicles, or UAVs) can cache and deliver content when ground infrastructure is down, but existing caching schemes rarely account together for shifting demand, content deadlines, and uneven energy use across UAVs. The authors first build `DE-UBAC`, an interpretable rule-based scheme for deadline- and energy-aware placement and replacement. They then propose `GRU-DEPPO`, which combines local and global GRU-based temporal features with a centralized `PPO` actor-critic. In simulation, `GRU-DEPPO` has the lowest deadline-miss rate and communication energy of all schemes compared, **cutting deadline misses by about 61%** and inter-UAV energy imbalance by about 40% relative to `DE-UBAC`.

papers.title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.
papers.summary: LLM agents in multi-agent systems respond to one another's choices, which creates feedback loops prone to herding. Replicating the classic `Music Lab` experiment, the authors had large populations of LLM agents recommend unfamiliar songs, with or without seeing cumulative recommendation counts. Seeing the counts triggered runaway cascades that produced extreme, unpredictable outcomes increasingly detached from each song's intrinsic appeal. **LLM populations were far more susceptible to herding than humans and less able to self-correct**, which bears on multi-agent recommender systems, automated evaluation, and collaborative problem-solving.

papers.title: One Pretrained Decision Model Is Enough for Training-Free Generalist Graph Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to identify irregular entities in graph-structured data, yet heterogeneous anomaly patterns and distributional differences across graphs challenge generalizable detection. Existing training-free approaches avoid task-specific optimization but primarily rely on predefined numerical scoring rules, leaving the semantic interpretation of heterogeneous anomaly evidence largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose Jev-GAD, a training-free generalist graph anomaly detection framework that bridges heterogeneous numerical evidence and pretrained decision mechanisms. To address heterogeneous anomaly patterns, we construct complementary structural, attribute, and neighborhood evidence and transform heterogeneous statistics into graph-relative anomaly percentiles. To move beyond predefined numerical scoring rules, we leverage a single frozen pretrained language model for evidence-conditioned anomaly assessment. To bridge the semantic gap between numerical evidence and pretrained models, we design a semantic Graph-to-State (G2S) transformation that organizes graph context and semantically labeled node evidence into structured decision states for non-generative option-logit readout. The resulting decision scores are integrated with four complementary statistical scores through equal-weight rank-based fusion, without GAD-specific gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments on seven graph anomaly detection benchmarks spanning citation, social, and co-review networks demonstrate the effectiveness of Jev-GAD, achieving average AUROC and AUPRC scores of 89.18\% and 52.40\%, respectively. Further analyses validate the contributions of pretrained decision readout and semantic evidence grounding.
papers.summary: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to spot irregular nodes in graph data, but anomaly patterns and data distributions vary widely between graphs, and existing training-free methods depend on fixed numerical scoring rules. `Jev-GAD` builds structural, attribute, and neighborhood evidence for each node and converts it into percentiles relative to the rest of the graph. A semantic Graph-to-State (`G2S`) transformation then turns that evidence into structured text, which a single frozen pretrained language model scores by reading the logits of answer options instead of generating text. These scores are combined with four statistical scores through equal-weight rank fusion, with no gradient training for GAD, and reach **an average AUROC of 89.18%** across seven citation, social, and co-review benchmarks.

papers.title: Where meanings converge and diverge: Revisiting linguistic relativity across 81 languages
papers.abstract: Do people who speak different languages organize concepts in similar ways? This question lies at the heart of the Sapir--Whorf hypothesis and debates about linguistic relativity. Shared basic meanings, however, need not imply shared relations among them. We compared relations among 196 basic concepts across 81 languages, using word embeddings from two multilingual models to quantify conceptual structure expressed in language. Cross-language correspondence was greater for sociocultural meanings than for meanings concerning nature and motion, a contrast recurring across models and classifications. Within the sociocultural domain, relational differences increased with geographic separation; less closely related languages differed more across all domains. These findings suggest that universality and relativity are interwoven across conceptual domains. They inform an account in which shared cognitive resources interact with linguistic and local experience, and predict greater cross-language correspondence in human semantic judgments for sociocultural than for nature and motion meanings.
papers.summary: The authors test the linguistic relativity (Sapir-Whorf) question of whether speakers of different languages organize concepts the same way. They use word embeddings from two multilingual models to compare how 196 basic concepts relate to one another across 81 languages. **Languages agreed more on sociocultural meanings than on meanings about nature and motion**, and this held across models and concept classifications. Within the sociocultural domain, differences grew with geographic distance, and less closely related languages differed more in every domain, which suggests that universal and language-specific structure coexist.

papers.title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. Mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by quantizing different model components at different bit widths, but existing methods often struggle to preserve generation quality under tight bit budgets. We identify two key challenges: (1) nonlinear quantization errors at extremely low precision are underestimated when cross-layer propagation is ignored; (2) direct router fine-tuning may cause routing drift, and calibration gains may not generalize to downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose ProQuant, a weight-only PTQ framework for MoE models. Prune-or-Prioritize Mixed-Precision Allocation (PoP) jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width assignment. It allows higher-precision experts to substitute for severely degraded ones while improving bit-budget utilization. Routing-Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (RoCo) adapts expert input representations through mathematically equivalent transformations. It compensates for quantization errors to reduce routing drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProQuant outperforms existing methods across diverse generative tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ThrowBug/ProQuant.git.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token but still need a lot of storage, and mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) struggles to keep output quality at very low bit budgets. The authors point to two causes: existing methods ignore how quantization errors propagate across layers, and fine-tuning the router directly can shift which experts get selected. `ProQuant` addresses these with Prune-or-Prioritize (`PoP`), which jointly decides which experts to prune and how many bits each remaining expert gets, so that higher-precision experts can stand in for badly degraded ones. It adds Routing-Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (`RoCo`), which compensates for quantization error through mathematically equivalent transformations that keep routing stable, and the method **outperforms existing quantization methods across diverse generative tasks**.

papers.title: MixJudge: Learning a Language-Queryable Critic for Vocal Mixing
papers.abstract: Mixing requires not only applying processing but also assessing the resulting mix. Audio-language models can provide conversa- tional mixing advice, but existing evaluations do not separately test whether they can judge specific mixing issues. Since professional supervision for such judgments is scarce, we construct a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at multiple severity levels and use it to train MixJudge, a language-queryable audio critic. MixJudge shows its ability to retrieve mixing issues, distinguish opposite issues, and order the severity of an issue. Moreover, its judgments transfer to menu selection: given a set of processing candidates, MixJudge often favors versions acoustically closer to a held-out professional version, demonstrating how explicit mixing judgment can support comparison and downstream mixing decisions.
papers.summary: Audio-language models can give conversational advice on mixing, but no existing evaluation checks whether they can judge specific mixing problems, and expert labels for that are scarce. The authors build a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at several severity levels and use it to train `MixJudge`, an audio critic that answers natural-language queries. `MixJudge` can retrieve mixing issues, tell opposite issues apart, and rank how severe an issue is. When choosing among candidate processing settings, it **often prefers the versions that sound closest to a held-out professional mix**.

papers.title: Invisibilization as a Source of Probability Bias in Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models are aligned to avoid using protected attributes such as race, ethnicity, and gender to inform their responses. Therefore, they increasingly refuse or hedge when such attributes appear in a prompt. However, if a system must decide how much to learn from what people tell it, it is costly to refuse valuable information because of its source. In this article, we measure the cost of declining information in a two-urn game with an exact Bayesian answer. We present leading LLM models from two developers (OpenAI and Anthropic) with a prompt that requires them to decide how far to trust an unverifiable report from a participant whose description we randomize across ten configurations (6,600 sessions). We show that leading models often decline to assess the reporter, treating information as worthless at rates set by the description rather than by the evidence. At its widest, models decline a Black-described reporter 46% of the time and a white-described reporter 9%; yet, when they do assess the information, the Black-described reporter receives slightly more trust. The bias is invisible to audits that compare average trust or look only at assessed cases. It grows with reasoning effort, follows words rather than categories (models invoke race for "Black" but not for its Spanish translation negro, and never for "Indigenous"), and worsens under warning instructions a practitioner would try first. We also present a scoring option that reduces the refusal rate bias. When a model's trust is scored against revealed truth over repeated rounds, it credits identical records equally. In four of five configurations from Anthropic and OpenAI, the racial gap in trust falls below 0.02 by the last rounds.
papers.summary: Language models are aligned to avoid using protected attributes such as race, and as a result they often refuse to weigh information when those attributes are mentioned. The authors measure the cost of this in a two-urn game that has an exact Bayesian answer, running 6,600 sessions with leading OpenAI and Anthropic models in which models judge an unverifiable report from a reporter described in ten different ways. Models frequently declined to assess the reporter at rates driven by the description rather than the evidence, **declining a Black-described reporter 46% of the time versus 9% for a white-described one**. Audits that compare only average trust miss this bias, which grows with reasoning effort and gets worse under warning instructions. Scoring the models' trust against revealed outcomes over repeated rounds shrinks the racial gap in trust to below 0.02 in four of five configurations.

papers.title: An Introduction to World Models for Generalist Agents
papers.abstract: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.
papers.summary: "World model" is used loosely for many things, from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to systems that generate future observations and actions together. This introductory tutorial starts from the partially observable Markov decision process (`POMDP`) framework and connects world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. It compares world-modeling approaches by the knowledge they capture, the objectives they learn, and how they support decisions. A central argument is that **world modeling and policy learning can be unified through conditional prediction without separate models**, and the paper favors core principles over an exhaustive survey.

papers.title: Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization
papers.abstract: LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed, producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning, using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.
papers.summary: LLM agents can improve by turning past experience into reusable knowledge such as skills and memories, but different ways of analyzing the same experience can produce knowledge of very different usefulness. `SPLICE` borrows the idea of consistency regularization: it varies how an experience is analyzed to produce several knowledge candidates, then keeps updates whose usefulness gains hold up consistently across those variations. Model updates combine reinforcement learning with self-distillation of the evolved knowledge, using knowledge that consistently hurts performance as a contrastive reference, and knowledge updates and model updates alternate. `SPLICE` beats knowledge-evolution and model-training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points of average accuracy, and its evolved knowledge **cuts output tokens per correct solution by up to 44%** while transferring across model sizes and families.

papers.title: Gandalf: Flash Shall Not Die! Increasing Flash Storage Lifetime for KV Cache Offloading in LLM Serving
papers.abstract: KV caching reduces the serving cost of large language models (LLMs), but the growing KV cache footprint is increasingly exceeds GPU and host-memory capacity. Therefore, people use SSD to expand the KV cache storage capacity with high I/O bandwidth. However, in production LLM workload, such as multi-round conversation and LLM agents, the total amount of KV cache writes significantly exceeds SSD capacity, shortening SSD lifetime from years to months. To improve SSD lifetime, a natural solution is to reduce the KV cache writes by gating the KV cache writes via historical access patterns. However, that significantly lowers the KV cache hit rate (and increase the LLM serving cost) since KV caches from different attention types might have identical historical access pattern but different future access patterns. Our insight is that, to reduce KV cache writes without hurting KV cache hit rate, one need to not only consider the access pattern, but also application-level information such as the attention type of KV cache. Leveraging this observation, we propose Gandalf , the first SSD KV cache offloading system with SSD life time awareness. Gandalf prioritize the admission of full-attention KV cache into SSD over the cache generated by other types of attention, which significantly increases SSD lifetime without sacrificing cache hit rate. Our evaluation shows that Gandalf extends the SSD lifetime by 7.3X on average, while having negligible impact on cache hit rate across multiple workload traces and wide range of hardware capacity. Gandalf design can be extended to other flash-based storage, such as High Bandwidth Flash (HBF).
papers.summary: LLM serving systems increasingly offload the key-value (KV) cache to SSDs, but multi-turn chat and agent workloads write so much KV data that SSD lifetime can drop from years to months. Filtering writes by past access patterns alone lowers cache hit rates, because KV caches from different attention types can have similar histories but different future reuse. `Gandalf` also uses application-level information and gives full-attention KV caches priority for SSD admission over caches from other attention types. Across workload traces and hardware capacities, this **extends SSD lifetime by 7.3x on average** with negligible effect on cache hit rate.

papers.title: Trace2World: Reconstructing App Worlds from Real Interaction Traces for Scalable GUI Agent Training
papers.abstract: Scaling GUI reinforcement learning requires environments that preserve real-app behavior. Yet coupling behavior inference with coding can turn partial traces into runnable mocks with incorrect state transitions. We introduce \textbf{Trace2World}, which separates global behavior reconstruction from implementation. It reconciles traces into a shared, source-linked app model, then compiles an executable environment. Independent replay of source workflows localizes mismatches for bounded implementation repair. Validated worlds then support learner-adaptive task and environment augmentation within source-supported behavior. From 1,570 traces, Trace2World constructs 50 environments. On 200 workflows across ten apps, 91.1% are reproduced end to end, versus 59.8% for the strongest matched task-local baseline. Source-grounded validation retains 94.0% of simulated training gains on real devices, versus 54.7% under self-validation. Learner guidance raises benchmark success from 56.9% to 61.1%. Training in Trace2World further improves the model by 20.2 points on our benchmark, 5.4--16.2 points across four external GUI benchmarks, and 16.3 points on 100 real-device tasks. Reliable reconstruction separates what behavior source evidence supports from whether the implementation preserves it.
papers.summary: Scaling reinforcement learning for GUI agents needs training environments that behave like real apps, but generating mock apps directly from partial interaction traces often produces incorrect state transitions. `Trace2World` first merges traces into a shared app model linked to its source evidence, then compiles that model into an executable environment, and it replays source workflows to find mismatches that need repair. From 1,570 traces it builds 50 environments that **reproduce 91.1% of 200 workflows end to end**, compared with 59.8% for the strongest baseline, and validation against the source evidence keeps 94.0% of simulated training gains on real devices. Training in these environments improves a model by 20.2 points on the authors' benchmark, by 5.4 to 16.2 points on four external GUI benchmarks, and by 16.3 points on 100 real-device tasks.

papers.title: VLTest: Finding Joint Image-Text Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. Mutating either input can change the expected answer, so an output change is not by itself a failure. Some failures appear only when both inputs are mutated; attributing them to the combination requires testing each mutation alone. We present VLTest, a black-box VLM testing approach.
