It generates image variants by editing VQGAN latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, filters variants likely to change the expected answer, and tests each variant alone before testing combinations, so every joint failure has four matched cells. A VLM judge confirms a failure only after checking that the input keeps the expected answer. On three tasks with eight VLMs, including two commercial API models, the oracle confirms 81.7% of the candidates, with 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates. Under the same budget, VLTest's generators find 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as SINVAD and TextFooler, and its joint tests find 91 to 197 attributed joint failures per 1,000 joint calls, 1.3 times as many as the same pairing applied to the baselines' variants.
papers.summary: Testing vision-language models (VLMs) is hard because changing an input can legitimately change the correct answer, and some failures only appear when the image and the text are both changed. `VLTest` is a black-box tester that creates image variants by editing `VQGAN` latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, and it discards variants likely to change the expected answer. It tests each variant on its own before testing combinations, so every joint failure can be attributed using four matched cases, and a VLM judge confirms each failure. Across three tasks and eight VLMs, the judge reaches 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and with the same budget **`VLTest` finds 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as `SINVAD` and `TextFooler`**.

papers.title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL
papers.abstract: Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome-grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token-level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation-focused distillation can conflict with the outcome-driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose \textbf{GIFT} (\textbf{G}radient-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{F}il\textbf{T}ering for Distillation-Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. Code: https://github.com/lilifree/GIFT
papers.summary: Training LLMs for reasoning often combines sparse, outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) with dense, token-level distillation from a teacher, but imitating the teacher can conflict with the RL objective. `GIFT` splits each token's distillation gradient into a component parallel to the RL gradient, which measures conflict and serves as a safety filter, and an orthogonal component, which measures new guidance and serves as a value score. Tokens are ranked by this score, and a coverage-annealing schedule gradually shrinks the set of distilled tokens, dropping the most conflicting first, until training is pure RL. Across model scales on math and logic benchmarks, `GIFT` beats strong baselines, with **relative gains of up to 9.5% on difficult math tasks**.

papers.title: Amplifying Latency and Cost of LLM Inference via Rowhammer Attack
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high inference efficiency using optimized GPU kernels generated by just-in-time (JIT) compilation frameworks such as Triton. Triton compiles GPU kernels through an MLIR/LLVM-based pipeline. We investigate whether a Rowhammer-induced bit-flip in the CPU's DRAM can degrade GPU-based LLM inference performance while preserving output correctness. We present LLVMhammer, the first Rowhammer attack that causes LLM inference slowdown by inducing a bit-flip in Triton's compilation pipeline. A bit-flip in a performance-critical optimization pass causes Triton to generate a functionally identical but suboptimal GPU kernel. Since Triton caches the generated kernel on disk, a single successful bit-flip causes persistent slowdown across subsequent inference executions. Triton's target-independent stages are shared across GPU vendors, which makes our attack GPU vendor-agnostic. To identify exploitable bit-flip locations without manual inspection, we build Karnage, a tool that isolates useful bit-flip locations in Triton's target-independent compilation pipeline. We evaluate LLVMHammer across a diverse set of LLMs, including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Deepseek-llm-7B-chat, across NVIDIA RTX 4090 and AMD RX 7900 XTX GPUs. LLVMhammer increases inference latency of an LLM inference server running on a single GPU by 4-16\%, which, in turn, can translate into additional annual operating costs at the scale of multi-GPU deployments. We further show that LLVMhammer can also corrupt LLM outputs across different GPU vendors, reducing BERTScore to as low as 25\%, illustrating the broader security implications of bit-flips in Triton's compilation pipeline.
papers.summary: `LLVMhammer` is a Rowhammer attack that flips a bit in CPU memory during `Triton`'s just-in-time GPU kernel compilation, which leaves output correct but makes LLM inference slower. Because the flip hits an optimization pass, `Triton` produces a functionally identical but slower kernel and caches it on disk, so a single successful flip causes lasting slowdown. Since the targeted compiler stages are shared across GPU vendors, the attack works on both NVIDIA and AMD hardware. A companion tool, `Karnage`, finds exploitable bit locations automatically. On `Qwen2.5-7B`, `Llama-3.1-8B`, `Mistral-7B`, and `DeepSeek-7B` running on RTX 4090 and RX 7900 XTX GPUs, the attack **increases inference latency by 4 to 16%**, and variants can also corrupt outputs, lowering `BERTScore` to as little as 25%.

papers.title: A Computationally Efficient and Rate-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial Linear MDPs with (Aggregate) Bandit Feedback
papers.abstract: We study episodic linear Markov decision processes with unknown transitions, adversarial losses, and bandit feedback. The state-of-the-art result for this setting (Liu et al., 2024) either achieves $\sqrt{K}$ regret with a computationally inefficient algorithm or achieves suboptimal $K^{3/4}$ regret, where $K$ is the number of episodes. Our work gives the first $\sqrt{K}$ regret with a polynomial-time algorithm. Our method reduces adversarial linear MDPs to adversarial linear bandits whose action set consists of policies' expected feature vectors. The central challenge is that this action set is unknown and can be estimated only through exploration. We address this challenge by constructing an approximate separation oracle for the action set that either generates executable policies from queried features, or refines an outer approximation of the action set. This approach draws inspiration from the reduction of van Erven et al. (2025) for linear contextual bandits and the oracle-efficient linear bandit algorithm of Ito et al. (2019), but additionally deals with the imprecision of the oracle. The resulting algorithm requires only aggregate loss feedback, and to our knowledge. This is the first polynomial-time algorithm for adversarial MDPs with aggregate feedback beyond the tabular case.
papers.summary: The setting is episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions, adversarially chosen losses, and bandit feedback, where earlier methods achieved either optimal square-root-of-K regret with an inefficient algorithm or a weaker K^(3/4) regret, K being the number of episodes. The authors **give the first polynomial-time algorithm with square-root-of-K regret** by reducing the problem to an adversarial linear bandit whose actions are the expected feature vectors of policies. Because that action set is unknown, they build an approximate separation oracle that either produces an executable policy from a queried feature or tightens an outer approximation of the set. The algorithm needs only aggregate loss feedback, making it the first polynomial-time method for adversarial MDPs with aggregate feedback beyond the tabular case.

papers.title: Is spectral predictability enough? Testing {\Omega}-matching for synthetic pretraining under distribution shift
papers.abstract: Synthetic pretraining under distribution shift requires deciding what synthetic data to use. A natural criterion is to match the spectral predictability $\Omega$ of the source to the target, but is $\Omega$ sufficient? We test this hypothesis, which we call predictability-aware pretraining, across three architectures (LSTM, PatchTST, TCN) and three seeds. Under ideal synthetic-to-synthetic conditions, $\Omega$-matched pretraining can outperform even an oracle baseline (+46.8% MSE reduction, LSTM), though the benefit is already architecture-dependent. On the real-world ETTm1 benchmark, however, this relationship does not hold: sine-plus-noise pretraining at matched $\Omega$ yields only a marginal mean improvement +2.3% averaged over all three architectures, up to +65.5% on individual channels), whereas $\Omega$ matched chaotic ODE trajectories systematically degrade performance -13.2%). The two sources agree on the direction of transfer for only 53% of configurations across all three architectures (Pearson r=-0.02), indicating that $\Omega$ carries little information about which source will transfer beneficially. We further observe an architecture-dependent asymmetry in the response to the direction of the $\Omega$ gap. We conclude that $\Omega$ matching can help in controlled settings but is not sufficient to predict transfer across sources, and we discuss additional signal properties that a source-selection criterion may need to consider.
papers.summary: When pretraining time-series models on synthetic data, one natural rule is to choose synthetic data whose spectral predictability (Omega) matches the target. The authors test this rule with `LSTM`, `PatchTST`, and `TCN` models over three seeds. In synthetic-to-synthetic tests, Omega-matched pretraining can beat an oracle baseline, but on the real `ETTm1` benchmark, matched sine-plus-noise data helps only marginally (+2.3% on average) and matched chaotic ODE trajectories hurt performance (-13.2%). The two synthetic sources agree on whether transfer helps in only 53% of configurations, so **Omega matching is not sufficient to predict which source will transfer well**.

papers.title: What Lies Beyond Perception: A Partition Theory of the Limits of AI Evaluation and Oversight
papers.abstract: Replacing the judge can move a benchmark score, and models can be trained to hide capabilities. Both put the evaluator in question: what can it certify? We develop a partition theory of evaluation from one principle: judgement is bounded by perception. An agent's discrimination is the partition of its inputs into classes it cannot tell apart. Discrimination is necessary for capability but not sufficient, so bounds on it bear directly on whether evaluation can show that a model lacks an ability. We prove a one-sided bound. An examinee whose partition refines its evaluator's has the discrimination to pass every test the evaluator can grade, provided each input has an acceptable reply. We define the echo test, which accepts any reply the evaluator perceives as identical to the input, and show that it is complete for the tests the evaluator can grade. Passing therefore certifies at most a floor on discrimination, never a ceiling, and only a sharper evaluator can raise it. Used to detect concealment, echo-test failure points the wrong way: under exhaustive probing it flags every honestly weaker examinee and no concealer that presents as the evaluator's peer. Exact imitation of a weaker model is undetectable by any behavioural evaluator. We extend the bound to ensembles of monitors and to channels a model controls, explain published findings on judge disagreement and sandbagging, and derive testable predictions. A safety case that argues from behavioural evaluation alone that a model lacks an ability must assume the model's cooperation.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores can change when the judge model changes, and models can be trained to hide capabilities, which raises the question of what an evaluator can actually certify. The authors develop a theory in which an agent's ability to discriminate is the partition of its inputs into classes it cannot tell apart, and they prove that any examinee at least as discriminating as its evaluator can pass every test that evaluator can grade. As a result, passing a test certifies only a lower bound on ability, never an upper bound, and **exact imitation of a weaker model cannot be detected by any behavioral evaluator**. The bound extends to ensembles of monitors and helps explain published findings on judge disagreement and sandbagging, implying that safety arguments based only on behavioral evaluation must assume the model cooperates.

papers.title: xVGAE: A Hierarchical Variational Graph Autoencoder for Exchangeable Graphs
papers.abstract: Graphs play a crucial role in many applications, ranging from drug discovery to social network modeling and astronomy. Generative models for graphs have substantially advanced in recent years, but we identify relatively simple scenarios where state-of-the-art models struggle to converge within a standard compute budget, or exhibit prohibitively slow generation times. We propose a generative architecture that achieves quality competitive with state-of-the-art models and is orders of magnitude faster at generation. Our approach is inspired by the Aldous-Hoover theorem, a classic representation theorem that characterizes any probability distribution of graphs that is invariant to permutations of node indices or exchangeable. This theorem establishes that three ingredients suffice: a graph-level latent variable, a set of exchangeable node-specific latent variables, and a so-called graphon function that maps graph- and node-level variables to the probability of an edge between any node pair. Given a training set of graphs, our exchangeable Variational Graph AutoEncoder (xVGAE) learns an approximation to their underlying graphons, as well as graph- and node-level latent variables. We show that our xVGAE encodes latent representations that correlate with graph- and node-level properties, and can (quickly, in one shot) generate new graphs that closely match key training set statistics.
papers.summary: State-of-the-art graph generative models can fail to converge within normal compute budgets even in fairly simple settings, or they generate graphs very slowly. `xVGAE` is based on the Aldous-Hoover theorem, which says that any distribution over graphs that ignores node ordering can be described by a graph-level latent variable, per-node latent variables, and a graphon function that gives the probability of each edge. The variational autoencoder learns approximations of these components from training graphs, and its latent variables correlate with graph-level and node-level properties. It generates graphs in one shot with quality competitive with leading models while being **orders of magnitude faster at generation**.

papers.title: TESSA: A Governance-Oriented Custom GPT for SME Guidance under the EU AI Act: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.
papers.summary: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) struggle to apply the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, and `TESSA` is an OpenAI Custom GPT built to teach governance and give compliance guidance to them. Following a design science approach, the authors compare it with baseline `ChatGPT` on 100 benchmark scenarios using LLM-assisted scoring, human expert review, and consistency tests. LLM-assisted scoring rated governance alignment at 90% for `TESSA` and 83% for `ChatGPT`, but **an AI-regulation lawyer rated them nearly the same, at 71% and 70%**. Its clearest advantage was higher consistency across repeated runs.

papers.title: Neural Spectral Capacity with Residual Context for Heterogeneous Resource Allocation within Transformers
papers.abstract: Predicting relative trained performance from architectural specifications can guide design when training costs limit experimentation. Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC) provides such a heuristic, but scores projections independently and assigns identical scores to compatible reorderings of the same layer configurations. We introduce Residual-Aware Neural Spectral Capacity (ResNSC) for Transformers, using a specification-derived statistical reference for accumulated residual updates to determine the input and residual-state statistics in each projection's capacity calculation, while retaining additive evaluation without data or instantiated weights. When residual widths vary, earlier choices affect later scores, so we augment NSC's allocator (NSC-DP) with residual history beyond its layer-and-budget state. ResNSC-DP jointly allocates residual and feed-forward widths under a resource budget, with certified bounds on the best numerically evaluated ResNSC score within a specified finite candidate set. At the 121M and 374M pretraining scales, selected architectures achieve lower mean perplexity than uniform, variable-width, and tapered allocations on FineWeb-Edu, WikiText-2, and LAMBADA at comparable parameter budgets. In inherited-weight LLaMA-7B pruning using the LoNAS supernet, ResNSC-DP improves eight-task average accuracy over NSC by 3.28--5.46 percentage points across eight matched parameter budgets. Paired reversals preserve the projection shapes and NSC scores yet worsen performance in both settings, exposing performance differences hidden by position-independent scoring. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/Optima-CityU/neural-spectral-capacity.
papers.summary: Neural Spectral Capacity (`NSC`) estimates how well a Transformer architecture will perform from its specification alone, but it scores each projection independently, so reordering the same layers gives the same score. Residual-Aware NSC (`ResNSC`) adds a statistical model of the accumulated residual stream to each projection's score, still without needing data or weights. A matching allocator, `ResNSC-DP`, jointly chooses residual and feed-forward widths under a resource budget. At 121M and 374M parameters, the selected architectures reach lower perplexity than uniform or tapered designs, and when pruning `LLaMA-7B` they **improve eight-task average accuracy over `NSC` by 3.28 to 5.46 points**.

papers.title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
papers.abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.
papers.summary: Editing real images usually requires inverting the image into noise and then sampling iteratively, and fast one-step editors still evaluate the model at several noise levels. The authors show that in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step generator, a single source-and-target query at one noisy state gives both a semantic direction and an estimate of the clean endpoint shift. Their method, Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (`ECT`), follows the semantic direction to produce the edit and uses the endpoint estimate to correct its error. It is a closed-form, training-free editor that needs **only one model evaluation and one latent update**, with no inversion or iterative optimization, and it shows stable quality gains at very short editing times.

papers.title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI-tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case-specific scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open-ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple-choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context-specific adaptation, especially for open-weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for LLM tutors rarely cover the difficult behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. `TutorCaseBench` builds scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and grading rubrics from qualitative case studies in pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education, producing 923 dialogues across five types of challenging behavior. Across 11 leading LLMs, **even the best model meets a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases**. Models do better at choosing an appropriate strategy from a list than at writing a response that fits the situation, and the gap is larger for open-weight models.

papers.title: Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks: Enhancing Flexibility in Node Dependencies via penalized B-Splines
papers.abstract: Bayesian networks for continuous variables often rely on restrictive assumptions: linear Gaussian models lack flexibility to capture nonlinear dependencies, while non-parametric approaches provide greater flexibility at a high computational cost. This creates a gap for modeling scenarios where variables are approximately Gaussian but exhibit nonlinear relationships. We introduce Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks (SLGBN), a novel class of continuous Bayesian networks designed to bridge this gap, preserving Gaussian conditional distributions while introducing nonlinear conditional mean functions. The proposed framework provides a unified probabilistic framework combining linear Gaussian and nonlinear Gaussian conditional models within the same Bayesian network Nonlinear conditional mean functions are estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with penalized B-splines. We present parameter estimation procedures for both types of nodes, as well as a greedy hill-climbing algorithm for learning the network structure under the SLGBN framework. To assess its performance, we compare SLGBN with other continuous Bayesian network models, including semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBN) and Linear Gaussian Bayesian networks (LGBN). Experimental results evaluate both goodness of fit and the ability to recover the underlying network structure. The results show that, in the presence of nonlinear Gaussian relationships, SLGBN achieves better fit and improved structure recovery compared to alternative models, particularly when combined with the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC*) score. Furthermore, by retaining Gaussian conditional distributions, SLGBN offers computational advantages over fully semiparametric approaches.
papers.summary: Bayesian networks for continuous variables usually force a choice. Linear Gaussian models are cheap but cannot capture nonlinear dependencies, while non-parametric models are flexible but computationally expensive. Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks (`SLGBN`) keep Gaussian conditional distributions but let some nodes have nonlinear conditional means, which are fitted with generalized additive models (GAMs) using penalized B-splines. The authors also give a greedy hill-climbing algorithm for learning the network structure. Compared with semiparametric (`SPBN`) and linear Gaussian (`LGBN`) networks, `SLGBN` **achieves better fit and better structure recovery when relationships are nonlinear but Gaussian**, especially when paired with the `EBIC*` score, and it is cheaper to compute than fully semiparametric models.

papers.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
papers.summary: Most multimodal benchmarks test recognition or reasoning on inputs that are already unambiguous. `TRIAD` instead tests whether omni-modal models can resolve ambiguity spread across text, image, and audio. It contains 327 hand-written text–image–audio items in 86 scene groups covering 18 ambiguity categories, and each item has a unique answer only when all three modalities are considered. Across 14 omni-modal systems, **the best model still trails humans by more than 20 points in scene-level group accuracy**, and without answer options model group accuracy drops to single digits while humans stay robust. Ablations show that models tend to underuse audio cues when text and image are also present.

papers.title: Lean Finder V2: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Disambiguates User Queries
papers.abstract: We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. In contrast, existing Mathlib search engines unrealistically assume context-rich queries. The scarcity of real-world short queries paired with ground-truth Mathlib statements makes this ambiguity even more intractable. We argue that this is essentially a data problem. Through adversarial training, we scale up the generation of labeled short and ambiguous queries, and learn to disambiguate user queries at both model-level fine-tuning and input-level query rewriting. On the human-curated MathlibQR benchmark, our Lean Finder V2 sets a new state of the art, with at least 11% relative improvement over the previous best Mathlib semantic search engines. On top of our state-of-the-art retriever, optimized query rewriting further improves MathlibQR retrieval. On unlabeled queries from human and coding-agent interactions, Lean Finder V2 is ranked as the strongest system. Integrated with Claude Code, Lean Finder V2 improves proof success on downstream theorem-proving task. Lean Finder V2 is available at: https://leanfinder.github.io/
papers.summary: Mathematicians and coding agents usually search the `Mathlib` library of formal mathematics for the theorem prover `Lean` with short, ambiguous queries such as a property, a notation, or an alias. Existing search engines assume detailed, context-rich queries instead. `Lean Finder V2` treats this as a data problem: it uses adversarial training to generate large amounts of labeled short queries, then disambiguates queries both by fine-tuning the retriever and by rewriting queries at input time. On the human-curated `MathlibQR` benchmark it sets a new state of the art with **at least 11% relative improvement over the previous best Mathlib search engines**. When integrated with `Claude Code`, it also improves proof success on a downstream theorem-proving task.

papers.title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits
papers.abstract:
Reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood. In particular, the effects of two design choices remain unclear: Does access to the teacher's full action distribution provide an advantage over observing only the probability it assigns to the sampled action? Must training trajectories come from the student (online distillation), or can teacher-generated trajectories (offline distillation) suffice? Our work takes a first step toward understanding the theory underlying these questions.
  We study the sample complexity of online reverse-KL distillation under two feedback models: the teacher reveals either its full action distribution or only the probability of the student-generated action. We establish minimax bounds for the former and show that substantially more data may be required for the latter. In contrast, offline reverse-KL distillation can attain the same minimax rate whether the teacher reveals its full distribution or only its probability of the teacher-generated action. The key distinction is that teacher-generated actions themselves reveal the teacher's preferences, while queries at student-selected actions can leave those preferences unobserved. This highlights an additional statistical challenge for online distillation compared to offline distillation.
  These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories. We develop trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques together with policy-space learning to achieve optimal online distillation guarantees.
papers.summary: Reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation is widely used to train language models, but its statistical properties are poorly understood. The authors analyze sample complexity in two settings: online distillation on student-generated trajectories and offline distillation on teacher-generated ones, each with either the teacher's full action distribution or only the probability of a single sampled action. They prove minimax bounds and show that **online distillation with only sampled-action probabilities may need substantially more data**, whereas offline distillation reaches the same rate under either feedback model, because teacher-chosen actions themselves reveal the teacher's preferences. They also show that common online objectives can fail, and they propose trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques that achieve optimal online guarantees.

papers.title: Bifurcations from Weight Space: JEPAWG on Parametric Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract:
Trained network weights are increasingly treated as data, but there is rarely ground truth about what a population of models should encode, which hampers systematic validation of weight-space methods. This makes parametric dynamical systems a natural test-bed: the dynamics change qualitatively at submanifolds of parameter space that are, in well-studied families, known analytically or numerically. Fine-tuning a forecasting network at each point of a parameter grid yields a model zoo indexed by a physical parameter, against which weight-space diagnostics can be checked.
  We build such model zoos for four dynamical systems and analyse them with JEPAWG, a recently proposed joint-embedding hypernetwork built around a learned parameter--weight representation. It was first introduced for neural samplers for lattice field theories, where its latent geometry located the phase transition and estimated the 2D Ising critical exponent. Applied to dynamical systems, JEPAWG is competitive on forecasting with a hypernetwork trained directly for that task, despite being supervised on the parameter--weight correspondence rather than on forecasts. Beyond forecasting, the norm of the parameter-derivative of the decoded weights locates Hopf points and curves, tracks a period-doubling cascade closely enough to give a qualitative estimate of the Feigenbaum constant, and detects a global bifurcation, which has no eigenvalue signature and is therefore invisible to linearisation. As such, JEPAWG provides interpretable insight into the dynamics that is not available from other hypernetworks. Together, these results indicate that JEPAWG is a workable instrument for reading physical structure off a population of trained networks.
papers.summary: Weight-space methods treat trained networks as data, but there is rarely ground truth for checking what such methods recover. Parametric dynamical systems provide one, because their qualitative behavior changes at known bifurcations. The authors build zoos of forecasting networks fine-tuned at each point of a parameter grid for four dynamical systems and analyze them with `JEPAWG`, a joint-embedding hypernetwork. `JEPAWG` forecasts about as well as a hypernetwork trained directly for forecasting. Its parameter derivatives of the decoded weights **locate Hopf bifurcations, track a period-doubling cascade well enough to roughly estimate the Feigenbaum constant, and detect a global bifurcation that linearization cannot see**.

papers.title: ADAPT for Science: A Multi-Agent System for Self-Evolving Scientific Optimization
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery often requires identifying a small number of high-performing designs in vast, constrained search spaces. This is difficult when evaluations are costly, feasible solutions are sparse, parameters are strongly coupled, and physical constraints are strict. Recent AI for AI methods can automatically improve algorithms and optimization procedures. However, general purpose approaches are not designed around scientific priors, physical constraints, and limited evaluation budgets. We introduce ADAPT for Science, a multi-agent framework that treats scientific optimization as two coupled decisions: where to search and how to search. ADAPT uses historical designs to identify promising and diverse initial conditions, progressively concentrates computation on favorable search directions, and evolves the optimization procedure from execution feedback. We evaluate ADAPT on the design of gravitational wave detectors using a differentiable physics simulator and eight unseen detector topologies. Under matched scientific evaluation budgets, ADAPT achieves a mean loss of 0.204 +/- 0.101, reducing loss by 54.9% relative to the best classical optimizer and by 62.2% relative to the best general purpose agentic evolution baseline. ADAPT achieves the lowest loss on all unseen topologies among the evaluated baselines. ADAPT provides a step toward scientific optimization systems that continuously learn from prior experience and their own search outcomes.
papers.summary: Scientific design problems involve costly evaluations, sparse feasible solutions, and strict physical constraints, which general-purpose agentic evolution methods are not built to handle. `ADAPT for Science` is a multi-agent framework that splits optimization into deciding where to search, by seeding from diverse promising historical designs, and how to search, by evolving the optimization procedure from execution feedback. On gravitational-wave detector design with a differentiable physics simulator and eight unseen detector topologies, it reaches a mean loss of 0.204 under matched evaluation budgets. That is **54.9% lower than the best classical optimizer and 62.2% lower than the best general-purpose agentic evolution baseline**, and it has the lowest loss on every topology.

papers.title: Training Mixed-Monotone Neural Networks for Verification Without Set Propagation
papers.abstract: Most formal verification approaches for neural networks conservatively enclose the output set of the neural network. However, computing a tight output enclosure is in general computationally hard. We sidestep this challenge with a novel neural network architecture that realizes mixed-monotone functions as the difference of monotone subnetworks. By utilizing the theory on mixed-monotone systems, this reduces the computation of a tight output enclosure from complicated set propagation to two simple forward passes of opposite corners of an input interval. Moreover, because the size of the resulting enclosure is a closed-form function of the weights of the neural network, we can directly minimize it during training. We prove a lower bound on the size of any such enclosure, given by the total variation of the represented function generalized to several inputs, which makes it possible to compare the tightness of the enclosure against the optimum. Our evaluation on regression and dynamical-system benchmarks demonstrates that our training reduces the enclosure size to within 0.5% of the lower bound without sacrificing prediction accuracy. Computing our enclosure is orders of magnitude faster than CROWN and $\alpha$-CROWN and on deep networks it is also tighter than zonotope propagation and CROWN, while its size exceeds that of $\alpha$-CROWN by only 5.1%.
papers.summary: Formal verification of neural networks usually requires enclosing the network's output set, and computing a tight enclosure is hard in general. The authors propose an architecture that represents mixed-monotone functions as the difference of two monotone subnetworks, so a tight enclosure takes only two forward passes at opposite corners of the input interval. Because the enclosure size is a closed-form function of the weights, it can be minimized directly during training, and the authors prove a lower bound on it based on generalized total variation. On regression and dynamical-system benchmarks, training brings **the enclosure to within 0.5% of the lower bound without hurting accuracy**. Computing it is orders of magnitude faster than `CROWN` and `α-CROWN`, and the result is tighter than `CROWN` and zonotope propagation on deep networks.

papers.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
papers.abstract: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule. For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.
papers.summary: The authors measure how much economic value AI systems produce per unit of energy. They define Net Value per Joule (NVJ), the dollar value of the output minus execution cost divided by energy, and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), expert time saved divided by energy. They evaluate 220 `GDPval` tasks across 44 occupations using five open-weight models served locally on four accelerator types. Occupations with the highest value per task are not always the most energy-efficient: engineering yields more net value per task, but software development yields about 27% more per joule. `GLM 5.2` delivers the most net value per task, while **`Gemma 4 31B` achieves about 2.5 times the NVJ using 23% of the energy**. Hardware choice changes `Qwen3.6-27B`'s NVJ by a factor of 4.32, with `B200` leading.

papers.title: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark
papers.abstract: Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) on conversational speech that mixes Nepali and English suffers from script confusion between Devanagari and Latin and from errors where speakers switch languages. The authors release a benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 hours) and test a two-stage adaptation: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 0.95 hours of synthesized speech, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) with transcription and script rewards. **Synthetic SFT provides most of the gain**, cutting mixed error rate from 23.40% to 21.52% and switch-point error rate from 35.89% to 28.77%. `GRPO` adds only small but statistically significant adjustments, and the auxiliary script reward has no effect because rollouts show almost no variation in script.

papers.title: Direct Forcing: A Single-Stage Training Recipe for Few-Step Autoregressive Text-to-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.
papers.summary: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable low-latency streaming, but training them normally separates causal adaptation from distribution matching into two stages. `Direct Forcing` merges these into a single stage that uses reference videos in two ways. Causal Continuation Alignment learns how a reference history continues, and Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to pull the model's own rollouts toward the distribution of reference videos, with Dynamic Gradient Balancing weighting the two signals. Starting from bidirectional `Wan2.1-1.3B`, it learns **a four-step autoregressive generator in only 250 updates**, scoring 84.63 `VBench` Total without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision.

papers.title: Separate Field Scoring Protects Unused Tools When Agents Pool Tool-Use Experience
papers.abstract: Agents that call tools from a shared catalog can pool what they learn about which tool serves which request. We measure what pooled usage examples do to tool retrieval, reporting separately the held-out tools, for which no agent has usage, and all other tools. Adding usage examples to the index as extra entries for used tools raises Hit@5 (whether a gold tool is in the top five) for those tools and lowers it for held-out tools, by a large margin on two of three catalogs and with both embedders we tested. Giving used tools the same number of equally long entries filled with other tools' text lowers held-out Hit@5 about as much, but gives little or none of the gain. We call our method of scoring usage as its own field SYNAPSE. On StableToolBench, the held-out gold tool appears in its top five more often than with a router that reserves slots for usage (0.785 against 0.683), and this held-out lead holds on all three catalogs with both embedders. This protection persisted when we replaced each tool's usage with other tools' text, and a constant score offset for tools with usage gives similar held-out Hit@5 in most settings. The gain for tools with usage, in contrast, needs usage about the right tool. The router keeps more of the gain on labeled queries on TOUCAN with both embedders and on ToolRet with one, so the better choice depends on the workload. Splitting the usage among ten simulated agents shows that pooling helps exactly as much as giving one agent the same records.
papers.summary: Agents that share a tool catalog can pool usage examples to improve tool retrieval. However, adding those examples as extra index entries raises retrieval of tools that have usage and substantially lowers retrieval of held-out tools that no agent has used yet. `SYNAPSE` avoids this by scoring usage as a separate field. On `StableToolBench`, **held-out gold tools land in the top five 0.785 of the time versus 0.683 for a router that reserves slots for usage**, and this lead holds across three catalogs and two embedders. A reserved-slot router sometimes keeps more of the gain on labeled queries, so the better choice depends on the workload. Splitting usage across ten simulated agents helps exactly as much as giving one agent all the records.

papers.title: MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback
papers.abstract: Mix-policy optimization incorporates off-policy expert data into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop to transcend the capability boundary of on-policy RL. However, existing methods either provide static full-trace guidance that suppresses self-exploration, or adopt expert prefix guidance without correctness guarantees, leading to suboptimal performance or even training collapse. In this paper, we propose MOER, a mix-policy optimization framework that harmonizes expert guidance with self-exploration. MOER injects a decaying expert chain-of-thought prefix into the prompt and lets the model complete the remaining reasoning, with the prefix length progressively annealed to encourage self-exploration. A selective rollback mechanism replaces failed completions with the original full expert trace, guaranteeing the correctness of every off-policy trajectory. Furthermore, a harmonized mix-policy objective optimizes on-policy tokens with a GRPO loss while supervising both expert prefix and completion tokens with a trust-region SFT loss, substantially stabilizing training. Extensive experiments show that MOER achieves the highest average scores in mathematical and general domain reasoning tasks, outperforming all basic and mix-policy baselines, and generalizes consistently across diverse tasks, model scales, and base model categories. Codes are available at https://github.com/CityU-MLO/MOER.
papers.summary: Mixing expert demonstrations into reinforcement learning (RL) for reasoning models can push models past what on-policy RL learns alone. Existing methods either suppress exploration with full expert traces or risk collapse with expert prefixes that may lead to wrong answers. `MOER` adds an expert chain-of-thought prefix to the prompt, shrinks it over training so the model completes more of the reasoning itself, and replaces failed completions with the full expert trace so every off-policy trajectory is correct. It trains on-policy tokens with a `GRPO` loss and expert tokens with a trust-region supervised fine-tuning loss. The authors report **the highest average scores on math and general reasoning benchmarks among all on-policy and mix-policy baselines**, consistent across model scales and model families.

papers.title: One Teacher, Many Views: Reducing Reference Sensitivity in On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a model on its own trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a privileged copy conditioned on a reference solution. Existing methods typically use a single teacher distribution conditioned on the complete reference. We identify a limitation of this formulation: a reference is only one realization of the reasoning process. Although it provides evidence about the answer, it also encodes an ordering, phrasing, and solution path. Full-reference conditioning can therefore produce correct targets that depend excessively on information unavailable to the student at inference. We show that replacing one valid reference with another, while holding the problem and student state fixed, can substantially alter the teacher distribution, a phenomenon we call reference-induced target instability. To address this instability, we introduce Monte Carlo Privileged Distillation (MCPD), which models privileged context as a distribution over partial reference views and distills the marginal teacher distribution. MCPD evaluates the teacher under multiple views and averages the resulting next-token distributions. We show that this probability-space average is the exact target induced by minimizing the expected teacher-to-student KL divergence over privileged views. Across mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, we show that MCPD produces more reference-consistent supervision and consistently improves over full-reference OPSD.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a reasoning model on its own outputs, using token-level targets from a copy of itself that sees a reference solution. The authors show that **swapping one valid reference solution for another can substantially change the teacher's targets**, because the reference also encodes a particular ordering, phrasing, and solution path. Monte Carlo Privileged Distillation (`MCPD`) instead conditions the teacher on multiple partial views of the reference and averages the resulting next-token distributions. The authors prove this average is the exact target for minimizing expected teacher-to-student KL divergence. Across math and science reasoning benchmarks, `MCPD` gives more consistent supervision and outperforms full-reference OPSD.

papers.title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is often credited with teaching reasoning models to say "wait" before reconsidering a step. The authors trace the word through open models' training histories and find that **RL from a base model almost never invents it**: on bases that lack the word, RL substantially raises `MATH-500` accuracy while "wait" stays nearly absent. The marker comes from training data, through mid-training in `OLMo-3` or fine-tuning on reasoning traces, and RL recipes amplify, reshape, or even erase it depending on KL regularization and on whether fine-tuning came first. The authors warn that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning, and that LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics can reverse trends labeled by humans.
papers.highlight_summary:
RL is widely credited with teaching reasoning models to say `wait` before reconsidering a step, but the marker usually comes from training data instead. The authors trace it through the open training histories of 120 model endpoints using label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage, plus an injected-error test, all computed only from sampled outputs on `MATH-500`.
- Zero-RL almost never coins the marker: across **18 runs from 9 marker-free bases** (`Qwen2.5`, `Mistral`, `Qwen3`), accuracy rises by a **median of 42.9 points** while `wait` stays below 0.05 per 1k tokens in **17 of 18**, with `General-Reasoner-Qwen3-4B` (0.29 per 1k) the lone exception.
- The marker arrives with data: in `OLMo-3` it jumps from 0.04 to **4.03 per 1k tokens during mid-training**, and **13 of 14** models fine-tuned on reasoning traces from marker-free bases adopt it.
- When the base already writes `wait`, the released `RL-Zero` recipes (`OLMo-3`, `MiMo`) multiply it (OLMo-3: 4.9 to a peak of **17.0 per 1k**), but KL-free `GRPO` from the same base does not; the authors' `GRPO` recipe even erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning (7.52 per 1k down to zero), and `OLMo-3` RL-Zero erodes the canonical `Wait,` form from 88.9% to 37.5% of uses.
- In the injected-error test, `RL-Zero` makes revision markers a more sensitive but more liberal alarm (d′ from **0.57 to 1.09**, criterion from 0.11 to −0.24), and in a 60-sentence blind audit one LLM judge reversed the human-labelled revision trend (26.0% to 12.9%, against expert consensus of 1.3% to 15.9%).
- The evidence is observational, and each open series is a single training run; all RL runs use 0.5B–32B models trained on English mathematics with outcome rewards, and the measurements capture the word itself rather than the underlying reflective behaviour.

papers.title: Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining
papers.abstract: Large language models trained on data generated by other models can sometimes inherit traits unrelated to that data, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. We study both hard label distillation, where students train on numbers generated by a biased teacher, and on-policy soft label distillation, where students generate the data and the teacher's logits provide the learning signal. Using Pythia, PolyPythia, and DataDecide OLMo models, we find that transfer persists in both settings across differences in weight initialization, pretraining data order, pretraining corpus, model size, and architecture. Across pretraining checkpoints, the ability to transmit a preference and the ability to acquire one develop separately: some checkpoints are more effective teachers but weaker students, and vice versa. Consistent with this distinction, cross-model transfer can be strongly asymmetric in magnitude when teacher and student roles are reversed. To investigate what carries the preference signal, we construct synthetic number sequences that match the teacher's generated number frequencies but have no dependence on the prompt or preceding numbers and find that these still induce substantial transfer in the hard-label setting. In top-$K$ soft-label distillation, removing animal tokens from the loss reduces transfer, although not completely in the same-model setting. In our experiments, soft label distillation produces more consistent transfer with less extensive training than hard label distillation. The growing use of on-policy distillation in model post-training makes this a particularly relevant setting for assessing unintended preference transfer.
papers.summary: Subliminal learning is when a language model trained on another model's outputs picks up traits unrelated to that data, such as a preference for an animal. Using `Pythia`, `PolyPythia`, and `DataDecide` `OLMo` models, the authors show it persists in both hard-label distillation on teacher-generated numbers and on-policy soft-label distillation, across different initializations, data orders, pretraining corpora, model sizes, and architectures. Across pretraining checkpoints, a model's ability to transmit a preference and its ability to acquire one develop separately, so transfer can be strongly asymmetric. **Synthetic number sequences that only match the teacher's number frequencies still induce substantial transfer**, and soft-label distillation transfers more consistently with less training.

papers.title: From Perpetrators' Digital Footprints to Behavioral Communities: An Ontology-Driven Framework for Bengali Cyberbullying Analysis--- FULL VERSION
papers.abstract: Cyberbullying involves behavioral and contextual patterns beyond isolated abusive messages. However, existing approaches remain fragmented across content detection, semantic representation, and network analysis, with limited interpretable perpetrator representations, multi-scale structural modeling, and explanations of behavior-driven similarity and influence propagation. These limitations hinder the identification of persistent perpetrators, characterization of behavioral communities, and assessment of potentially influential users. This paper proposes Ontology-Driven Cyberbullying Behavior and Network Analysis (ODCBNA), a perpetrator-centric framework integrating requirements-driven ontology design, knowledge graph construction, behavioral modeling, community analysis, and influence modeling. Using the Bengali Contextual and Diverse Cyberbullying (BenCoDiC) corpus as a use case, ODCBNA identifies $1{,}063$ users with at least three bullying comments or replies as perpetrators and represents each through a $64$-dimensional behavioral and contextual feature vector. Cosine similarity and $k$-nearest-neighbor modeling produce a weighted network with $27{,}554$ edges. Louvain analysis identifies six communities with a modularity of approximately $0.495$ and $27$ sub-communities. Feature-contribution analysis identifies the Video, Impact, and User Profile groups as the strongest contributors to behavioral similarity and community separation, while contextual dimensions support interpretation. Community-constrained influence analysis shows that IM Greedy achieves small positive gains in all six communities, although different seed-selection methods produce comparable diffusion spreads despite limited seed overlap. These findings provide an interpretable basis for understanding perpetrator behavior, community organization, and potential influence patterns in Bengali online environments.
papers.summary: Cyberbullying analysis tends to treat detecting abusive content, representing its meaning, and analyzing social networks as separate problems. Ontology-Driven Cyberbullying Behavior and Network Analysis (`ODCBNA`) combines them in a perpetrator-centric framework built on an ontology and knowledge graph. On the `BenCoDiC` Bengali corpus, it represents 1,063 repeat perpetrators as 64-dimensional behavioral feature vectors and links them into a similarity network with 27,554 edges. **Louvain community detection finds six communities with modularity of about 0.495**, with video, impact, and user-profile features driving the separation. Influence analysis shows the `IM Greedy` seed-selection method gives small gains in every community.

papers.title: Building Presentation Intelligence for High-Quality Slide Generation
papers.abstract: PowerPoint presentations (PPTs) are a dominant medium for communication across diverse domains, yet high-quality PPT generation still depends heavily on labor-intensive human effort. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for agentic tasks have created both new opportunities and challenges (Chen et al., 2026) for automatic PPT generation. In this work, we present a unified training framework for automatic PPT generation toward presentation intelligence, integrating cross-validated data synthesis, guided teacher enhancement, and verifiable reward optimization. We first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis, with explicit control over both difficulty and validity. We then develop a teacher-enhancement framework grounded in rules and prior knowledge to substantially strengthen the instructional capacity of teacher models. Building on this, we further improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through a mixed-teacher strategy and a lightweight outcome-driven trajectory filtering method. Finally, based on the resulting SFT models, we introduce a suite of verifiable aesthetic metrics together with a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to optimize slide-level visual attributes beyond text-only supervision. Experiments show that our enhanced SFT pipeline improves Qwen-3.6-27B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B by 7.45 and 9.35 points on PresentBench, respectively, surpassing GLM-5.2 while maintaining strong generalization. Reinforcement learning further improves performance across five aesthetic dimensions, compensating for the limitations of SFT in visual refinement. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for high-quality PPT generation.
papers.summary: Generating high-quality PowerPoint slides still requires a lot of human effort. The authors present a training framework for slide generation that combines cross-validated data synthesis with control over difficulty and validity, teacher models strengthened with rules and prior knowledge, mixed-teacher supervised fine-tuning with outcome-based filtering of trajectories, and `GRPO` reinforcement learning on verifiable aesthetic metrics. **Fine-tuning improves `Qwen-3.6-27B` and `Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B` by 7.45 and 9.35 points on `PresentBench`**, surpassing `GLM-5.2`. Reinforcement learning then improves five aesthetic dimensions that text-only supervision cannot reach.

papers.title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.
papers.summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are Bayesian regression models that become harder to optimize as layers are added. The authors instead treat depth as continuous: the latent representation evolves under a stochastic differential equation whose drift has a Gaussian process prior. They propose two versions, `CDGP`, which places a GP prior directly over the drift, and `FlowDGP`, which uses a flow-evolved prior that is cheaper to train. They show that the standard training objective becomes increasingly sensitive as layers are stacked, which residual DGPs only partially fix. On synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks, **`CDGP` and `FlowDGP` outperform both plain and residual DGPs overall**.

papers.title: Equilibria and Learning in Competitive Market Making
papers.abstract: We propose a market-making game played among $N \ge 2$ strategic market makers and a single non-strategic representative trader. In a continuous quote space, standard finite-game arguments do not apply, while non-convex and discontinuous payoffs rule out classical continuous existence results and complicate learning. Nonetheless, we characterize pure-strategy Nash equilibria (PSNEs) and show that at least one PSNE always exists under minimal assumptions on the underlying asset value distribution, and that the equilibrium bid-ask spread widens strictly with asset value volatility. To obtain a tractable learning framework, we discretize prices and, under an additional regularity condition, show that the time-averaged play of no-internal-regret learners approaches the continuous Nash price envelope as the tick size vanishes. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical results through numerical simulations.
papers.summary: The authors model market making as a game among N strategic market makers quoting continuous prices to one non-strategic trader. In this setting, discontinuous, non-convex payoffs rule out standard equilibrium-existence results. They prove that **a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium always exists under minimal assumptions**, and that the equilibrium bid-ask spread widens strictly as the asset's volatility increases. With discretized prices, they show that the time-averaged play of no-internal-regret learners approaches the continuous equilibrium price envelope as the tick size shrinks, and numerical simulations confirm the theory.

papers.title: Parameter Learning in Active Inference via Variational Message Passing
papers.abstract: Active inference casts perception, learning and planning as variational inference, where the Expected Free Energy (EFE) defines the planning objective. Recent work showed that EFE minimization can be written as Variational Free Energy (VFE) minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors, and that the resulting entropy-corrected objective is minimized by sum-product message passing (SP-MP) on modified factor functions. These formulations treat model uncertainty as inference over a finite set of known models. We extend them to planning during learning, where beliefs over the observation and transition parameters $\theta_A$, $\theta_B$ are Dirichlet priors. Closed-form Dirichlet updates are usually obtained by a structured mean-field factorization between parameters and states, but under exactly that factorization the information-gain corrections vanish. We resolve this by giving every factor its own parameter prior, frozen during a rollout. Conjugacy then makes each factor belief a product of a marginal over the categorical variables and a one-step Bayes posterior of the parameters. This reintroduces the datum-dependent parameter posteriors that mean-field factorization destroys. We show that evaluating the epistemic priors under the resulting Bethe joint recovers the information gains. Stationarity of this single closed-form objective yields SP-MP whose factor functions are augmented by the information-gain weight. Experiments on two grid POMDPs, in which only a planner that learns the model finds the safe route, show that the method plans to efficiently learn $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$. It reaches the goal on every episode, whereas SP-MP planners with the same inference update plateau or take the risky route.
papers.summary: Active inference treats perception, learning, and planning as variational inference, and planning minimizes Expected Free Energy (EFE). Earlier message-passing formulations only handled uncertainty over a finite set of known models. The authors extend them to planning while learning Dirichlet beliefs over observation and transition parameters. The standard mean-field factorization makes the information-gain terms vanish, so they give each factor its own parameter prior, held fixed during a rollout, and show this **recovers the information gains within sum-product message passing**. On two grid partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), the planner learns the model efficiently and reaches the goal in every episode, while baselines plateau or take the risky route.

papers.title: Silicon Samples Match the Answers but Not the Respondents
papers.abstract: Silicon sampling generates survey respondents by having a large language model (LLM) answer a survey as a person with given demographic attributes, and the resulting synthetic populations are increasingly used in place of human ones. Existing evaluations focus on individual-answer accuracy, per-question answer distributions, and correlations across questions. None of these compares the respondents themselves, so a generator whose respondents have combinations of answers found in no human respondent can still score well if it reproduces every answer distribution. We propose the respondent coverage gap (RCG), which represents each respondent as a point defined by their complete answer profile and measures how far each human respondent is from the nearest generated one, relative to the distance between human samples. On two US social surveys, all six LLMs we evaluate leave human respondents uncovered, and under our main settings, they fall behind a baseline that samples each answer independently from the human marginals. Across the prompting and inference settings we test, every LLM has a higher RCG than a Gaussian copula fitted to the human data.
papers.summary: Silicon sampling has a large language model (LLM) answer a survey while posing as a person with given demographic attributes, and the synthetic respondents it produces are increasingly used in place of human ones. Standard checks look at individual answers, per-question answer distributions and correlations between questions, so a generator can pass them while producing answer combinations that no real person gives. The authors propose the `respondent coverage gap` (RCG), which treats each respondent's full answer profile as a point and measures how far each human is from the nearest synthetic respondent, relative to the distance between human samples. On two US social surveys, all six LLMs tested leave human respondents uncovered, and in every prompting and inference setting tried, **every LLM has a higher RCG than a Gaussian copula fitted to the human data**. Under the main settings they also do worse than a baseline that samples each answer independently from the human marginals.

papers.title: Beyond Phenotypic Similarity: Relation Refinement and Selective Population Graph Learning for Multimodal Brain Disorder Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Population graph learning supports brain disorder diagnosis by sharing information across subjects. Its effectiveness, however, depends on whether the relationships guiding this exchange are relevant to diagnosis. Similarity in demographic or acquisition attributes does not necessarily indicate diagnostic agreement, and heterogeneous subjects may require different representation updates within the same population graph. We propose PopDRP, a framework that combines diagnosis-guided relation refinement with hierarchical selective state-space learning. Using only training labels, Contrastive Affinity Refinement calibrates attribute-based affinities according to diagnostic agreement. Neural Graph Rectification then refines these relationships using fused functional-connectivity and non-imaging representations, guided by graph reconstruction and dual-view alignment objectives. On the resulting graph, a Selective Pyramid State-Space backbone integrates input-dependent state updates, graph diffusion, and hierarchical pooling and unpooling to learn population representations at multiple resolutions.
