The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models trained with token-level likelihood on radiology reports reward fluent text over getting the diagnoses right, so they can miss findings or invent them. Diagnostic Loss (`DLoss`) is a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective computed on decoder token probabilities. It **pushes supported diagnoses to receive enough probability at some position in the report while suppressing probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses at every position**. Trained on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D models, it improves diagnostic faithfulness on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks while keeping standard text-generation metrics competitive, and it adds no inference cost.

papers.title: A Reality Check of Inference-Time Context Augmentation Methods
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to utilise the context given in the input, resulting in hallucinations or a fallback to parametric knowledge. Context augmentation methods aim to improve model performance by modifying the input, from inserting filler tokens that add computational time to adding relevant content such as elaboration of a context during inference. However, these methods have been evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains, leaving it unclear how they compare and whether they reliably improve performance. In this paper, we present an evaluation framework spanning five methods that differ in how informative the inserted content is and apply them at the sentence level across seven models spanning multiple sizes on three datasets. We find that accuracy gains are not always genuine improvements but undirected perturbations: the methods correct some predictions while breaking others, particularly when the inserted text allows only for more computational time. Our analysis reveals that methods that bring no additional content primarily change model predictions near the decision boundary. Our findings highlight the need to evaluate the reliability of the accuracy gains before adopting them in practice.
papers.summary: Inference-time context augmentation methods change the input to help language models use their context, either by inserting filler tokens that buy extra computation or by adding content such as elaborations. Until now each method has been judged in isolation and only by accuracy gains. The authors compare five such methods across seven models of different sizes and three datasets. They find that **many apparent gains are undirected perturbations that fix some predictions while breaking others**, especially for methods that add no new content, which mainly flip predictions near the decision boundary. They recommend checking how reliable a gain is before adopting such methods.

papers.title: Interpretive Variation and Discourse Structure in Detecting Enthymemes in Controversial Political Discourse
papers.abstract: Enthymemes are arguments that leave a premise or conclusion unstated, and they are a common persuasion device on social media. Because readers must fill in the missing part themselves, they often disagree on whether a text contains one. This paper asks how to detect and evaluate enthymemes when such disagreement is part of the task. On tweets about vaccination and immigration, each labeled by five annotators, F1 stalls around 0.67 for every fine-tuned model we train, regardless of data size, added features or label type. We therefore ask how these models should be evaluated instead, and propose metrics that compare predictions with the full distribution of annotator votes, together with a model that predicts this distribution directly and captures disagreement better at no cost in F1. We then ask what role discourse structure plays. Models learn to rely on explicit argumentative structure: they reliably recognize tweets without an enthymeme but rarely commit on tweets that contain one. Both the models and a discourse parser miss arguments whose links are left implicit and must be inferred by the reader. Finally, we discuss what these blind spots mean for content moderation systems trained on majority labels.
papers.summary: Enthymemes are arguments with an unstated premise or conclusion, and annotators often disagree about whether a given text contains one. On vaccination and immigration tweets labeled by five annotators each, **every fine-tuned model plateaus at about 0.67 F1** regardless of data size, added features or label type. The authors propose metrics that compare predictions with the full distribution of annotator votes, along with a model that predicts that distribution directly. Their analysis shows that models depend on explicit argumentative structure and miss arguments whose links the reader must infer, a blind spot with implications for content moderation trained on majority labels.

papers.title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents
papers.abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.
papers.summary: Personal agents must use a user's long interaction history both to decide what outside knowledge a request needs and to apply that knowledge to the user's situation. `ColaBench` is a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living with 349 tasks, 10 user profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. An evidence graph links each answer requirement to personal disclosures and to the documents that support it. The accompanying `MemKB` method uses state summaries and memory-document links and **reaches 86.25% accuracy with about four interaction rounds per task**. Errors come mostly from unsupported assumptions about the user and from misapplied rules.

papers.title: EEG-Captioner: Grounding EEG-to-Language Generation in Fundamental Signal Properties
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-to-language models offer a promising approach for translating complex neural signals into human-readable descriptions. However, generating plausible language does not necessarily demonstrate that a model has learned to interpret the underlying EEG signal. A direct way to assess such interpretation is to probe objectively measurable properties of the signal itself. We therefore construct an EEG-language dataset of 160,781 segments annotated with signal-level question answering (QA) pairs, where each question targets one of five property families and requires a quantitative comparison involving spectral, spatial, temporal, or lateral signal properties. Each segment is also paired with a feature-grounded EEG caption. We further propose a Dual-Domain EEG Encoder that jointly models temporal waveforms and spectral-spatial representations, and introduce EEG-Captioner, a unified EEG-to-language framework trained with both signal-level QA and EEG caption supervision. Experiments show that the proposed encoder achieves the highest overall macro-averaged balanced accuracy (Macro-BA) among the compared EEG encoders, while EEG-Captioner achieves a Macro-BA of 88.81% on signal-level QA and improves caption factual consistency from 82.06% to 83.46% over caption-only language adaptation, demonstrating the complementary benefits of signal-level QA and caption supervision.
papers.summary: Fluent text from electroencephalography (EEG)-to-language models does not show that they have actually interpreted the brain signal. The authors build a dataset of 160,781 EEG segments with question-answer pairs that probe objectively measurable spectral, spatial, temporal and lateral properties of the signal, plus a feature-grounded caption for each segment. They also propose a dual-domain encoder that models raw waveforms and spectral-spatial features together. Their `EEG-Captioner` framework, trained on both question answering and captions, **reaches 88.81% macro-averaged balanced accuracy on signal-level questions** and slightly improves the factual consistency of its captions.

papers.title: Padding to k: A Minimum Count in the Schema Makes Open-Weight Models Pad Their Extraction Lists
papers.abstract: Extraction pipelines ask language models for JSON that follows a schema, and the schema can set a minimum number of list entries. We ask what models do when the document holds fewer items than that minimum. Under a preregistered plan, we test eight open-weight models on 558 real documents from nine annotated datasets, with six more models on hosted services as a reference. Three findings stand out. First, models treat the count as a target: a minimum shown in the schema, but not enforced, raises the share of lists longer than the true count from 34.5% to 55.4%. Second, the padding is hard to catch, because most added entries are real text taken from the document; about half of them pass a check that each entry occurs in the source. Third, common fixes help only partly: a line saying fewer items are fine removes the effect on average but misses more true items, a count in prose ("up to k") also raises over-counting, an "N/A" option under an enforced minimum still leaves half the lists padded, and re-asking with the validation error makes padding far more common. We release the code, answer lists and run records at https://github.com/AbhishekBarali/padding-to-k
papers.summary: Extraction pipelines often ask language models for JSON that follows a schema, and the schema can set a minimum number of list entries. In a preregistered study of eight open-weight models on 558 real documents, the authors find that models treat that minimum as a target. **Showing an unenforced minimum raises the share of over-long lists from 34.5% to 55.4%**, and about half of the padded entries are real text from the document that passes source-occurrence checks. Common fixes help only partly, and re-prompting a model with the validation error makes padding much more common.

papers.title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
papers.abstract:
Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering.
  Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-\delta)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $\delta$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.
papers.summary: When AI assistants place sponsored ads inside their answers, an ad's click rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This makes truthful bidding hard to guarantee. The authors propose click thinning, which omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's click probability no longer depends on ad order. Welfare maximization then reduces to a matching problem solved with VCG-style payments. The resulting mechanism is **truthful in expectation and reaches at least half the optimal welfare**, with a sharper approximation factor that they prove is the best any order-preserving rule can achieve.

papers.title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.
papers.summary: Existing datasets for analyzing cybersecurity logs with large language models (LLMs) are small, draw evidence from a single source, and label only the attack type without annotating the reasoning behind it. `SecLog-Bench` addresses this with an extensible simulation platform covering 29 attack scenarios. The platform generates logs from multiple sources (audit logs, application logs, and network traffic) labeled with attack stages, and each sample is annotated with essential context and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. Across eight mainstream LLMs asked to reason about how far an attack has progressed, the best model reaches **only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1** even when given scaffolded evidence. The best Stage Reasoning F1 is 54.87%, and correct predictions often rest on flawed reasoning.

papers.title: Agri-SCHOLAR: Simulation-Grounded In-Season Rolling Advisories for Agricultural Crops Using LLM-Bounded Optimization
papers.abstract: Existing agricultural advisories to farmers suffer from several limitations: (a) remain largely expert-driven, (b) do not adequately account for in-season weather, and (c) do not scale to individual farms. In this paper, our objective is to close these gaps by developing Agri-SCHOLAR (Simulation-Grounded Crop Harvest Optimization with LLM-Guided In-Season Advisory Rollouts). Agri-SCHOLAR is a rolling, in-season advisory framework that issues, at intervals of every few days or every week, a personalized advisory using the following information: soil and crop properties, observed weather to date, short-range forecast of weather, and a season extrapolation of weather based on historical analogs. The novelty and depth of Agri-SCHOLAR lies in each advisory being produced by a closed-loop system which couples multiple LLM agents with a powerful crop simulator (such as APSIM in our case). The simulator crucially serves as an evaluation oracle. In Agri-SCHOLAR, the LLM agents propose agronomically sound and feasible bounds on actionable parameters and an optimizer searches within those bounds against a multi-objective reward spanning yield, resource utilization, and economic feasibility. We conduct a detailed 11-year analysis of the maize crop in two selected locations of South Asia and show that Agri-SCHOLAR consistently outperforms the region's standard packages of practice and satisfactorily addresses the limitations of existing agricultural advisories.
papers.summary: Agricultural advisories for farmers tend to be expert-driven, ignore in-season weather, and do not scale to individual farms. `Agri-SCHOLAR` issues personalized rolling advisories every few days or weekly by coupling multiple LLM agents with the `APSIM` crop simulator, which serves as an evaluation oracle. The agents propose agronomically sound bounds on actionable parameters, and an optimizer searches within those bounds against a multi-objective reward covering yield, resource use, and economic feasibility. In an 11-year study of maize at two South Asian locations, the system **consistently outperforms the region's standard packages of practice**.

papers.title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
papers.abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA
papers.summary: The authors identify a failure mode in long-text image-text alignment that they call saliency collapse: models over-rely on text describing visually prominent content and underuse the rest of the description, so retrieval degrades sharply when salient content is reduced. `RoSA` is a fine-tuning framework that splits image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views. It pairs object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition and uses auxiliary objectives to align the views. It **greatly improves long-text retrieval and robustness to saliency collapse** across benchmarks, and its auxiliary objectives add consistent gains when plugged into existing tuning methods.

papers.title: Evaluating Artificial Wisdom (AW): A Trajectory-Based Framework for Context-Sensitive Decision Regulation
papers.abstract: Capability benchmarks measure what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations remain appropriate as decision conditions change. This paper proposes a trajectory-based measurement framework and prospective validation protocol for artificial wisdom, defined behaviorally as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. Versioned reference specifications determine admissible responses and transition materiality before evaluation. Seven stage-level criteria assess judgment under current conditions, while two transition components assess material-update adequacy and commitment-preserving stability. Stability requires prior adequacy; switching within registered commitment classes is permitted, and persistent error earns no stability credit. A nine-component profile is primary, with a secondary bottleneck score and separate critical-failure reporting. Three simplified simulations examine precision, bottleneck estimation, and sensitivity to model-family count. A single-criterion simulation met its precision criteria at 24 scenarios per domain. Near a bottleneck tie, the estimated minimum had a downward bias of 0.55 points at that size. A simplified incremental-prediction simulation detected a Brier improvement of 0.027 with probabilities of .508 and .742 using eight and twelve families, respectively; it does not establish power for the operational protocol. An exploratory predecessor-rubric study comprising 71 evaluation records illustrates aggregation sensitivity but does not validate the proposed instrument. The twelve-family target remains provisional pending feasibility assessment and calibration of the complete analysis. Whether the profile predicts independent decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open empirical question.
papers.summary: Capability benchmarks show what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations stay appropriate as decision conditions change. The authors propose a trajectory-based framework for measuring "artificial wisdom," defined as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. It scores responses with seven stage-level criteria and two transition components (adequacy of updates when conditions change, and stability of prior commitments), which combine into a nine-component profile. Simplified simulations suggest **24 scenarios per domain** meet precision criteria for a single criterion, but the authors stress that the full protocol is not yet validated. Whether the profile predicts real decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open question.

papers.title: Multi-Tool Selection for Robotic Systems: Comparing Semantic Retrieval and LLM
papers.abstract: Natural-language interfaces allow users to command robotic systems without interacting directly with mission planners or robotics middleware. Their reliable use depends on robot tool routing, defined here as the selection of the smallest complete subset of predefined executable capabilities required to satisfy a request. This task is particularly difficult for compound instructions, where incomplete selection may omit necessary sensing or monitoring capabilities, while excessive selection may expose irrelevant tools. We compare four routing strategies: three progressively refined ChromaDB-based methods - fixed-threshold retrieval, relative-distance retrieval, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval - and a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter language-model baseline. The methods are evaluated on 164 manually annotated prompts organised into three complexity levels, from direct single-tool requests to compound requests requiring at least three tools. Using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency, CDB-v3 achieves the best macro-average score among the retrieval-only methods, with 0.7822, compared with 0.8869 for the large-model baseline. Although the LLM provides higher routing quality, CDB-v3 exhibits substantially lower latency and can be deployed locally without requiring cloud connectivity. These results identify a quality-latency trade-off between direct large-model selection and clause-aware semantic retrieval for privacy-sensitive, connectivity-constrained, and resource-constrained robotic systems.
papers.summary: Natural-language control of robots requires tool routing, which means picking the smallest complete set of predefined capabilities a request needs; this is hard for compound instructions. Three increasingly refined retrieval strategies built on `ChromaDB` (fixed-threshold, relative-distance, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval) are compared against a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter LLM on 164 annotated prompts at three complexity levels. The clause-aware method `CDB-v3` scores **0.7822 versus 0.8869 for the LLM baseline** on a completeness-weighted composite. However, it has much lower latency and can run locally without cloud connectivity, which makes this a quality-latency trade-off for resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive robots.

papers.title: XALIGN: A Human-centric Visual Analytics Approach to Understanding AI Explanations
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods are usually evaluated for technical properties such as faithfulness and robustness. In high-stakes application domains, experts also need to check model predictions against established knowledge. Different explanation methods often disagree, and this disagreement is hard to see when each method is inspected separately. We propose XALIGN, a visual analytics workflow and interface that shows rule-based explanations and several feature attribution methods (TreeSHAP, KernelSHAP, and LIME) side by side for the same Random Forest model. Agreements and contradictions between the methods become visible signals that users can explore and compare with domain knowledge. We apply XALIGN in two case studies: the German Credit dataset and a meteorological dataset, in which events derived from ICON model output and Cloudnet observations are classified. In both, the views reveal discrepancies between the rule-based explanation and the attribution methods that a single method would not show. In an expert evaluation with three specialists, participants found XALIGN useful for identifying influential features and for avoiding over-trust in predictions. Linking rules to attributions was harder for the participant without an XAI background.
papers.summary: Different explainable AI (XAI) methods often disagree, and the disagreement is hard to spot when each method is inspected on its own. `XALIGN` is a visual analytics interface that shows rule-based explanations alongside `TreeSHAP`, `KernelSHAP`, and `LIME` attributions for the same Random Forest model, so agreements and contradictions are visible and can be checked against domain knowledge. Case studies on the `German Credit` dataset and a meteorological dataset **reveal discrepancies that any single method would hide**. In an evaluation with three experts, participants found the tool useful for avoiding over-trust in predictions, though linking rules to attributions was harder for the participant without an XAI background.

papers.title: Mostly Reading: What Open-Book Scores Measure in Document-Level LoRA Adapters
papers.abstract: Single-document LoRA adapters have been proposed as units of knowledge to be merged and retrieved; yet open-book scoring, with the document in the prompt, can credit a document's own adapter (its specialist) for reading that document as readily as for holding it. Training one adapter for each of 150 Wikipedia articles on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that open-book scores mostly measure a reading behaviour every adapter shares: a random adapter trained on another document recovers 82 % of the specialist's open-book advantage over the base model but only 2 % of its advantage on a cloze probe that asks for the same document's facts without providing the source text, a share we cannot distinguish from zero. Content does reach the weights, since the specialists beat the base model in cloze recall by 0.094, and the geometry of their updates follows the documents they read; yet, in a test of 30 queries, adapters chosen by weight-space proximity or text embedding are not distinguishable from random ones on either probe, although that test cannot exclude an advantage of about four fifths of what a query's own adapter gains over a random one. At 16 documents or more, correctly scaled merges recover 87 % to 89 % of the specialists' open-book advantage but only 12 % to 16 % of their cloze advantage, with intervals that run from below zero to at most 32 %, against 94 % for joint training.We also report four silent errors, each of which produced a clean, wrong result.
papers.summary: Single-document LoRA adapters have been proposed as mergeable, retrievable units of knowledge, but open-book evaluation (with the document in the prompt) cannot tell whether an adapter holds a document's content or simply reads it well. With one adapter per Wikipedia article for 150 articles on `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, a random adapter trained on a different document **recovers 82% of a specialist's open-book advantage but only 2% of its advantage on a closed-book cloze probe**. Content does reach the weights, but selecting adapters by weight-space proximity or text embedding is indistinguishable from random selection. Merges of 16 or more adapters keep most of the open-book gain but little of the cloze gain. The authors also document four silent errors that each produced clean but wrong results.

papers.title: Chunk Recomputation under Real Document Revisions: Measuring Update Cost and Retrieval Quality of Fixed, Recursive, and Content-Defined Chunking
papers.abstract: Chunking strategies for retrieval-augmented generation are almost always evaluated on a static snapshot, yet the documents underlying a knowledge base continue to change. Because chunks are embedded independently, a boundary that moves after an edit forces unchanged text to be re-embedded. We measure this update cost on 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions for three stateless chunkers (non-overlapping fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking) under a strict byte-identical reuse rule and a frozen dense encoder. On the 116-article common-success pool, with frozen, length-calibrated parameters, fixed-size chunking recomputes 57-68% of its full new-version embedding-input workload, recursive chunking 38-56%, and content-defined chunking 43-54% (it failed on 4 of 62 Chinese articles), while at these parameters mean evidence recall under a fixed 2048-token retrieval budget differs by less than two percentage points within either language. A cost-only parameter grid shows that the ranking of the two content-aware chunkers changes with chunk-length settings, whereas non-overlapping fixed-size chunking has the highest recomputation cost in every length-matched condition. Controlled edits and a verbatim-presence diagnostic support boundary drift as one contributor to recomputation of text already present in the previous version. Update cost is therefore a substantial, parameter-sensitive dimension that static retrieval evaluations do not expose and that should be reported alongside retrieval quality.
papers.summary: Chunking strategies for retrieval-augmented generation are usually evaluated on static snapshots, yet when a document is edited, shifted chunk boundaries force unchanged text to be re-embedded. Using 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions, the authors measure this update cost for fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking. **Fixed-size chunking recomputes 57-68% of the new version's embedding workload**, compared with 38-56% for recursive and 43-54% for content-defined chunking, while retrieval recall differs by under two percentage points. Fixed-size chunking is the most expensive in every length-matched setting, and the ranking between the two content-aware chunkers shifts with chunk-length parameters.

papers.title: NN-Based Transistor Modeling for Ultra-Fast SPICE Simulation and Standard Cell Library Characterization
papers.abstract: Neural network (NN)-based transistor models have proven to be a promising solution to accelerate device modeling. Although these models demonstrated remarkable speedup in circuit simulations, they were not rigorously tested in complex tasks within standard EDA tool flows for chip design, which require very high transistor model precision to provide accurate results and converge properly. To investigate their full potential and promise, we develop NN-based transistor models that accurately predict the drain current and various charges for a 3nm nanosheet, and employ the models for a standard cell library characterization. This enables us to evaluate the accuracy and speedup under a very wide range of SPICE simulations, benchmarking our models against an industry-standard implementation. Since standard cell library characterization involves thousands of SPICE simulations, it serves as a great benchmark for transistor model quality and consistency. To further evaluate model accuracy, we also perform analog- and digital-level simulations for various complex circuits. Our experiments reveal that NN-based models are a valid alternative to existing transistor compact models, capable of producing accurate delay and power estimates with a much higher speed and convergence time compared to the conventional Verilog-A-based industry-standard (BSIM-CMG) transistor compact model. Our NNs achieve sub-0.11% and 0.76% errors for delay and total power evaluation on a wide range of circuits, while taking up to 8 times less time during the standard cell library characterization. Additionally, we provide comprehensive information and guidance on NN accuracy, unveiling the relationship between NN size and its effect on circuit simulation precision.
papers.summary: Neural network transistor models speed up circuit simulation, but they had not been rigorously tested in the demanding, precision-sensitive flows used in chip design. The authors build neural network models of drain current and charges for a 3nm nanosheet transistor and use them for full standard cell library characterization and for analog and digital circuit simulations, benchmarking against the industry-standard `BSIM-CMG` Verilog-A model. The models achieve **under 0.11% delay error and 0.76% total power error while running up to 8 times faster** during characterization. The paper also gives guidance on how network size affects simulation precision.

papers.title: CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU
papers.abstract: Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data. We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, CAKE's aggregated results achieve $100\%$ case pass rate on the standard set (1,060/1,060) and $98.28\%$ on the hidden set (4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an average performance speedup of $1.334\times$ over the baseline. Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts aggregate device time by $46.6\%$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves the mean roofline gap. These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.
papers.summary: AI agents approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks but struggle to write `AscendC` kernels for Huawei's Ascend NPUs, likely because little training data exists for them. `CAKE` is an agentic system that combines adaptive routing across multiple domain-specific languages, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through a curated knowledge base (`CAKE Book`) and a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 `CANN-Bench v1.1` operators it passes **100% of standard cases and 98.28% of hidden cases**, with an average 1.334x speedup over the baseline. The Evolution mode cut aggregate device time for one fused operator by 46.6% over 20 rounds.

papers.title: Multichoice Modeling: Exploring Decision Configuration Space under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Decision support has become sophisticated at exploring uncertainty, but much less so at representing the architecture of the decision itself. As a result, the decision space is often narrowed before uncertainty is analyzed, leaving interactions among choices and the effects of alternatives they imply largely invisible. This paper introduces multichoice modeling, a framework for making large decision configuration spaces explicit and computationally explorable under uncertainty. Drawing on the logic of rugged landscapes, we conceptualize such problems as contingent performance landscapes, where interdependent choices generate configuration-specific outcomes whose value changes across uncertain futures. The computational framework combines multidimensional decision and uncertainty spaces in a single simulation. Further, variance-based sensitivity analysis is used for identifying influential choices, and conditional distribution analysis for comparing configuration-specific performance profiles. We demonstrate the framework through three case studies: a manufacturing process upgrade, M&A strategy, and mortgage design. By contrasting conventional uncertainty-only analysis with multichoice modeling, the cases show how opening the decision configuration space can reveal unexpected complementarities, near-best configurations with different risk profiles, and strategies that were not apparent as alternatives at the outset.
papers.summary: Decision-support tools are good at exploring uncertainty but often narrow the set of choices before analysis begins, which hides interactions between choices. Multichoice modeling treats such problems as rugged performance landscapes: it simulates large spaces of interdependent decision configurations together with uncertain futures, then uses variance-based sensitivity analysis and conditional distribution analysis to find influential choices. Case studies on a manufacturing upgrade, M&A strategy, and mortgage design show that opening up the configuration space **reveals complementarities and near-best alternatives with different risk profiles** that uncertainty-only analysis misses.

papers.title: Algorithmic drift in generative adaptive learning
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence promises to democratize personalized tutoring, yet the longitudinal stability of adaptive systems remains under-theorized. Current ethical discourse focuses on static bias. This paper argues that a distinct threat lies in algorithmic drift: a feedback loop in which minor, demographically asymmetric observation errors compound over time into systemic inequities. We make three contributions. First, we formalize algorithmic drift as a coupled learner--tutor dynamical system. Second, we corroborate this theory with an agent-based Monte Carlo simulation in which either a transparent online tracker or an LSTM deep-knowledge-tracing network drives an IRT-based curriculum policy. Third, we introduce the temporal fairness stabilizer (TFS), a targeted intervention that periodically re-probes learner capability, and benchmark it against standard exploration baselines with explicit group-fairness metrics and replication-level inference. Within the modeled environment, TFS closes the achievement gap where generic exploration does not, and we characterize the conditions under which it succeeds. We separate what is established analytically, what is demonstrated in simulation, and what remains to be validated with real learners. Our results reframe algorithmic fairness in education as a temporal property of a closed loop rather than a deployment-time checkbox.
papers.summary: Ethics discussions of generative AI tutors focus on static bias, but the authors argue that small observation errors that differ across demographic groups can compound over time into systemic inequity, a feedback loop they call algorithmic drift. They formalize drift as a coupled learner-tutor dynamical system and reproduce it in agent-based Monte Carlo simulations. In these simulations, either a transparent online tracker or an `LSTM` deep knowledge-tracing network drives a curriculum policy based on item response theory (IRT). A proposed temporal fairness stabilizer, which periodically re-probes learner ability, **closes the achievement gap where generic exploration does not**, though only within the simulated environment.

papers.title: Conflict-Aware Logit Adapters for Utility-Preserving Anti-Distillation
papers.abstract: While reasoning traces improve model capability, they also provide supervision signals for downstream distillation. Initial efforts to mitigate this issue rely on decoding-time interventions, but they incur high inference overhead and can harm the teacher model's natural fluency. We propose Conflict-Aware Logit Adapters (CALA), a lightweight training-time defense. CALA attaches a small residual adapter to a frozen teacher model and trains only the adapter. A proxy student identifies positions where imitation is most sensitive, and the adapter perturbs the output distribution at these positions while remaining within high-probability regions. A conflict-aware optimization strategy balances anti-distillation and utility objectives, while regularization preserves the teacher's performance and fluency. At inference time, CALA incurs modest overhead and requires no auxiliary model. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that CALA substantially reduces successful student imitation while maintaining near-original teacher performance and generation quality. These results establish CALA as a practical and efficient alternative to decoding-time approaches.
papers.summary: Reasoning traces from a teacher model make it easy for others to distill a student from it, and existing decoding-time defenses are slow and hurt fluency. `CALA` (Conflict-Aware Logit Adapters) trains only a small residual adapter on a frozen teacher. A proxy student identifies the positions where imitation is most sensitive, and the adapter perturbs the output distribution there while staying within high-probability regions. A conflict-aware optimization balances the anti-distillation goal against utility. On reasoning benchmarks it **substantially reduces successful student imitation while keeping near-original teacher performance**, with modest inference overhead and no auxiliary model.

papers.title: Harm Is Behavioural, Moderation Is Lexical: How Language and Culture Decide Whom Automated Safety Systems Protect and Whom They Silence
papers.abstract:
Content warning: this paper quotes slurs and hateful statements from published test suites; the racial slur among them is masked.
  Automated systems decide at scale which messages are harmful, and they decide unevenly. Classifiers label African American English as offensive up to twice as often as other English, the accounts of prominent drag queens can score as more toxic than those of white nationalists, and safety behaviour that holds in English collapses in low-resource languages. We argue that over-flagging and under-protection share one cause: deciding harm from vocabulary and surface form rather than from what a message does. We organise the evidence into seven failure modes and argue, as testable hypotheses, that harmful behaviours (a request for secrecy, a demand for payment, an attempt to isolate someone) travel across languages better than the words that express them. We propose an evaluation protocol that makes the gap between the best- and worst-served language communities a headline result, and show that the naive gap is inflated under equal service and that its usual bootstrap interval is unreliable. Applied to five open systems in eleven languages, from a keyword lexicon to two current multilingual guard models, the protocol finds that none reaches native-speaker accuracy at separating harmful function from harmless form (51 of 55 system-language pairs fall short); that greater capability raises discrimination in nine languages while leaving Arabic and romanised Hindi near chance, so the gap between the best- and worst-served languages grows with capability; that one system both over-flags and under-protects the same language most; and that a language a system reads worst can look the most fairly treated when only false positives are reported.
papers.summary: Automated content moderation both over-flags (labeling African American English as offensive up to twice as often, for example) and under-protects speakers of low-resource languages. The authors argue that both problems share one cause: judging harm by vocabulary rather than by what a message does. They organize the evidence into seven failure modes and propose an evaluation protocol that makes the gap between the best- and worst-served languages a headline metric. Applied to five systems, from a keyword lexicon to multilingual guard models, across eleven languages, **51 of 55 system-language pairs fall short of native-speaker accuracy**. More capable systems widen the gap, leaving Arabic and romanised Hindi near chance.

papers.title: Directing to Diversify: Multi-Directional Search for Automatic Heuristic Design
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong potential to automate heuristic design for NP-hard combinatorial optimization (CO) tasks without human intervention. Recent methods predominantly rely on evolutionary computation (EC) frameworks, where heuristic diversification is mainly induced through EC-like operators or downstream selection, while the direction of heuristic transformation remains largely unharnessed. In this paper, we propose a multi-directional Perturbation-Rewrite Search (PRS) framework for automatic heuristic design that factorizes heuristic transformation through directional search primitives at the generation level. Specifically, PRS operates on heuristic ideas through three complementary directions: expansion toward richer and more expressive designs, compression toward simpler and less specialized designs, and steering for fine-grained refinement, together enabling broader and more sustained exploration of diverse regions in the heuristic design space. PRS further organizes candidate exploration within a breadth-first search-based process with adaptive operator control, which ensures thorough candidate utilization and sustained exploration, and maintains strong search dynamics while preventing premature convergence. Extensive empirical results across diverse CO tasks show that PRS consistently discovers high-quality heuristics, demonstrating the effectiveness and generality of explicitly directional exploration design.
papers.summary: LLM-driven automatic heuristic design for NP-hard combinatorial optimization usually relies on evolutionary operators for diversity and leaves the direction in which heuristics change uncontrolled. `PRS` (Perturbation-Rewrite Search) transforms heuristic ideas along three explicit directions: expansion toward richer designs, compression toward simpler ones, and steering for fine-grained refinement. It runs these within a breadth-first search with adaptive operator control to avoid premature convergence. Across diverse combinatorial optimization tasks, PRS **consistently discovers high-quality heuristics**.

papers.title: Diagnosing the Explicit-to-Applied Theory of Mind Gap in LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in high-stakes roles such as therapy, education, and personal assistance, their social cognition must be assessed reliably. Current Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks report aggregate scores that conflate two distinct competencies: explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) and applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). Building on this distinction, we investigate the gap and its recoverability using four structurally diverse benchmarks. Aggregate reporting obscures uneven competence: on SimpleToM, Llama-3.1-8B scores 51.5 percent overall while recognizing mental states at 99.4 percent and predicting behavior at only 28.9 percent. To assess recovery, we compare structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and our proposed Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters on answered support questions through action reconstruction. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GPT-oss-20B, recovery depends on the model, task, and intervention. On SimpleToM, reminders combined with BSTTT improve Llama's behavior prediction by 40.8 percentage points; reminders account for most of the overall improvement, with BSTTT adding 1.3 to 5.5 points beyond reminders across models. Contextual examples often outperform weight updates, while BSTTT remains stronger in specific model-benchmark settings. Temporal belief tracking remains difficult despite partial recovery. These findings show that aggregate ToM scores can overstate applied competence while hiding performance recoverable through targeted assistance. We recommend decomposed reporting of explicit and applied accuracy alongside intervention comparisons that establish which failures are recoverable and under what conditions.
papers.summary: Aggregate Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmark scores mix explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) with applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). On `SimpleToM`, `Llama-3.1-8B` **recognizes mental states 99.4% of the time but predicts behavior only 28.9% of the time**. The authors compare structured prompting, in-context learning, and a proposed Belief-State Test-Time Training (`BSTTT`) across `Qwen2.5-7B`, `Llama-3.1-8B`, and `GPT-oss-20B`. Reminders plus BSTTT improve Llama's behavior prediction by 40.8 points, most of it from the reminders. The authors recommend reporting explicit and applied accuracy separately.

papers.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs
papers.abstract: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. Additionally, we validate the key components of our method through an ablation study. SCOPE thus enables reliable, interpretable, and efficient policy enforcement at production scale.
papers.summary: Enforcing compound, application-specific policies over multi-turn LLM agent transcripts and tool calls is hard: fine-tuned guardrail models degrade on such policies, and LLM-as-a-judge is costly and unstable. `SCOPE` compiles a natural-language policy into an executable program of neural predicates, run by small models and deterministic extractors and composed by code. The program is optimized jointly with its training data through adversarially generated counterexamples. It achieves the highest average accuracy against prompt-optimization, decomposition, and workflow-generation baselines. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models, which lets **inexpensive models reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models** with more stable and interpretable verdicts.
papers.highlight_summary:
Guardrail models fine-tuned for policy enforcement lose accuracy when a policy combines many conditions, exceptions and counts, while frontier LLM judges are expensive and give inconsistent verdicts across runs. `SCOPE` compiles a natural-language policy into Python code that combines narrow yes/no-style predicates answered by small non-reasoning models with deterministic extractors, and it optimizes this program together with a training pool that grows through adversarially generated counterexamples.

- Strong LLM agents (`Claude Opus 4.8`) run the search: they trace each failure back to a specific predicate or to the composition code and revise it, while two adversaries generate counterexamples aimed at a single predicate ("local") or at the whole program ("systemic"), and a teacher labels each one; a counterexample is kept only when the teacher's label agrees with the adversary's intended label.
- With `gpt-5.4-nano` as the executor, `SCOPE` scores **0.85 / 0.82 / 0.87 / 0.78** on the four benchmark tasks (`Coaching`, `Escalation`, `Plan`, `Tile-match`), beating `GEPA`, `MIPROv2`, `CheckEval` and `RLIE` everywhere, and it ranks first or ties in **10 of 12** task–executor settings, losing the other two to `AFlow` (for example 0.82 vs 0.86 on `Escalation` with `gpt-5.4-nano`).
- Decomposition makes accuracy much less dependent on the executor: moving from the weakest to the strongest executor adds only **0.09** accuracy under `SCOPE` versus **0.26** under prompt optimization, and weaker executors lead the search to split the policy into more predicates.
- Programs compiled for `gpt-5.4-nano` transfer without re-optimization to open-weight models running without reasoning, which gain an average of 0.13–0.22 per model; `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` reaches **0.78 / 0.91 / 0.86 / 0.89** against `gpt-5.5` with high reasoning effort at 0.94 / 0.89 / 0.89 / 0.82, at a fraction of the cost, and only **5–7%** of its `Tile-match` predictions change across five runs compared with **37%** for `gpt-5.5` and **26%** for `gemini-3.1-pro`.
- Removing the adversaries significantly lowers accuracy on three of the four tasks (for example `Plan` drops from 0.865 to 0.813, p=0.005) and has no effect on `Escalation`. Limitations: correctness depends on how the teacher model reads the policy rather than on formal verification, and the benchmark is small, with only four tasks of 163–371 samples each.

papers.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
papers.abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.
papers.summary: Studying how multimodal agents and world models help each other requires measuring action selection and state prediction separately. `Dual Exam` tests agents against fixed environment responses (1,088 items) and world models against fixed action interventions (400 cases), across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. `GPT 6 Astra` leads the agent track with an index of 31.3 and `GPT-Image-2` leads the world-model track at 21.7, though the two scores are not comparable. A 150-case pilot coupling one agent with one world model records **zero task successes**, and results show frequent failures to preserve task-relevant state.

papers.title: Federated Differentially Private Optimization via Low-Rank Preconditioning
papers.abstract: We consider differentially private (DP) optimization in the federated setting, where a DP estimate of the feature covariance matrix serves as a Hessian approximation for generalized linear models. Existing central DP methods for covariance estimation have communication cost that grows quadratically in the data dimension, while existing baselines with linear communication cost are only locally private and degrade as the number of clients increases. As a remedy, we propose a federated DP-PCA framework that achieves linear communication cost while providing central DP guarantees under secure aggregation. It consists of a DP rank selection step, a DP power method, and a noisy release of the covariance projected onto the selected low-dimensional subspace. We give error bounds for this covariance estimate and for the resulting low-communication preconditioned DP gradient descent. Empirically, our proposed DP optimization method matches a centralized baseline with quadratic communication cost at a fraction of the communication.
papers.summary: In federated differentially private (DP) optimization, a DP estimate of the feature covariance can serve as a Hessian approximation for generalized linear models. However, central DP covariance estimation costs communication that grows quadratically with data dimension, and existing linear-cost methods are only locally private. The authors propose a federated DP-PCA (principal component analysis) framework with linear communication and central DP guarantees under secure aggregation. It combines DP rank selection, a DP power method, and a noisy projected covariance release, and the authors prove error bounds for it. The resulting preconditioned DP gradient descent **matches a quadratic-cost centralized baseline at a fraction of the communication**.

papers.title: When Forgotten Facts Return: Relearning-Aware Unlearning of Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Tangent Kernels
papers.abstract: Approximate unlearning answers a deletion request on a knowledge-graph embedding by editing entity embeddings instead of retraining from scratch. These embeddings keep being updated as new facts arrive. Under this ordinary continued training, forgotten facts recover more than in the exact-unlearning baseline, a model retrained without them and given the same continued training. We trace this relearning to entity embeddings shared by forgotten and new facts. To our knowledge, this is the first study of relearning in knowledge-graph embeddings. Relearning-robust methods developed for deep networks do not account for the graph structure underlying this recovery. We propose Kernel-Anticipated Unlearning (KAU), which uses the tangent kernel to model how continued training changes forgotten facts' scores through these shared parameters. KAU expresses this first-order response in closed form and differentiates through it inside the forgetting loss. The objective steers edits toward directions that continued training reverses less. We compare KAU with state-of-the-art knowledge-graph unlearners and relearning-robust methods under identical continued training, measuring leakage beyond the exact-unlearning baseline. Across three backbones, KAU reduces the strongest knowledge-graph unlearner's leakage by 46-63% on FB15k-237 and 50-82% on CoDEx-L, at higher retained utility.
papers.summary: When facts are approximately unlearned from a knowledge-graph embedding and training then continues on new facts, the forgotten facts recover more than they do in a model retrained from scratch without them. The authors trace this relearning to entity embeddings shared between forgotten and new facts. Kernel-Anticipated Unlearning (`KAU`) uses the tangent kernel to model in closed form how continued training will shift forgotten facts' scores, and it steers unlearning edits toward directions that continued training reverses less. Across three backbones, KAU **reduces leakage of the strongest existing unlearner by 46-63% on `FB15k-237` and 50-82% on `CoDEx-L`** while retaining more utility.

papers.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
papers.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. Code: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nninteractive-agent
papers.summary: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as `nnInteractive` can turn a few points, scribbles or boxes into a volumetric mask, but a person still has to find each structure, place the prompts and correct the result. The authors show that general-purpose AI agents can do that work without additional training. They release `nninteractive-agent`, which exposes `nnInteractive` as tools over the Model Context Protocol (`MCP`) along with a skill that encodes how expert users prompt it. On a benchmark of 14 images and 51 targets covering CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant, `Claude Code` and `Codex` reach a **mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from a plain-language request alone**, and they stay accurate on targets where the text-prompted 3D model `VoxTell` fails outright.

papers.title: MQAScore: Fine-Grained Text-Music Alignment Evaluation via Large Audio Language Model
papers.abstract: Text-to-music alignment is commonly evaluated by the global similarity between text and audio embeddings, which collapses all described attributes into a single score and obscures which ones are missing. We instead introduce MQAScore, which verifies each atomic musical concept along five clip-level dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage) by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers affirmatively to a binary question. To assess evaluator reliability, we construct verification labels from presence/absence annotations and LLM-guided concept substitutions, and propose the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator responds to meaning-changing substitutions. Experiments show that concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, and MQAScore can be a more reliable and interpretable fine-grained complement to global similarity for evaluating text-to-music alignment.
papers.summary: Text-to-music alignment is usually measured as the global similarity between a text embedding and an audio embedding, and a single score like that cannot show which described attributes are missing from the music. `MQAScore` breaks a description into atomic musical concepts across five dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal and usage). It scores each concept by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers yes to a binary question about it. The authors also introduce the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator reacts to substitutions that change the meaning. They find that **concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators**, which makes `MQAScore` a more interpretable complement to global similarity.

papers.title: Transformers with CoT Discover Heavy-Ball Acceleration Through Training
papers.abstract: Modern transformers often solve complex tasks by generating and refining intermediate reasoning steps. To develop a theoretical understanding of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, a notable recent study by Huang et al. (2025) viewed transformers as algorithm executors, and showed that when transformers' CoT steps are supervised by a gradient-descent teacher, they can learn to implement gradient descent for in-context weight prediction in linear regression. In this paper, we study the same in-context weight prediction task but ask whether CoT reasoning can go beyond merely imitating the teacher algorithm. We show that, after initial supervision from a gradient-descent teacher, further trajectory-level supervision using the true regression weights leads the model to implement the Heavy-Ball method, thereby achieving acceleration over the original teacher. Notably, this accelerated algorithm emerges without supervision from any Heavy-Ball teacher. Our results provide a concrete theoretical example in which transformer reasoning can discover new algorithms through training, rather than merely imitate the algorithm used for supervision.
papers.summary: Earlier theoretical work showed that transformers whose chain-of-thought (CoT) steps are supervised by a gradient-descent teacher learn to carry out gradient descent for in-context linear regression. This work asks whether CoT reasoning can go beyond imitating its teacher. After initial supervision from gradient descent, the model is given further trajectory-level supervision that uses only the true regression weights. Under that training the model **learns to implement the Heavy-Ball momentum method and converges faster than its teacher**, even though no Heavy-Ball teacher was ever used. The authors present this as a concrete theoretical case of transformer reasoning discovering a new algorithm through training.

papers.title: What Pairwise Evaluation Misses: Reward Scores across Prompts
papers.abstract: Reward models score responses for preference optimization, filtering and ranking, and pooling scores across prompts needs them to be comparable. Yet pairwise evaluation compares two responses to the same prompt, so any score component shared by a prompt's responses cancels and goes untested. We study this component by comparing between-prompt variation in model scores with the same variation in human ratings of the same responses. We propose a human-referenced audit, built from a between-prompt variance share, a sibling-rating regression and prompt substitutions, and apply it to eighteen released scorers and six matched training conditions. We find that scores cluster by prompt more than the ratings do: on HelpSteer2, six reward models have between-prompt shares of 0.34 to 0.64 against a human share near zero. Replacing the original prompt with a fixed instruction keeps substantial clustering but weakens agreement with prompt-level human ratings, so clustering alone does not show agreement with humans. Part of that variation is useful: subtracting prompt means lowers the helpfulness of globally selected responses, and scores stay sensitive to a wrong prompt even when training shuffles prompt means. We propose that reward evaluation check between-prompt variation, sensitivity to a wrong prompt and usefulness for selection separately.
papers.summary: Reward models are normally evaluated pairwise, by comparing two responses to the same prompt, so any part of the score that all of a prompt's responses share cancels out and is never tested. That shared part matters whenever scores are pooled across prompts for filtering or ranking. The authors build a human-referenced audit that combines a between-prompt variance share, a sibling-rating regression and prompt substitutions, and apply it to eighteen released scorers and six matched training conditions. On `HelpSteer2`, **six reward models put 0.34 to 0.64 of their score variance between prompts, while human ratings put close to none there**. Some of that variation is still useful for selecting responses, so the authors recommend checking between-prompt variation, sensitivity to a wrong prompt and usefulness for selection as separate properties.

papers.title: Co-Recursive Semantic Self-Extension: A Mathematical Foundation for Open-Ended Intelligence
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has advanced through scale, data, and computation, yet remains bounded by its representational framework. We ask what makes intelligence open-ended. Every inferential system selects meaningful distinctions, limiting what it can learn. Within a fixed purpose, performance reaches a ceiling set by its semantic domain. Teleological succession, in which purposes arise from earlier ones, faces a similar limit: Boolean-closed purpose-transformations exhaust their reachable semantic territory. We shift from purposes to inferential systems. Drawing on Kant and G\"odel, we model cognitive states as partial evaluations over a formal language. Unresolved propositions may be undecided or undecidable. Reasoning can resolve the former but not the latter, leaving a frontier for extension. Non-trivial reductions of undecidable propositions expose undecidable intermediate premises whose reflective reification supports multiple decisive extensions. Finite trace-guided generation remains fallible, requiring meta-level selection and polycontextural exploration. Using Kolmogorov complexity, we show that no architecture with a fixed state description, transition mechanism, and initial condition can generate histories incorporating irreducible algorithmic information. Because physical systems are fixed in this sense, we examine collectives. Coupling finitely many finite agents does not remove the bound. Extension requires persistent external memory preserving semantic content and historical coordinates. Collective generative capacity depends on balancing overlap for transfer with difference for generation. We propose semantic self-extension as a design principle: intelligence should not merely resolve ambiguity within existing meanings, but transform unresolved structures into new spaces of meaning, generating new distinctions, questions, representations, and purposes.
papers.summary: This is a theoretical account of what would make intelligence open-ended, drawing on Kant, Gödel and Kolmogorov complexity. It models cognitive states as partial evaluations over a formal language, where unresolved propositions are either undecided, which reasoning can settle, or undecidable, which leaves a frontier for extension. The central claim is that **no architecture with a fixed state description, transition mechanism and initial condition can generate histories that contain irreducible algorithmic information**, and that coupling finitely many finite agents does not remove this limit. The author argues that going further requires persistent external memory, and proposes 'semantic self-extension', meaning the creation of new distinctions and purposes, as a design principle.

papers.title: RIFT: KV Cache Compression for Draft Models with Complementary Compressibility Training
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular decode acceleration method. As such, it is particularly relevant to long-output generation, which requires an increasingly large KV cache. KV cache compression offers a way to constrain costs in long-context drafting. However, compression methods that focus on prefill information can lose relevance as the output length grows. We term this phenomenon decode staleness and show that it degrades draft model accuracy under selection-based KV cache compression. We introduce RIFT, a family of selection-based KV cache compression strategies that balance prefill information and recent generated tokens. We show that refreshing the KV cache selection during token generation significantly improves the drafter's quality at the cost of additional decode latency. To alleviate the refresh costs, we propose an adaptive KV refresh strategy that reduces the number of score calculations while retaining the drafter's quality. We further demonstrate how a compressibility-driven drafter training phase, based on sparse attention masks, can improve the drafter's quality under a compressed KV cache. Combined with compressibility training, RIFT enables Qwen3.5-4B, drafting for Qwen3.5-122B, to retain over 98% of its full-cache acceptance length on 32K-token inputs, 4K-token outputs, and an 8K-token KV cache budget.
papers.summary: In speculative decoding with long outputs, the draft model's key-value (KV) cache keeps growing. Compression methods that select entries based on the prompt (the prefill) gradually become less relevant as generation goes on, a problem the authors call 'decode staleness'. `RIFT` is a family of selection-based KV cache compression strategies that balance prefill information against recently generated tokens. It refreshes the selection during decoding, uses an adaptive schedule to cut the cost of those refreshes, and adds a training phase with sparse attention masks so the drafter works better under compression. With `Qwen3.5-4B` drafting for `Qwen3.5-122B` on 32K-token inputs and 4K-token outputs, **an 8K-token cache budget keeps over 98% of the full-cache acceptance length**.

papers.title: Solving Flood-It Puzzles: A Comparison of Tailored A* Search with Declarative Solver Approaches
papers.abstract: We present an optimized approach for finding minimal move sequences to solve Flood-It puzzles using A* search and compare it with approaches using SAT, Integer Programming, and Constraint Programming solvers. The performance of A* search is considerably improved by using an appropriate heuristic and sophisticated equivalences of game states to limit the search space. Each aspect is systematically evaluated, providing insights that generalize to other problems. By comparing the best variant of each approach, the A* search is the fastest in finding a minimal solution in about 75 % of the Flood-It instances tested. This result is in line with our expectation since A* specifically looks for a minimum solution. In contrast, the SAT-based approach is designed to solve the decision problem of whether a solution with a given length exists. An iterative search is required to determine a minimum solution length using a SAT-based approach. However, with increasing complexity, quantified by the minimum solution length, the SAT-based approach outperforms A*. We also compared the different approaches to the decision problem, where A* again performed best for the largest number of puzzles. Here, again, SAT supersedes A* for higher complexities, albeit with a lower crossing point.
papers.summary: The authors look for minimal move sequences that solve Flood-It puzzles. They compare a tailored `A*` search, made faster with a well-chosen heuristic and with equivalences between game states that shrink the search space, against SAT, integer programming and constraint programming solvers. **`A*` finds a minimal solution fastest on about 75% of instances**, but the SAT-based approach overtakes it on harder puzzles with longer minimum solutions. The same crossover appears for the decision version of the problem (whether a solution of a given length exists), where it happens at lower complexity. The authors also evaluate each optimisation separately and argue that the lessons carry over to other search problems.

papers.title: DeepOpen: Decision-Oriented Intent Classification on BANKING77 and CLINC150
papers.abstract: We present DeepOpen, a decision-Oriented intent-classification framework with dataset- specific systems for BANKING77 and CLINC150. On BANKING77, a single English classi- fier continued with sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) achieves 94.1234% test accuracy (2,899/3,080).
