This is the best observed result among three fixed SAM seeds, selected for display after test evaluation; their mean is 94.0368%. On the 150 in-scope CLINC150 classes, probability fusion of one Laya specialist and three DeBERTa-v3-large classifiers achieves 98.0222% (4,411/4,500). We describe the two configurations, reproduce the reference com- parisons displayed in the accompanying evaluation explorer, and separate headline scores from evidence about improvement. Under a uniform BANKING77 evaluation path, the SAM mean exceeds the historical checkpoint by 0.0433 percentage points, with a shared-row 95% interval of [-0.2273, +0.3247]. Thus, the continuation does not establish a reliable accuracy gain. The report documents strong observed task-specific performance, selection effects, and unresolved historical execution-path differences, rather than a new backbone or a unified algorithmic advantage.
papers.summary: `DeepOpen` is a set of intent-classification systems built separately for the `BANKING77` and `CLINC150` datasets. On `BANKING77`, a classifier further trained with sharpness-aware minimization (`SAM`) reaches 94.12% test accuracy at best and 94.04% on average across three seeds. On `CLINC150`, combining the probabilities of one `Laya` specialist and three `DeBERTa-v3-large` classifiers reaches 98.02%. The report is candid about its limits: **the `SAM` gain over the earlier checkpoint is 0.04 percentage points, with a 95% interval that includes zero**, so the authors present strong task-specific scores rather than evidence of a general improvement.

papers.title: Who Is the Influencer? Consensus Dynamics in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used in practice, but their behavior is complex and hard to understand. We design a simple task to ask which model has the most influence on the final consensus when several models are mixed in one system. Experimentally, across seven model families, we find that the opinions of the other models are absorbed into the opinion of the stronger model, the one with more parameters. This happens even though the task requires no pretraining knowledge and has no correct answer. To understand this phenomenon, we interpret the agents as weighted particles moving on a simplex. Larger models carry a larger weight and therefore occupy a deeper well in the energy landscape. A large weight means strong in-context learning: a model with a large weight amplifies the majority of its context. Larger models are generally better at in-context learning, and this is what makes the larger model the influencer. We hope that this work helps to interpret multi-agent systems, whose behavior is becoming too complex for humans to understand.
papers.summary: The authors ask which model sets the final consensus when several different large language models (LLMs) are mixed in one multi-agent system. They use a simple task that needs no pretraining knowledge and has no correct answer. Across seven model families, **the other models' opinions are consistently absorbed into the opinion of the larger model**. To explain this, they model the agents as weighted particles moving on a simplex, where a larger weight corresponds to stronger in-context learning that amplifies the majority of the context and gives a deeper well in the energy landscape. Because larger models are generally better in-context learners, they end up as the influencers.

papers.title: Learning What to Ask for Tomorrow: Active Preference Acquisition for Long-Term Personalized Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents increasingly serve the same user across repeated online tasks such as booking travel, shopping, and scheduling, so their long-term usefulness depends on how well they know the user's preferences. Passive memory and personalization methods cannot obtain preferences the user never reveals, and clarification methods that value a question by its benefit to the current task overlook the benefit of reusing the answer in later tasks. We study Active Preference Acquisition (APA): which missing preferences are worth the cost of asking? We define the Prospective Personalization Value (PPV) of a missing preference as its expected cumulative utility gain over future tasks minus the effort and disclosure-risk cost of asking, and select questions under a per-interaction budget. We characterize when cumulative reuse justifies acquisition despite insufficient single-task benefit, and evaluate this regime with an initial-profile diagnostic. APA computes the counterfactual gain of each candidate preference on public task prototypes with the agent's own task solver and aggregates it by the expected reuse of each task family. We evaluate it on ActiveWebPref, a controlled longitudinal benchmark with hidden but queryable user profiles and exact task utilities. At a horizon of 20 tasks, 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable missing preferences are amortization-dependent; APA acquires 80.3% of them, whereas current-task value of information acquires 5.1%. Under per-user asking-cost caps matched to APA's realized expenditure, APA achieves higher net utility than four heuristic selection baselines. In our cost setting, asking about every unknown preference yields lower net utility than not asking, while APA recovers 84.2% of its utility gain with 27.6% of its questions. The value of acquiring a user preference should account for its reuse across future tasks, not only its benefit to the task at hand.
papers.summary: Web agents that serve the same user across many tasks need to know that user's preferences. Existing clarification methods judge a question only by how much it helps the current task, and so they ignore the value of reusing the answer later. Active Preference Acquisition (`APA`) scores each missing preference by its Prospective Personalization Value: the expected utility it adds over future tasks, minus the effort and disclosure risk of asking, chosen under a per-interaction budget. On the new longitudinal benchmark `ActiveWebPref` with a 20-task horizon, **`APA` acquires 80.3% of the valuable preferences that only pay off through reuse, compared with 5.1% for current-task value of information**. It also recovers 84.2% of the utility gain from asking about everything while using only 27.6% of the questions.

papers.title: DRAFT: Decoding and Reconstructing 3D Room Layouts from fMRI and Camera Trajectories
papers.abstract: While functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) decoders reconstruct images and 3D objects, recovering the metric geometry of rooms from a moving viewpoint remains an open challenge. We introduce, to our knowledge for the first time, the task of reconstructing 3D layouts of held-out scenes using only the known camera trajectories and the fMRI signals of participants watching indoor walkthroughs, without any visual frames. The task is hard because of the temporal mismatch between rapid visual changes and blurred fMRI signals. Our method, DRAFT (Decoding and Reconstructing 3D room lAyouts from fMRI and Trajectories), extracts a compact layout representation from the early visual cortex and fuses this neural code with the geometric free space derived from camera motion. To evaluate it, we propose layout r, the Pearson correlation between predicted and ray-cast log depths. On ten held-out scenes (20 participants), DRAFT reaches a layout r of 0.480, outperforming the camera path alone (0.446) and seven fMRI decoders (at most 0.429). DRAFT also works as a plug-in that improves all seven decoders without retraining, raising their layout r from 0.171-0.429 to 0.487-0.493. Brain activity and camera motion can thus recover the metric layout of unseen rooms, a first step toward reconstructing the 3D spaces people see.
papers.summary: The authors introduce a new task: reconstructing the 3D layout of unseen rooms from the functional MRI (fMRI) signals of people watching indoor walkthrough videos, plus the known camera trajectory, without using any video frames. The difficulty is that the scene changes quickly while fMRI signals are slow and blurred. `DRAFT` extracts a compact layout code from the early visual cortex and fuses it with the free space implied by the camera's motion. It is scored with 'layout r', the correlation between predicted and ray-cast log depths. On ten held-out scenes with 20 participants, **`DRAFT` reaches a layout r of 0.480, compared with 0.446 for the camera path alone and at most 0.429 for seven existing fMRI decoders**. Used as a plug-in, it also raises all seven decoders to between 0.487 and 0.493.

papers.title: Can AI Co-Design Structures? An AI Agent for Early-Stage Structural Design
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models and agentic workflows offer a new paradigm to early-stage structural design translating design intent into structural models. Although text-to-3D approaches have demonstrated that natural language can be used to produce visual, mesh-based geometric models, structural design requires domain-specific geometric arrangements and semantically rich data types. This paper introduces a proof-of-concept workflow for prompt-to-structure generation using an AI agent connected to a COMPAS-based structural modelling API through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Through controlled modelling operations, the agent creates and modifies a graph-based structural data model composed of explicit building elements. The resulting artifacts can be inspected, modified, serialised, and further connected to downstream AEC workflows. The approach is demonstrated through selected prompt-to-structure examples and by progressive and editable design sequences that resemble typical iterative structural design workflows. The results are preliminary, but demonstrate the possibility of combining natural language, agentic workflows, and domain-specific structural data structures as a first step toward AI-assisted structural co-design.
papers.summary: This proof of concept turns natural-language prompts into structural engineering models for early-stage building design. An AI agent connects through a Model Context Protocol (`MCP`) server to a `COMPAS`-based structural modelling API. Using controlled modelling operations, the agent builds and edits a graph-based data model of explicit building elements, and the result can be inspected, serialised and passed to downstream architecture, engineering and construction workflows. Selected examples and step-by-step editing sequences show that **an agent can produce editable, semantically rich structural models rather than plain visual meshes**, although the authors describe the results as preliminary.

papers.title: What Comes Next and Why: Interpretable Next-Event Prediction with Neuro-Symbolic Rules
papers.abstract: In real-world applications, being able to explain why a prediction is made is often as important - if not more so - than achieving high accuracy. However, existing methods for sequential event prediction typically prioritize accuracy at the expense of interpretability. Neuro-symbolic approaches offer a promising direction to improve interpretability by learning symbolic rules, but extending them to next-event prediction is challenging due to the presence of temporal dependencies. We introduce RULES, a neuro-symbolic model that learns sequential rules directly from data, and combine it with a residual network to form RUNES (Rule Network for Event Sequences). RULES accurately recovers ground truth rules from synthetic data and discovers compact, interpretable rule sets on real data. RUNES combines these rules additively with a residual network, achieving competitive accuracy while providing transparent access to active rules and how residuals adjust predictions.
papers.summary: Methods for predicting the next event in a sequence usually trade interpretability for accuracy. `RULES` is a neuro-symbolic model that learns sequential rules directly from data while handling temporal dependencies. `RUNES` (Rule Network for Event Sequences) adds the output of a residual neural network to those rules. **`RULES` recovers the ground-truth rules on synthetic data and finds compact rule sets on real data**, and `RUNES` reaches competitive accuracy while showing which rules fired and how the residual adjusted each prediction.

papers.title: A Grammar of French Civil Cassation: A Ground-Level Dataset and Tool
papers.abstract: This paper presents a dataset of 121,536 ground-reasons pairs across 86,464 rulings of the five civil chambers of the French Court of Cassation (2016-2025). An appeal on points of law cannot itself be appealed and often decides a case for good. Understanding how the Court rules is thus crucial and can help lawyers who draft those appeals. Inside a ruling, every ground of appeal (a distinct legal complaint against the appealed decision) has its own answer from the Court. This answer is called the reasons and it belongs to one of a few doctrinal families. Using a deterministic pipeline, we pair each ground with its reasons and attach the pair to its family, according to the established French taxonomy. We obtain a descriptive grammar of civil cassation that shows which grounds succeed, which legal texts they refer to, and how both evolve over the decade. We release the dataset, the code and an interactive consultation tool.
papers.summary: The authors release a dataset of **121,536 pairs of grounds and reasons drawn from 86,464 rulings of the French Court of Cassation's five civil chambers between 2016 and 2025**. A ground is a distinct legal complaint against the decision under appeal, and the reasons are the Court's answer to it. A deterministic pipeline pairs each ground with its reasons and assigns the pair to a doctrinal family from the established French taxonomy. The result shows which grounds succeed, which legal texts they cite and how both changed over the decade. The code and an interactive consultation tool are released alongside the dataset.

papers.title: Through a PRISM, Clearly: Step-Sequence Reasoning for Mistake Recognition in Procedural Videos
papers.abstract: Procedural mistake recognition requires identifying deviations from valid multi-step activities. We study post-completion recognition from videos with benchmark-provided step boundaries. We introduce PRISM (Procedural mistake Recognition via Interpretable Semantic Modeling), which grounds video segments in language and maps their descriptions to procedural states using a lightweight hidden Markov model trained on correct executions. Reference alignment and semantic checks identify errors in step content and order. To support evaluation across heterogeneous benchmarks, we map dataset-specific annotations to four edit-based error types: insertion, deletion, substitution, and transposition. Across three benchmarks, we compare gold and VLM-generated descriptions in raw, semantic-role, and action-object forms. Decoder controls show consistent gains from the trained local decoder over nearest-candidate matching, with additional, dataset-dependent benefits from sequence decoding. Semantic role labeling improves Any-F1 in all six matched grounded comparisons, although the gains vary across datasets and do not translate into uniform improvements under separate configuration selection. These results establish language grounding as an effective interface for explicit procedural mistake reasoning and characterize the contributions of representation and decoding.
papers.summary: `PRISM` (Procedural mistake Recognition via Interpretable Semantic Modeling) detects mistakes in videos of multi-step activities once they are finished, using step boundaries supplied by the benchmark. It describes each video segment in language, maps those descriptions to procedural states with a lightweight hidden Markov model trained only on correct executions, and then uses alignment against a reference and semantic checks to find errors in step content and order. To compare across benchmarks, the authors map each dataset's annotations to four edit types: insertion, deletion, substitution and transposition. Across three benchmarks, **the trained local decoder consistently beats nearest-candidate matching, and semantic role labeling improves Any-F1 in all six matched comparisons**, although the size of the gains varies by dataset.

papers.title: ProductWebBench: Evaluating Website Continuity Beyond Task Completion
papers.abstract: Frontend coding agents are usually graded on one question: did the requested target get built. Real engineering changes carry a second obligation, because the rest of the site has to keep working. We call that second obligation website continuity, and introduce ProductWebBench, a benchmark that scores both on living frontend repositories: 320 Change tasks over existing code and 80 long-horizon Build tasks. Every task freezes a repository snapshot, staged requirements, browser evidence and deterministic checks before evaluation, and enters only once a reference passes every check and plausible-wrong ones fail. A simulated user reveals the requirements one stage at a time, and every check cleared earlier stays armed for the rest of the run. Across 8,737 runs from 13 models the two come apart: of the Change runs passing every requested-work check, 28.2% still fail a continuity check -- a blank route, horizontal overflow, console errors -- and 10.8% push a browser state they had already passed back to failing. Because the same checks also run on the untouched repository, each regression carries exact provenance, not a post-hoc label: on the 586 runs where both readings exist, 18.3% are caught breaking a verified state. Interaction is a further blind spot, failing in 29.5% of runs whose static DOM already passes. ProductWebBench therefore scores a patch against the living system it lands in, not the target alone.
papers.summary: Frontend coding agents are usually graded only on whether they built what was asked, not on whether the rest of the website still works afterwards, which the authors call 'website continuity'. `ProductWebBench` includes 320 change tasks on existing repositories and 80 long-horizon build tasks. A simulated user reveals requirements in stages, and every deterministic browser check that passed earlier stays active for the rest of the run. Across 8,737 runs from 13 models, **28.2% of change runs that pass every check on the requested work still break continuity**, for example with blank routes, horizontal overflow or console errors, and 10.8% turn an earlier passing state back into a failure. Because the same checks also run on the untouched repository, every regression can be traced exactly to the agent's patch.

papers.title: Constraint Reasoning and Large Language Models Join Forces: Providing Contrastive Explanations for Real-World Optimisation-Based Applications
papers.abstract: We focus on optimisation-based Decision Support Systems in real-world applications. In this context, we aim to provide contrastive explanations that answer users' questions about recommendations based on the solution of an optimisation problem, specifically a Mixed-Integer Program (MIP). Addressing this endeavour is crucial to ensure human oversight of the decisions implemented, as required by international guidelines on trustworthy and responsible automated decision-making systems. We propose a novel methodology that combines constraint reasoning techniques and Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate contrastive explanations for optimisation problems encoded as MIPs. Although LLMs have shown impressive capabilities in Natural Language processing, they can produce incorrect answers due to reasoning limitations. To overcome these limitations, we leverage constraint reasoning techniques to distil the information necessary to produce an explanation, which is then passed as input to an LLM as the so-called graph of reasons. Such a graph captures the semantics and the relationships among constraints of the optimisation problem. Results on real-world scheduling domains show that incorporating constraint reasoning improves explanations generated by the LLM. In particular, using the graph of reasons enables the LLM to produce natural-language explanations that include more relevant reasons while reducing errors compared to explanations generated without this structure.
papers.summary: Decision support systems built on mixed-integer programs (MIPs) need to answer users' 'why this and not that' questions, but large language models (LLMs) asked directly often get the reasoning wrong. The authors first use constraint reasoning to extract the information an explanation needs, packaged as a 'graph of reasons' that captures how the optimisation problem's constraints relate. They then give this graph to an LLM to write the natural-language explanation. On real-world scheduling problems, **explanations built from the graph of reasons include more relevant reasons and contain fewer errors** than explanations the LLM produces without it.

papers.title: SetCommit: Coordinated Token Commitments for Few-Step Diffusion Language Model Decoding
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models generate multiple token positions in parallel, but few-step decoding makes parallel commitment difficult: tokens that appear reliable individually may be jointly inconsistent, while premature commitments can prevent later context-dependent refinement. In this paper, we introduce SetCommit, a training-free method for coordinated parallel token commitment. Instead of selecting tokens independently by confidence, SetCommit selects a commitment set that balances token reliability against local joint commitment risk, preserving conditioning opportunities for subsequent denoising steps. It further performs budget-neutral local exchanges, replacing vulnerable earlier commitments when newly revealed context supports more reliable alternatives. SetCommit requires no retraining or architectural modification and is compatible with existing diffusion decoding strategies. Experiments with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on GSM8K, MATH-500, MBPP, and HumanEval show accuracy/pass@1 gains of up to 7.4 percentage points over native decoding at 32 model evaluations. At common quality targets, geometric-mean incremental speedups range from $1.44$ to $1.74\times$. Code is available at https://github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models generate many token positions in parallel. With only a few decoding steps, tokens that each look reliable can turn out to be inconsistent with one another, and committing to them too early blocks later refinement. `SetCommit` is a training-free method that chooses a whole set of tokens to commit at each step, balancing each token's reliability against the risk of committing them together. It also swaps out weak earlier commitments when new context supports better alternatives, without changing the commitment budget. With `LLaDA-8B` and `Dream-7B` on `GSM8K`, `MATH-500`, `MBPP` and `HumanEval`, it **improves accuracy or pass@1 by up to 7.4 percentage points at 32 model evaluations** and gives geometric-mean speedups of 1.44 to 1.74 times at matched quality.

papers.title: Delta N-gram: Forward-Only Continual Writing into a Language Model's Native N-gram Memory
papers.abstract: Our previous analysis found that a model's native hashed N-gram table is where continual updates disturb the base least, but its writes needed backpropagation and changed the pretrained table. We present Delta N-gram, a forward-only write path into that table. The pretrained table T^0 is never modified. Evidence is written into a sparse patch \Delta on the rows it addresses: a 4.1M-parameter writer emits a target and a gate per (position, hash head) event, and a block-averaged delta rule keeps each row a convex combination of its old value and the gated targets. The writer is trained offline on raw text with the pretraining objective; at use time writing takes forward passes only, and clearing \Delta restores the original model. A 0.6B prototype trained to answer questions keeps 16/16 facts after a second write; online gradient writes keep 2--4/16. We study two writers: a plain writer that encodes evidence with the T^0-only model, and a delta writer that reads its current memory while encoding. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the plain writer's memory is document-specific: on 64 held-out news events it lowers continuation NLL by 0.068 nats/token against empty memory and by 0.024 against another document's memory, and 0.063 and 0.013 after 16 intervening articles. The delta writer's memory is more document-specific and keeps more of it under distraction (70% vs 54%). Over 35,000 writes on our previous seven-task chain both writers stay stable and the delta writer drifts less (layer-2 math drift 176% vs 188%); later accuracy changes by -0.26/-0.52pp (-7.29pp for gradient updates) and small-k_i drift is 17.9/17.5% (39.2%). Acquisition is negative, and general-input drift reaches 32.8% (20.75%): format rows read by every example grow to 4--12 times their pretrained norm. Zeroing eight such rows removes over 98% of layer-2 drift on math inputs, together with their NLL gain.
papers.summary: `Delta N-gram` writes new knowledge into a language model's built-in hashed N-gram table using only forward passes. Instead of changing the pretrained table, it stores updates in a sparse patch that can be cleared to restore the original model. A 4.1M-parameter writer, trained offline with the pretraining objective, produces a target and a gate for each table row it touches, and an averaged update rule mixes those targets with the row's previous value. In a 0.6B-parameter prototype, **all 16 stored facts survive a second write, compared with 2 to 4 for online gradient updates**, and the memory stays stable and specific to its source document over 35,000 writes on `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next`. The authors also report limits: the model does not gain new task skills this way, and a few rows that every input reads drift substantially and cause most of the side effects on unrelated inputs.

papers.title: Post-Audit Mirage: Identifiability Limits of Offline Agent Verification
papers.abstract: Offline tests can fail to reveal whether an agent update will remain safe after deployment. We operationalize this post-audit mirage using matched safe and harmful lifecycles that expose identical verifier-visible evidence while an isolated scorer records opposite deployment truth. Our theorem applies standard observational-equivalence and indistinguishability ideas to this executable audit boundary and states the resulting error-abstention tradeoff. The Post-Audit Mirage benchmark makes that boundary executable across authorization, scheduling, and shared-capacity environments. IdentifiedRangeMonitor uses fresh group-labelled harm outcomes to return deploy, hold, cannot determine, or unsupported. Experiments show that monitoring can recover the missing distinction in favorable settings but may remain undecided for rare groups, small effects, or missing observations. Verifier-agent evaluation must therefore test both calculation validity and whether the available evidence supports the deployment decision.
papers.summary: Offline audits may not reveal whether an update to an AI agent will stay safe after deployment. The authors call this the 'post-audit mirage' and demonstrate it with matched safe and harmful scenarios that give the verifier identical evidence but have opposite outcomes in deployment. A theorem built on standard observational-equivalence arguments formalizes **an unavoidable tradeoff between making errors and abstaining from a decision**. A benchmark spanning authorization, scheduling and shared-capacity environments makes the problem concrete. A proposed monitor, `IdentifiedRangeMonitor`, uses fresh harm outcomes labelled by group to choose between deploy, hold, cannot determine and unsupported, and it can resolve the cases in favourable settings but stays undecided when groups are rare, effects are small or observations are missing.

papers.title: Is High Local Accuracy Enough? Geometric Consensus with Support-Adaptive Statistical Personalization for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Real-world deployment of personalized federated learning (PFL) requires adapting to heterogeneous clients while preserving recognition performance beyond local distributions. However, high local accuracy can conceal failures on locally rare or absent classes. Effective personalization should therefore strengthen global recognition while raising the personalization floor. We propose an evaluation protocol that complements local accuracy with global, rare-class, and unseen-class evaluations to reveal generalization obscured by local scores, and assesses personalization floors among the worst-performing clients to expose weaknesses hidden by aggregate performance. To meet these deployment challenges, we propose FedGRC, a unified PFL framework integrating generalization and personalization through (i) Consensus-Guided Representation Learning (CGRL), which learns discriminative representations through shared directional and magnitude guidance; (ii) Multilayer Metric Synthesis (MMS), which constructs a shared covariance metric from these multilayer representations for statistical classification; and (iii) Support-Adaptive Shrinkage Personalization (SASP), which adapts class means within this metric by shrinking local estimates toward shared means according to local sample support, enabling adaptation while retaining shared knowledge. Extensive experiments, including benchmarking against 21 methods across 5 heterogeneity settings on 3 datasets and comprehensive ablation studies, validate the effectiveness of FedGRC. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, FedGRC surpasses state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines in global recognition and personalization floors by at least 2.17% and 2.13%, respectively. On the real-world heterogeneous FedRS dataset, it outperforms the respective best baselines by 2.15%, 3.30%, and 4.61% in local adaptation, global recognition, and the personalization floor.
papers.summary: In personalized federated learning (PFL), a model can score well on each client's local data while failing on classes that client rarely or never sees. The authors propose an evaluation protocol that adds global, rare-class and unseen-class tests to local accuracy, and that also measures the worst-performing clients (the "personalization floor"). They pair it with `FedGRC`, which combines shared representation learning (`CGRL`), a shared multilayer covariance metric for statistical classification (`MMS`), and per-client class means that are pulled toward shared means according to how much local data supports each class (`SASP`). Against 21 methods, `FedGRC` beats state-of-the-art baselines on `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` by **at least 2.17% in global recognition and 2.13% in personalization floor**, and also leads on the real-world `FedRS` dataset.

papers.title: Mixing Matters: Evidence Position Bias Across Sequence Mixers in Long-Context Question Answering
papers.abstract: Long-context models often use answer-bearing evidence less effectively when it appears away from a prompt boundary. We compare this position bias across Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving one gold document through a fixed set of nine distractors. The evaluated Transformers show a beginning advantage that the evaluated state-space models lack, while both families favor evidence near the end. A matched pure-versus-hybrid Mamba comparison points in the same direction but remains statistically uncertain. The family difference appears among models that can answer the task. Transformer primacy reappears on synthetic retrieval, where state-space ceiling prevents a family comparison. A corpus swap within one state-space architecture changes overall accuracy without a detectable change in curve shape. Prompt changes can create or nearly remove a beginning advantage. Position remains decodable across architectures even when response curves differ, and attention concentration near initial tokens covaries with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformer family. These exploratory results show that effective context use depends on the evaluated architecture family, capability, task, and prompt, without isolating the sequence mixer as the sole cause.
papers.summary: Long-context models often make poorer use of answer-bearing evidence when it sits away from the edges of the prompt. The study compares this position bias across Transformer, state-space and hybrid `Mamba` models by moving one gold document through a fixed set of nine distractors. **The tested Transformers favor evidence at the beginning of the context while the state-space models do not, though both families favor evidence near the end.** The authors also find that prompt changes can create or nearly remove the beginning advantage, so they conclude that effective context use depends on architecture family, capability, task and prompt together rather than on the sequence mixer alone.

papers.title: GM-GReFEL: Geometry-Guided Spatiotemporal State-Space Learning for Robust Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions in unconstrained video suffers from two coupled problems: self-attention grows quadratically in cost with clip length, and crowdsourced labels are noisy. We present GM-GReFEL, a spatiotemporal state-space network with a geometry-aware decision stage. Its Modulated GroupMamba backbone replaces a spatiotemporal Vision Transformer. Six channel groups are scanned separately, four over the frame plane and two over time, so the cost grows linearly with sequence length ($\mathcal{O}(N)$); after each layer, a Channel Affinity Modulation gate mixes the groups again. On top of the backbone, a GReFEL reliability module turns the normalized entropy of each prediction into a mixing weight between the classifier output and a vote from trainable geometric anchors, so that facial geometry counts for more when the network is unsure. The model is initialized by static-to-dynamic weight transfer and trained with a Triple Loss. In five-fold cross-validation, the best fold scores 66.57\%/76.46\% UAR/WAR on DFEW, 0.3 points or less below the strongest compared method, and 45.66\%/62.27\% on MAFW, ahead of all compared methods; on FERV39k the mean over five splits, 42.30\%/52.66\%, is competitive. The five-fold means are 64.07\%/74.54\% on DFEW, on par with recent large pre-trained models, and 38.90\%/54.37\% on MAFW, below the best of them. A paired $t$-test on DFEW indicates a modest benefit of temporal modeling (+1.61 UAR points, one-sided $p=0.031$). Attention stays on plausible facial regions, and latency is close to a ViT-B/16 baseline (47.4 vs.\ 46.8 ms per clip). Code: https://github.com/ardiytama/GroupMamba-DFER.
papers.summary: Recognizing facial expressions in real-world video faces two problems: self-attention cost grows quadratically with clip length, and crowdsourced labels are noisy. `GM-GReFEL` replaces a spatiotemporal Vision Transformer with a `Modulated GroupMamba` state-space backbone whose cost grows linearly with sequence length. It adds a reliability module that relies more on trainable facial-geometry anchors when the classifier's prediction entropy is high. It reaches **45.66%/62.27% UAR/WAR on `MAFW`, ahead of all compared methods**, comes within 0.3 points of the best method on `DFEW`, and runs at roughly the latency of a `ViT-B/16` baseline.

papers.title: Rethinking Fisher Vectors for Second-order Multi-scale Deep Feature Aggregation in Scalable Scene Retrieval
papers.abstract: Aggregating CNN responses into a compact discriminative vector, given their lack of geometric invariance, is a challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a codebook-free method to encode second-order information of multi-scale CNN features within the Fisher Kernel framework. We use a scalable retrieval pipeline to show the efficacy of the proposed vector. The increased discriminative power is confirmed by experimental evaluation of our method on two difficult benchmarks (INRIA Holidays, UKBench). The significant improvement in retrieval accuracy over state-of-the-art approaches comes with only a slight dimension increase.
papers.summary: Image retrieval needs CNN features compressed into a compact vector that still discriminates well, which is hard because CNN responses lack geometric invariance. The authors propose a codebook-free way to encode second-order statistics of multi-scale CNN features within the Fisher Kernel framework and test it in a scalable retrieval pipeline. On `INRIA Holidays` and `UKBench` they report **a significant gain in retrieval accuracy over state-of-the-art approaches with only a slight increase in vector dimension**.

papers.title: PriMa-Causa: Causal Prescriptive Maintenance
papers.abstract: Automated manufacturing requires data-driven decisions under uncertainty and sparse observational records, and unplanned downtime is a dominant cost of getting them wrong. Prescriptive maintenance recommends a maintenance action against an impending failure rather than merely predicting it. Established reference architectures couple predictive models with rule- or optimisation-based recommendation logic. Selecting a corrective action, however, requires an interventional quantity: how the line behaviour would change if the action were set. Manufacturing data is observational, so a model fitted to predict the outcome estimates an associational quantity and may misdirect the choice of action without the prediction error revealing it. Causal estimators target the interventional quantity but require an expert-led causal study per case, for which the bounded decision window of operation leaves no room. This dissertation analyses how causal reasoning can be embedded into prescriptive maintenance so that actions are ranked by their estimated interventional effect. The result is PriMa-Causa, built from three components: a causal reasoning layer that integrates the estimate into the PriMa reference model, a parametric simulator that supplies the interventional ground truth absent from manufacturing data, and a graph-conditioned tabular causal foundation model that, pre-trained once on this synthetic production-line prior, answers interventional queries in a single forward pass. PriMa-Causa attains a lower prescription error than associational baselines, with the largest margin under weak overlap and sparse context, and a partially disclosed causal graph reduces this error further. The causal inductive bias of the synthetic prior and the graph conditioning can thus replace per-case estimator fitting, a step toward automating causal inference for autonomous and self-healing maintenance.
papers.summary: Prescriptive maintenance recommends an action against an impending equipment failure, but choosing that action requires knowing how the production line would respond if the action were taken. Models fitted to observational manufacturing data estimate only correlations, which can point to the wrong action. This dissertation presents `PriMa-Causa`, which combines a causal reasoning layer for the `PriMa` reference model, a parametric simulator that provides interventional ground truth, and a graph-conditioned tabular causal foundation model that answers interventional queries in a single forward pass after pre-training on synthetic production-line data. **It achieves lower prescription error than associational baselines, with the largest margin under weak overlap and sparse context**, and partially revealing the causal graph lowers the error further.

papers.title: Prompt Sensitivity in Tool-Augmented Model Comparisons
papers.abstract: Language models are compared on question-answering benchmarks that pose each question in one wording, and a reworded question can change which of two models scores higher. We ask whether giving the models tools makes such comparisons more stable. An accuracy gain cannot answer this, because tools change several steps between the question and the scored answer at once. We propose a matched protocol that separates those steps: the answer readout, reasoning, the decision to call, the tool's answer, and the report supplied without a call. We apply it to six open models in five domains under five wordings. We find that tools raise accuracy where a program answers the question and widen the wording sensitivity of many pairwise comparisons. The widening follows how often a model calls, and call frequency follows the wording for some models and not others. It also depends on the interface and the instructions: a native tool-calling interface and a second tool description leave no detected widening in molecules, and sensitivity persists where tools return intermediate results. These findings show that deterministic reports do not guarantee stable comparisons. We recommend reporting call frequency and comparison stability under several wordings beside accuracy.
papers.summary: Benchmarks phrase each question one way, and rewording it can change which of two language models ranks higher. The authors ask whether giving models tools makes these comparisons more stable. They build a matched protocol that separates the answer readout, reasoning, the decision to call a tool, the tool's answer and the report given without a call, and apply it to six open models across five domains and five wordings. **Tools raise accuracy where a program can answer the question, but they widen wording sensitivity in many pairwise comparisons**; the widening tracks how often a model calls tools and depends on the interface and instructions. The authors recommend reporting call frequency and comparison stability across several wordings alongside accuracy.

papers.title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
papers.abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.
papers.summary: Deep research agents write long reports from open-web evidence, but no existing benchmark evaluates research built around a source video. The authors define a task in which an agent takes a video and a user request, identifies research questions, gathers external multimodal evidence and produces an interactive report linked to moments in the video. They release `OmniDR-Bench`, with 50 Chinese and English tasks and 6,414 criteria organized into rubric trees (`Omni-ARTs`) that were built through an audited, human-reviewed process. **Across 18 agent configurations the best system scores only 63.3 out of 100**, and the main gaps are content coverage, causal reasoning across modalities and citation accuracy.
papers.highlight_summary:
Deep research agents can already write cited reports from web sources, but no existing benchmark tests research that is anchored to a specific source video. The authors define video-centered deep research report generation: an agent takes a video and a user request, finds research-worthy claims and procedures in it, gathers external text, image and video evidence, and produces an interactive HTML report linked to timestamps in the video. They pair this task with `OmniDR-Bench`, which scores reports against audited rubrics.
- Reports are graded with `Omni-ARTs` (Omni Atomic Rubric Trees). Each tree has three dimensions (content, citation and presentation), 23 shared directions and task-specific binary criteria, which are checked either by a multimodal judge (`GPT-5.6 Sol`) or by deterministic programs that probe the report in a browser.
- The criteria come from `ARC` (Audited Rubric Construction), which builds an independent library of video and web facts before writing any criteria, checks that scores rise with more evidence access, and runs rounds of human review; the final benchmark has **50 Chinese and English tasks**, **19 subcategories** and **6,414 criteria**, and 94% of sampled items were marked correct.
- Across **18 model and harness configurations**, the best score is **63.3/100**, from `Claude Opus 5` in `Claude Code`; `GLM-5.3` scores 62.0 with every task completed, and the confidence intervals overlap, so the ranking between the two is uncertain.
- Agents handle presentation (averaging **81.8**) much better than content (**45.4**) or citation (**47.8**): video faithfulness reaches 92.4%, but claim support is only **15.9%** and use of external evidence about **8.7%**, often because sources are listed at the end instead of cited next to the claims they support.
- In ablations, the full video-research skill adds **+7.3 points** over the individual skills alone, mostly through a **+20.7 gain in citation score**, but it roughly doubles cost (from 2.3M to 4.7M tokens and from 0.7 to 1.6 hours per report); the main limitations are the small task count, dependence on a single judge model, and only moderate agreement with human holistic ratings (Spearman **ρ = 0.64**).

papers.title: Towards Field-Deployable Wearable IMU Systems for Occupational Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) systems for construction worker human activity recognition (HAR) routinely report aggregate accuracies above 95 %, rarely under genuine subject-independent (leave-one-subject-out (LOSO)) evaluation, masking the per-individual variance that determines real-world deployment performance. Using the VTT-ConIoT benchmark, we conduct, to our knowledge, the first systematic configuration sensitivity analysis of this dataset: six classifiers across five sensor placements and three window sizes under a single LOSO protocol, a personalised-calibration pilot, and a validated comparison of tabular GAN-based and standard time-series augmentation. Per-subject LOSO accuracy for the main multi-sensor, 16-class configuration ranges from 61.9 % to 88.7 % (mean 77.5 %), a 27 pp spread, though all data are laboratory-collected. Multi-sensor fusion and longer windows both improve accuracy; standard augmentation gives small, consistent gains, while Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) augmentation actively harms accuracy with a demonstrated distributional-fidelity mechanism; and personalised calibration recovers 16.8 pp for the weakest participants from just 30 % of their own data. These findings provide evidence-grounded configuration guidance for scaling occupational body sensor networks towards field deployment
authors: Ihsan Ul Haq (Centre for Computational Science and Mathematical Modelling
School of Architecture and Built Environment Deakin University
James Brusey (Centre for Computational Science and Mathematical Modelling
Farnad Nasirzadeh (School of Architecture and Built Environment Deakin University
Chandan Karmakar (School of Information Technology Deakin University
papers.summary: Systems that recognize construction workers' activities from wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) often report accuracy above 95%, but rarely under leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation, which tests on people unseen in training. Using the `VTT-ConIoT` benchmark, the authors compare six classifiers, five sensor placements and three window sizes under one LOSO protocol, and also test data augmentation and per-user calibration. **Per-subject accuracy ranges from 61.9% to 88.7%, a 27-point spread hidden by the 77.5% mean.** `CTGAN` augmentation actually hurts accuracy, while calibrating on 30% of a person's own data recovers 16.8 points for the weakest participants.

papers.title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
papers.abstract: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.
papers.summary: Simulators are usually calibrated in order to make predictions, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (`KOH`) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference controls predictive error, especially when parameters are weakly identified or the model is misspecified. The proposed framework trains a conditional flow-matching model to produce an amortized posterior, using simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies. It then applies conformal risk control to select prediction bands that meet a target miscoverage rate in finite samples. **On a synthetic benchmark the bands are about 20% the width of `KOH-MCMC` bands while staying near the 10% miscoverage target.** In a measles-outbreak case study, the weeks the bands fail to cover reveal structural flaws in the epidemic model.

papers.title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.
papers.summary: Research on how conventions form among interacting large language model (LLM) agents has mostly assumed that every agent can interact with every other. Here, policies extracted from four LLMs play the naming game with 1,000 to 100,000 agents on fully connected, random and heterogeneous networks. Sparse networks slow consensus by up to twelvefold, but they can restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under all-to-all mixing. **When an adversary plants committed agents to overturn an established convention, targeting hub nodes takes about one-sixth as many as random placement** (3% versus 16% median on the most heterogeneous network). Networked populations are usually easier to tip than all-to-all ones, so estimates from all-to-all settings can overstate robustness.

papers.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
papers.summary: Whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies for humanoid robots see only the current frame, but in dynamic scenes the relevant cues can disappear as objects move, become hidden or leave the camera view. `WholeBodyMem` uses `SAM3` to track task objects and keeps key frames selected by object events within an adaptive budget, and the action model reads these frames through cross-attention alongside object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. The authors also release `HuMeGo`, a memory benchmark with six simulated and six real `Unitree G1` tasks. **Base-policy success rises from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot** (and from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation), outperforming both memoryless and uniform-memory baselines.

papers.title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
papers.summary: Prompting strategies for LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, such as Chain-of-Thought and role conditioning, are usually recommended based on English-only benchmarks. The authors test whether these strategies transfer using 9 strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, producing over 1 million scores validated against human judgments. **The choice of judge model matters more than the choice of prompting strategy, and a strategy's effect can reverse direction from one judge to another.** Stability also drops in low-resource languages in ways that aggregate scores hide, so the authors advise validating prompts for each intended evaluation setting.

papers.title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
papers.abstract: Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.
papers.summary: Particle physics experiments produce large volumes of sparse data that must be heavily reduced before analysis. The authors evaluate a foundation-model-based reconstruction pipeline on space points from a Time Projection Chamber, testing it on downstream tasks including charged-particle track finding and particle identification. They report that **the foundation-model approach significantly outperforms traditional methods** and can be adapted to tasks unrelated to its original training objective.

papers.title: RaSFNet: Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network for LiDAR Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation is a fundamental component of 3D perception for autonomous driving and robotics. Projection-based methods map 3D point clouds into 2D representations for feature extraction using 2D networks. However, aggregating multiple points during projection can obscure geometric differences within each frustum, while local feature extraction limits the modeling of spatial relationships across scanning regions. Moreover, proximity in the projected representation does not necessarily imply proximity in 3D space, and interactions between point and projected features may mix features from different ranges, reducing semantic discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose the Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network (RaSFNet), which incorporates point cloud geometry and LiDAR scanning characteristics into projection-based semantic segmentation. Specifically, the Ray-Aligned Geometric Distribution Encoding (RAGDE) module characterizes point distributions within each frustum using a ray-aligned coordinate system. To model spatial context, a Scan-Topology-Aware Mamba (STAM) block organizes frustum features according to the LiDAR azimuth sampling pattern and captures long-range dependencies across scanning regions. In addition, a Range-Constrained Point-Frustum Fusion (RCPFF) mechanism uses shared range information to guide feature exchange between point and frustum representations while maintaining spatial correspondence. RaSFNet achieves mIoU scores of 70.2% and 77.7% on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes validation sets, respectively, indicating competitive segmentation performance compared with the evaluated methods.
papers.summary: Projection-based LiDAR segmentation maps 3D point clouds to 2D images, but this blurs geometry within each projected cell and can mix features from points that look adjacent in 2D but are far apart in 3D. `RaSFNet` encodes the point distribution inside each cell in a ray-aligned coordinate system (`RAGDE`). It uses a `Mamba` block that orders features by the LiDAR's azimuth scan pattern to capture long-range context (`STAM`), and fuses point and projected features under range constraints (`RCPFF`). It reaches **70.2% mIoU on `SemanticKITTI` and 77.7% on `nuScenes`** validation sets, which is competitive with the methods it was compared against.

papers.title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
papers.abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.
papers.summary: Generating text from structured metadata is often treated as a task where more input fields should mean better-grounded output. The authors test this with LLM-written museum artefact descriptions, first by analysing natural variation across a large collection and then by running controlled probes that vary metadata quantity, field type and image access for the same object. **The number of metadata fields alone does not explain model behaviour; field type determines whether models ground, omit or invent information.** Images can support visual grounding but can also increase unsupported interpretation, so the authors argue evaluation should check support for each field and claim.

papers.title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space that are efficient for planning but hard to interpret. `Inside-JEPA` adds relational channels for ordered pairs of entities to the latent state and grounds them without relation labels by using an inverse-dynamics loss that recovers actions from changes in those channels. **On `Something-Something V2`, latent prediction alone does no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision improves relational AUROC by 0.065 to 0.103**, with similar gains on `RH20T` robot episodes. When asked which action achieves a one-step relational goal, a readout of the 16 channels places the correct action in the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, versus 24% for prediction-only latents.

papers.title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) produce text through repeated denoising steps, which makes quantization harder than for standard autoregressive models. The authors show that sensitivity to quantization varies by both task and denoising step, and that this pattern can be predicted without ground-truth labels. Their `T2Quant` framework uses that label-free signal to allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Across three DLMs and six benchmarks it improves existing quantization methods by **up to 6.7 percentage points in average accuracy at the same budget**.

papers.title: Investigating Multi-Cultural Value Selection Biases in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) serve users whose cultural identities are multi-layered, yet cultural evaluations commonly reduce identity to one label. In this work, we study LLMs under simultaneous identity cues, with a country persona in the system prompt and a second identity signaled in the user turn, either by naming a country (explicit cue) or through the query language (implicit cue). We test World Values Survey (WVS) multiple-choice probing and open-ended sociopolitical generation. In multiple-choice probing, language cues shift answers about three times more than explicit cues but away from the associated country's distribution, and explicit cues do not consistently move answers toward the named country. Across 1.6 million open-ended responses, naming a country closes 30-44% of the gap to the model's own responses for that country, and explicit cues produce more differentiated value changes than language cues. Our results suggest that country and language cues should be evaluated as distinct signals rather than interchangeable proxies for culture.
papers.summary: Cultural evaluations of large language models (LLMs) typically assign each user a single identity label, although real users have layered identities. The authors give models a country persona in the system prompt plus a second identity cue in the user turn, either by naming a country or through the language of the query. They test with `World Values Survey` (`WVS`) multiple-choice questions and 1.6 million open-ended responses. **In multiple choice, language cues shift answers about three times more than named countries, yet move them away from that country's actual value distribution.** In open-ended generation, naming a country closes 30 to 44% of the gap to the model's own responses for that country, which suggests language and country cues should be treated as distinct signals.

papers.title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.
papers.summary: Predicting the emotional arousal of music from audio works reasonably well, but valence (how positive or negative the music feels) remains hard to model. The authors use in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to refine predictions from a small task-specific model, using demonstrations drawn from an auxiliary dataset. They test a text variant using lyrics and generated audio captions and a multimodal variant using raw audio. On the held-out `MER60` dataset, **text-based ICL raises valence R² from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstrations**, and the multimodal variant reaches 0.346 with only 10.

papers.title: Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering with Shuffler-Based Anonymization
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel one-shot federated clustering approach based on evolving fuzzy clustering and shuffler-based anonymization. In federated clustering, each round reveals additional model information to the server and can increase the opportunity to infer properties of local datasets, even when raw samples are never shared. Consequently, fewer client-server exchanges and unlinkability are important, so transmitted information cannot be attributed to any single client. Data-stream clustering algorithms, which learn in a single pass over the data, align well with the one-shot federated learning paradigm, where a single communication round can be sufficient. The proposed Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering (eFDPC) method combines evolving fuzzy data-stream clustering and density peak clustering in a federated setting. Each client independently evolves micro-clusters from private data mini-batches through cluster addition and merging. To limit communication, density peak clustering is applied to the learned micro-clusters and only the selected peaks are transmitted, rather than the full local models. A shuffler-based layer is introduced between the clients and the server to anonymize contributions prior to reconstruction and global peak selection. We consider a peak-only variant, eFDPC-P, as well as eFDPC-G with server-side label propagation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets show that eFDPC outperforms recent federated clustering baselines in one-shot settings and scales to higher-dimensional, non-IID data.
papers.summary: Each communication round in federated clustering reveals more about clients' private data, so methods that need fewer rounds and cannot link updates to individual clients are preferable. `eFDPC` has each client build micro-clusters from its data stream in a single pass, applies density peak clustering locally and sends only the selected peaks to the server in one round. A shuffler layer between clients and server anonymizes these contributions before global peak selection, and the authors test a peak-only variant (`eFDPC-P`) and a variant with server-side label propagation (`eFDPC-G`). On synthetic and real benchmarks, **`eFDPC` outperforms recent one-shot federated clustering baselines** and scales to higher-dimensional, non-IID data.

papers.title: Trion-1: Unifying Language, Protein Sequence, and Structure with Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.
papers.summary: The goal is a single protein foundation model that can understand, generate and translate between protein sequence, 3D structure and natural language while keeping the instruction-following of general LLMs. `Trion-1` is a multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) that puts sequence, structure and text into one discrete token space. Instead of strict left-to-right generation, its tokens interact bidirectionally, which suits modeling long-range residue contacts. One model covers folding, inverse folding, sequence and structure understanding, and sequence and structure design. In folding it reaches **a TM-score above 0.8 from a single sample under strict homology control**, matching or beating an existing tri-modal model that uses 200 samples, and its sequence understanding is on par with `Claude Opus 4.7`.

papers.title: Local Discrimination of Binary Classifiers via Localized AUC Functional
papers.abstract: Risk prediction models are frequently evaluated with AUC, which means that during evaluation we are blind to performance heterogeneity, which could lead to bad decision-making in clinics. In this work, we aim to change that by identifying patient cohorts for whom the risk prediction model might not be an accurate predictor. To separate these cohorts, we use a version of the weighted AUC, which we call Localized AUC or LAUC. Using this metric, we build a method that we coin LOCATOR. This method is able to identify cohorts of patients for whom the risk prediction model is inaccurate. We test this method both in real-world data and in simulations. We also build a statistical background for the use of Localized AUC for our purposes.
papers.summary: Clinical risk prediction models are usually judged by one overall AUC (area under the ROC curve), which hides patient subgroups where a model performs poorly. The authors define a weighted variant called Localized AUC (`LAUC`) and build `LOCATOR`, a method that uses it to **identify patient cohorts for whom a risk model is inaccurate**. They test the method on simulations and real-world data and give a statistical justification for using `LAUC` this way.

papers.title: QICOM: Open-Source Software for Reproducible Image Quality Evaluation, Blinded Assessment, and Radiomic Comparison
papers.abstract: QICOM (Quality Image COMparator) is open-source software for quantitative image comparison, paired radiomics, and blinded assessment. It saves processing settings, image identities, measurements, and response mappings so a comparison can be reopened and recalculated. We evaluate reference agreement, responses to controlled perturbations, and recovery of saved analyses. Synthetic experiments cover 37 quantitative descriptors using independentnumerical references and separate upstream integration comparisons. The QICOM/MIRP backend meets the reference tolerances for all 482 numeric IBSI 1 digital-phantom entries and all 1,622 entries across configurations A-E of the public CT reference case; these comprise 1,804 feature/aggregation comparisons and 300 preprocessing diagnostics. Restricting masked SSIM and HFEN to complete kernel support removes the observed dependence on excluded pixels. In a synthetic filtering example, stronger smoothing increases SSIM while worsening MSE and HFEN relative to milder smoothing and changing GLCM contrast more strongly. Reopened radiomics projects reproduce all 43 feature pairs per comparison, and two blinded deliveries return four correctly mapped scripted responses. These experiments document the calculations and data transfers linking the three workflows.
papers.summary: `QICOM` (Quality Image COMparator) is open-source software for quantitative medical image comparison, paired radiomics and blinded reader assessment. It saves settings, image identities and response mappings so that any analysis can be reopened and recalculated. Its `MIRP`-based backend **meets reference tolerances for all 482 numeric `IBSI 1` digital-phantom entries and all 1,622 entries of the public CT reference case**. Reopened projects reproduce every feature pair, and blinded deliveries return correctly mapped responses.
