The framework integrates gated recurrent memory with graph message passing: local hidden states encode information beyond the instantaneous observables, while spatial coupling allows this information to propagate between sites. The observable and hidden fields evolve jointly through a shared local rule, providing a scalable representation of dynamics with spatial interactions and temporal memory. We demonstrate this framework on the emergent dynamics of charge-density-wave order in the semiclassical Holstein model, successfully reproducing temporal and spatial correlations and dynamical scaling during domain coarsening. By learning finite-time evolution directly, the GRNN offers a route to efficient, data-driven descriptions of collective dynamics with unresolved microscopic degrees of freedom.
papers.summary: In correlated electron systems, the observable patterns that emerge from microscopic dynamics may not follow a closed, memoryless equation of motion. The authors propose a graph-recurrent neural network (`GRNN`) that combines gated recurrent memory at each site with graph message passing between sites, and they train it directly on simulated trajectories. Applied to charge-density-wave ordering in the semiclassical `Holstein` model, it **reproduces temporal and spatial correlations and the dynamical scaling of domain coarsening**.

papers.title: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
papers.abstract: Feature flags are runtime configuration mechanisms used for gradual feature rollouts, experimentation, and kill switches. Once a feature is fully rolled out, the flag and its gated code become technical debt and can introduce operational risk through inadvertently enabling dormant code paths. At DoorDash, over 56,000 feature flags span 623 repositories, with 1,659 currently stale as of May 2026, with internal estimates of one to two hours per manual cleanup. Existing rule-based cleanup tools proved insufficient in DoorDash's codebases. Our contribution is an end-to-end automated LLM-based feature flag cleanup system that integrates querying live feature flag rollout data using MCP, Jira ticket processing, and end-to-end pull request creation. Our system successfully produced engineer-approved flag removal PRs for 45 (90%) of the 50 stale flags it was evaluated on, proving the system's operational viability at scale with each cleanup averaging only $4.79 and 13.8 minutes. We evaluated the system's quality and reliability boundary based on success rates, cost per cleanup and time metrics. Furthermore, we discuss our lessons learned when architecting this system, to provide practical guidance for developing similar multi-agent systems.
papers.summary: DoorDash has over 56,000 feature flags across 623 repositories, 1,659 of them stale, and each manual cleanup takes an estimated one to two hours. The authors built a multi-agent LLM system that queries live flag rollout data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), processes Jira tickets, and opens cleanup pull requests end to end. Evaluated on 50 stale flags, it **produced engineer-approved removal pull requests for 45 of them (90%), at an average of $4.79 and 13.8 minutes per cleanup**. The paper also shares lessons learned from designing the multi-agent architecture.

papers.title: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents
papers.abstract: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems often perform no better than single agents on goal-directed reasoning tasks, largely because agents exchange critical information poorly. `Muffin` (shared Memory bUFFer INference) replaces synchronous debate-style turn-taking with an asynchronous protocol. An orchestrator sends demanding queries to a group of agents, which post intermediate findings to a shared memory buffer while keeping their private reasoning local. It achieves the best accuracy in 17 of 20 benchmark settings and, compared with multi-agent debate, gains **19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens**, without sharing full reasoning traces.

papers.title: CrisiLangs: A Multilingual Resource for Crisis Warning Generation
papers.abstract: Communicating with the public during an emergency entails issuing warning messages promptly. In Europe, it often requires producing them in more than one language. Recent work has shown that language models can be trained to generate warning messages as a crisis unfolds, but the available data covers only English. To fill this gap, we present CrisiLangs, a multilingual extension of CrisiText (an English dataset of crisis events paired with warning messages written according to expert communication guidelines) to Italian, Bulgarian, German, and Greek. Expert native speakers translated the warning messages of 1,000 events drawn from 411 scenarios, for a total of 5,000 event-message pairs across five languages. We test the resource to fine-tune a multilingual model on all five languages jointly, with and without the emergency guidelines in the prompt, and compare it with a zero-shot baseline. The fine-tuned models outperform the baseline on ROUGE-L, BLEU and BERTScore in every language and configuration. In a human preference study, low decoding temperatures receive the most preferences in all five languages and in both configurations, while the effect of the guidelines varies by language.
papers.summary: Language models can generate public warning messages during emergencies, but existing training data covers only English, while European emergencies often need warnings in several languages. `CrisiLangs` extends the English `CrisiText` dataset to Italian, Bulgarian, German, and Greek. Expert native speakers translated the warnings for 1,000 events from 411 scenarios, giving 5,000 event-message pairs. A multilingual model fine-tuned jointly on all five languages **outperforms a zero-shot baseline on `ROUGE-L`, `BLEU`, and `BERTScore` in every language and configuration**. In a human preference study, low decoding temperatures were preferred in all languages, while the effect of including emergency guidelines in the prompt varied by language.

papers.title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.
papers.summary: LLM agents with persistent memory often derive extra state, such as summaries, from past interactions, so deleting an original record may leave its information alive in those derived copies. `AfterDeleteBench` measures this by comparing agents that saw and then deleted a synthetic secret with matched agents that never saw it. A single query recovers the deleted secret from `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` in about two thirds of cases, against zero for the controls. Even with no verbatim copy left, **exact reconstruction from separately stored components succeeds in 62-99% of cases** across `Qwen`, `Mistral`, and `Phi-3`. Provenance-aware closure, which also removes everything derived from a deleted record, eliminated recovery in the tested settings, while an exact-string write filter only stops the secret from being written back.

papers.title: RIDAR: Safeguarding Research Integrity in Autonomous Research Agents via Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention
papers.abstract: Autonomous research agents are increasingly used to automate large portions of scientific research, yet they are prone to research integrity violations (RIVs): behaviors that compromise the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research process. We present RIDAR, a framework for automated RIV detection and runtime intervention. First, we introduce RIVT, a comprehensive taxonomy of 14 RIV types spanning the full research lifecycle. Building on RIVT, we present RIDAR-post-hoc, a framework to detect RIVs within agent trajectories. RIDAR-post-hoc achieves 85.2% F1 performance on RIV-Gold, a benchmark for RIV detection with 60 expert-annotated trajectories. Applying RIDAR-post-hoc to RIV-Wild, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories across 50 distinct research tasks, we detect 3,964 RIV instances in 99.7% of trajectories, revealing the prevalence of RIVs in current agents. Finally, we present RIDAR-runtime, a framework for dynamically detecting and correcting RIVs during agent runtime. RIDAR-runtime effectively reduces agent RIVs remaining at task completion by 36.8%. We will release our code and data to facilitate future research.
papers.summary: Autonomous research agents can commit research integrity violations (RIVs), behaviors that undermine the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research they automate. The authors define `RIVT`, a taxonomy of 14 violation types across the research lifecycle, and build `RIDAR-post-hoc`, which detects violations in agent trajectories at 85.2% F1 on the expert-annotated `RIV-Gold` benchmark. Applied to 300 trajectories across 50 research tasks in `RIV-Wild`, it finds 3,964 violations, present in **99.7% of trajectories**. A runtime version, `RIDAR-runtime`, detects and corrects violations while the agent works, cutting the violations left at task completion by 36.8%.

papers.title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action
papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.
papers.summary: To defend LLM agents against prompt injection, the authors model the execution harness between the model and its tools as a supervisory control problem over Petri nets, where tokens represent capabilities, approvals, and budgets. Because an action fires only when the tokens it needs are present, an injected request with unmet or already spent preconditions is refused regardless of its wording. They introduce a replanning closed loop, in which an agent can propose again after a refusal at the cost of another inference call, and show that **the conventional maximally permissive supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one** in this loop. They characterize the least-intrusive safe supervisor as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one and demonstrate synthesis on an autonomous release agent.

papers.title: AI Risk Ontologies for the EU AI Act Compliance: AIRO, VAIR, and their Integration with DPV
papers.abstract: As the use of AI, and consequently its harms, becomes more prevalent, the global discourse around AI has become increasingly risk-aware. With new risks emerging more frequently than ever, a key challenge is how to represent, document, and catalogue AI risks in an effective, interoperable, and queryable manner. Additionally, the European Union (EU) AI Act's requirements for "high-risk" AI systems to manage and document the risks creates the need for open and interoperable tools, methods, and standards that facilitate AI risk management in an ever-changing environment. In this paper, we present ontologies and taxonomies developed to assist with risk management and documentation, in line with the requirements of the EU the AI Act. We developed the AI Risk Ontology (AIRO) to specify AI use cases and their associated risks, complemented by the Vocabulary of AI Risks (VAIR), which populates AIRO with taxonomies of concepts. Key international standards on AI and risk, namely ISO/IEC 23894 on AI risk management and ISO/IEC 22989 on AI terminology informed the development of the ontologies. To promote reuse and enable multi-regulatory compliance, AIRO and VAIR have been integrated in the Data Privacy Vocabulary (DPV) through a consensus-building process, expanding DPV's scope from data to AI.
papers.summary: The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to manage and document risks, which calls for interoperable, queryable ways to represent them. The authors present the AI Risk Ontology (`AIRO`), which describes AI use cases and their associated risks, and the Vocabulary of AI Risks (`VAIR`), which fills it with concept taxonomies; both draw on the ISO/IEC 23894 and ISO/IEC 22989 standards. Through a consensus-building process, **both have been integrated into the Data Privacy Vocabulary (`DPV`)**, expanding its scope from data to AI to support compliance across multiple regulations.

papers.title: A Task-Centric Survey of Long-Document Visual Question Answering: Taxonomy, Evolution, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Visual document understanding is essential for acquiring knowledge from visually rich documents and is attracting growing research interest. Existing surveys emphasize architectures or technical approaches, with limited attention to how task bottlenecks shape technical choices and research priorities. We present a task-centric survey that decomposes long-document visual question answering (VQA) into four components: document parsing, evidence organization and retrieval, generator organization and learning, and evaluation. For each, we develop a fine-grained taxonomy and trace motivations, technical responses, and cross-component connections. We focus on explicit retrieval while covering direct reading. Our temporal analysis traces expanding priorities from multimodal content understanding to sufficient, high-fidelity evidence acquisition and sustained evidence management. We outline future directions in evidence sufficiency, verifiable and correctable understanding, and budget-aware coordination, with an outlook on continual document understanding.
papers.summary: Existing surveys of visual document understanding are organized around architectures. This one is instead organized around the bottlenecks of the long-document visual question answering (VQA) task itself. It breaks the task into four components: document parsing, evidence organization and retrieval, generator organization and learning, and evaluation. For each it builds a fine-grained taxonomy, with a focus on explicit retrieval while also covering direct reading. A temporal analysis shows research priorities **expanding from multimodal content understanding toward sufficient, high-fidelity evidence acquisition and sustained evidence management**. Proposed future directions include evidence sufficiency, verifiable and correctable understanding, budget-aware coordination, and continual document understanding.

papers.title: Convex Equilibrium Potentials for Monge--Amp\`ere: Curvature Bounds and A Posteriori Evaluation
papers.abstract: Equilibrium neural networks define their hidden state as the fixed point of a contraction, so their effective depth is set at evaluation time rather than by the architecture. Using them for fully nonlinear PDEs raises two issues that explicit networks avoid: second derivatives may grow with the effective depth, and the potential is only ever evaluated approximately. We study nonnegative softplus equilibrium networks with contraction factor $q<1$, a convex class suited to the Monge--Amp\`ere equation. A positivity cancellation in the resolvent shows that the Hessian grows at most like $(1-q)^{-2}$, rather than the $(1-q)^{-3}$ of a direct estimate, and an explicit one-neuron family shows that this exponent is sharp; third derivatives satisfy a sharp $(1-q)^{-3}$ bound. Residual-based a posteriori estimates then control the state, its input derivatives and, in two dimensions, the Hessian determinant at an approximate equilibrium. Combined with interval arithmetic on complete covers of the domain, they yield rigorous uniform bounds on the Monge--Amp\`ere residual and, through a comparison argument, on the solution error of a fixed trained network. On two manufactured Dirichlet problems on the unit disk, all six trained models are certified with residual below $0.25$ and boundary error below $0.01$. Adaptive stopping halves float64 evaluation time at best, whereas certified adaptive evaluation remains costlier than fixed depth.
papers.summary: Equilibrium neural networks define their output as the fixed point of a contraction, so using them to solve the fully nonlinear Monge-Ampère equation raises two concerns: second derivatives might blow up with effective depth, and the fixed point is only ever computed approximately. For convex softplus equilibrium networks with contraction factor q<1, the authors prove that **the Hessian grows at most like (1-q)^-2, and that this bound is sharp**. Combining residual-based a posteriori estimates with interval arithmetic, they produce rigorous bounds on the residual and solution error of a fixed trained network. They certify all six trained models on two test problems on the unit disk.

papers.title: Auditing the Hand-Written Inputs of Learned Access Control
papers.abstract: Learned access control is typically deployed behind two hand-built artefacts: a hard-deny set enforced by a small trusted shield, and a region map that decides which requests mined rules answer and which the learner answers. Verifying the shield or measuring the learner validates neither. We audit both on the five public ABAC Lab policies. First, we formalise hard-deny soundness and check it exhaustively over relations of up to 794,250 tuples. Clauses that faithfully transcribe an explicit restriction are unsound at rates of 0.50-0.70 across four elicitors - an author and three blind language-model elicitors - because prose scopes restrictions to a section while the grant relation is a disjunction over all rules: 97% of counterexamples are granted by other rules. Shipped unchecked, these deny sets would withhold 16-78% of everything the policies grant; certified, they withhold nothing. Vacuity, a second silent failure, also occurs. Second, hybrid routing needs a two-class, abstaining rule set that ABAC miners do not emit, and ranking a mixed-effect candidate pool under a cap is one-class in all 24 cells for the two commonest ranking keys. Third, for additive losses the hybrid-versus-learner effect factorises into covered mass times a rule-learner risk contrast that must be reported on both false-non-grant and false-permit loss: on two real policies, most selection rules give opposite verdicts on the two losses, and the one favourable on both holds for one policy, one learner configuration and a band of noise levels. A released artefact regenerates and checks every reported number.
papers.summary: Learned access control systems usually depend on two hand-built inputs: a hard-deny set enforced by a trusted shield, and a region map that decides which requests are answered by mined rules and which by the learner. Auditing both on the five public `ABAC Lab` policies (ABAC is attribute-based access control), the authors find that deny clauses faithfully transcribed from the written policy are **unsound at rates of 0.50-0.70**, whether written by a human or by language models. This happens because a restriction stated in one section is overridden by grants from other rules. Shipped unchecked, these deny sets would withhold 16-78% of legitimate grants. The study also shows that standard rule miners do not produce the rule sets that hybrid routing needs, and that comparisons between hybrid and learner-only systems can reverse depending on which loss is measured.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models to a Low-Resource Agglutinative Language: A Corpus, Datasets, and a Reproducible Benchmark for the Bashkir Language
papers.abstract: Bashkir is a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic and remains poorly represented in modern LLMs. We present an open resource suite and a systematic benchmark of adaptation methods: the Bashkir Web Corpus (71,567 documents, 46.9M tokens, 16 sources) and three labelled datasets for binary, multiclass and multilabel text classification; the benchmark covers the first two. Experiments use eight architectures (82M-8B: DistilGPT2, GPT-2 base/medium, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B, mBERT, XLM-R) and three adaptation groups (full fine-tuning, QLoRA, in-context learning), plus continual pretraining (CPT). (1) QLoRA on 3.8-8B models outperforms encoder-only fine-tuning on binary classification: YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B with CPT reaches macro-F1 0.748 vs 0.653 (XLM-R) and 0.650 (mBERT); pairwise differences are significant after Holm correction (p<0.001). (2) YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B significantly outperforms Mistral-7B and Phi-3-mini on multiclass classification, BPB and native-speaker ratings (mean 3.28 vs 2.52 and 2.22; n=100; alpha=0.69-0.77; p<0.05); on binary classification its QLoRA advantage is not significant (p>=0.084). (3) CPT effects depend on model and task: perplexity improves for Phi-3-mini (+0.58) and YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B (+0.33) but worsens for Mistral-7B (-1.15, p<0.001); on binary classification CPT helps Mistral-7B most (+4.0 macro-F1). (4) Tokeniser fertility on Bashkir varies 2.67x (2.92-7.80) and tracks adaptation quality, while perplexity across tokenisers is not comparable. Cyrillic tokenisers with Russian pretraining are preferable; LLM judges reproduce native ratings for grammar and coherence (rho=0.33-0.46) but not language correctness (rho=0.16, p=0.11); native evaluation remains necessary. All artefacts are open-licensed.
papers.summary: Bashkir, a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic, is poorly served by current LLMs. The authors release the `Bashkir Web Corpus` (46.9M tokens) and three classification datasets, and benchmark eight models from 82M to 8B parameters under full fine-tuning, `QLoRA`, in-context learning, and continual pretraining. `QLoRA` on 3.8-8B models beats encoder-only fine-tuning, with **`YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B` plus continual pretraining reaching 0.748 macro-F1 versus 0.653 for `XLM-R`** on binary classification. Effects of continual pretraining depend on the model and task. Tokenizer efficiency on Bashkir tracks adaptation quality, and LLM judges fail to reproduce native speakers' ratings of language correctness.

papers.title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.
papers.summary: Continual learning methods that update weights suffer from forgetting, while methods that rely on prompts, skills, or harnesses are limited by context length and lossy text compression. `HERD` (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation) combines the two. It continually refines reusable skills in the harness and keeps the examples those skills fail to capture in a bounded memory, then distills this experience into the weights with drift constraints that reduce forgetting. On the 25-stage `TRACE+17` task stream under fixed budgets, HERD **matches the strongest weight-updating baseline on learning new tasks while showing the least forgetting** and the best retention of general capabilities.

papers.title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.
papers.summary: Existing phishing datasets were built for conventional detection and say little about how LLM email agents respond to persuasive malicious requests. `AgentPhishing` is a benchmark for this question. Alongside it, `PhishOpt` optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under realism constraints, and analysis of the resulting emails through Cialdini's persuasion principles is used to build a universal attack skill. Agents that safely handle pre-existing phishing emails remain vulnerable to adapted attacks: **four of nine agents detect fewer than 10% of phishing attempts and comply with over 45% of malicious requests**.

papers.title: Same Entity, Different Script: Diagnosing Cross-Script Entity Matching Failures in Language Models
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models can give different identity judgments when the same people's names are written in different scripts. We study this effect using 601 audited identity pairs with attested Devanagari and Latin forms, holding the question and relation fixed. Qwen2.5-7B's same-person accuracy falls from 35.1% in Latin to 8.5% in Devanagari under Marathi prompts, while different-person accuracy remains above 98%. Evaluation across five models reveals distinct response biases, and reduced tokenization fragmentation does not reliably close the gap. Replicating the design on 374 audited Malayalam pairs built from the same entities reproduces the effect in a second script and language family: same-person accuracy falls to 5.3%, about half the matched Devanagari rate, while the margin still ranks matching above non-matching names at 0.925 AUROC. Latin-trained probes recover label information from Devanagari states, exceeding a string-feature baseline under similarity-matched negatives. Scalar calibration recovers 87% of the raw model-probe balanced-accuracy gap, identifying decision criterion placement as a major contributor. Activation patching localises causal sensitivity to the second entity in Qwen's middle layers; one shared sensitivity direction transfers about half the full-state margin correction. A fact-independent intervention at this site raises held-out Marathi same-person accuracy from 6.5% to 33.5%, with 98.5% different-person accuracy. Together, these results distinguish script-dependent discrimination from criterion placement and identify a causal site for improving identity judgments.
papers.summary: Multilingual models can give different answers about whether two names refer to the same person depending on the script the names are written in. Using 601 audited Devanagari/Latin identity pairs, the authors find that `Qwen2.5-7B`'s same-person accuracy falls from 35.1% in Latin to 8.5% in Devanagari under Marathi prompts, and they replicate the effect in Malayalam. Probes and calibration show that the model's internal states still carry the identity information, and that much of the gap comes from where the decision threshold sits. Activation patching locates the effect in middle layers, and an intervention there **raises held-out Marathi same-person accuracy from 6.5% to 33.5%** while keeping different-person accuracy at 98.5%.

papers.title: SQuAT: Spherical Lattice Vector Quantization-Aware Training
papers.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.
authors: Tycho F. A. van der Ouderaa
papers.summary: Lattice vector quantization offers strong compression for low-bit LLMs, but how it behaves under quantization-aware training (QAT) at scale is poorly understood. `SQuAT` splits each weight block into a direction, quantized with a spherical codebook derived from the `E_8` lattice, and a magnitude, quantized with a low-bit scalar quantizer. Each part gets its own straight-through estimator (STE), which implicitly yields spherical optimization of the directions. A distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme **cuts QAT training time by 12.8x**, allowing training on 10B tokens. Across `LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B`, `Qwen3-4B`, and `Qwen3-1.7B`, it consistently outperforms standard STE-based vector-quantization QAT and reaches state-of-the-art accuracy for this class of method.

papers.title: Major Revision, Minor Accountability: LLMs as Reviewers of Published Articles in Top-Tier Journals
papers.abstract: With the growth of scientific output, the peer review system is approaching a breaking point: reviewers are increasingly hard to secure, and turnaround times lengthen accordingly. LLM-assisted or LLM-generated peer review has been proposed as a remedy, but how such models would treat manuscripts already published in top-tier journals, the closest thing the current system has to a gold standard of scientific validity, is not known. Here we assembled a corpus of 200 articles, each released under a CC BY 4.0 license and published in 2026, from 20 general-science, life-science, and clinical-medicine journals including Nature, Science, and Cell, and asked four current LLMs (two proprietary, two open-weight) to produce independent peer-review reports of each one under a blinded protocol. Their decisions were overwhelmingly harsh and starkly inconsistent with each other: 605 of 800 reviews (75.6%) recommended major revision or rejection, but the rate at which any single model did so ranged from 17.5% to 100% (p < 0.001), disagreement on manuscripts that had, by construction, already survived real editorial review at the journals in question. When the same manuscripts were doctored with one deliberately planted, field-specific methodological or statistical flaw, detection rates varied from 17.0% to 60.5% across models (p < 0.001). Recommending revision for papers that had already passed editorial review (low specificity) while missing flaws deliberately placed in front of them (low sensitivity), these models produce output that should be read for what it is: an uneven, framing- and model-dependent signal.

papers.title: SyRA-CS: Synthetic-to-Real Adaptation for Code-Switched ASR with Meta-Learning
papers.abstract: Code-switched (CS) automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains difficult because real CS speech is scarce and synthetic speech does not fully match it. We investigate whether synthetic CS speech is more useful for learning an adaptation-friendly initialization than for ordinary continual fine-tuning. We propose SyRA-CS, a pair-specific synthetic-to-real adaptation framework based on Reptile meta-learning. For each language pair and pretrained model, we meta-train on the corresponding synthetic CS-FLEURS subset and then adapt using one hour of labeled real target speech. We evaluate four architectural settings: Encoder-CTC, FastConformer-RNN-T, Attention Encoder-Decoder (AED) and Speech-LLM. Experiments cover on Arabic-, French-, German-, and Hindi-English, against synthetic-only transfer, real-only fine-tuning, and continual fine-tuning. SyRA-CS improves over continual fine-tuning on WER in all 16 model-pair comparisons and on CER in 15 of 16, with relative macro WER reductions of 17.7% for XLS-R and 5.3-5.8% for the other three models. The gains hold across the tested models but vary in size across architectures, language pairs and metrics.
papers.summary: PLACEHOLDER

papers.title: Post-Hoc Feature Selection Layer for Neural Networks Interpretability
papers.abstract: The interpretability of complex neural networks remains a critical challenge, especially for models already deployed in high-stakes domains. To address this, we adapted the Feature Selection Layer (FSL) to optimize feature weights post-training, a variant we term post-hoc FSL. Our approach reframes the FSL as a lightweight, trainable module that integrates with already frozen pre-trained models on tabular datasets to highlight the features the original model considers most important. This post-hoc FSL learns feature relevance by fine-tuning its weights based on the original model's learned outputs. Crucially, this process is non-invasive, operating without altering the original model's architecture or its learned parameters. We conducted our experiments using both statistical and visual metrics, including accuracy, F1 score, recall, precision, weighted t-SNE and silhouette score, and also analyzed the stability of the post-hoc FSL on high-dimensional synthetic and real-world tabular datasets. We compared the post-hoc FSL feature weighting method using these metrics against the original embedded FSL and other post-hoc interpretability methods, such as Integrated Gradients, Noise Tunnel, DeepLIFT, Gradient SHAP, and Feature Ablation. Experimental results demonstrate that the post-hoc FSL feature weighting method successfully identified relevant features across the different datasets, maintaining the predictive power of the original neural network while enhancing its interpretability.

papers.title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

papers.title: How Well Do Decision Models Transfer to Vietnamese? An Empirical Study of Text Classification
papers.abstract: Recent advances in specialized decision models have expanded the possibilities for zero-shot classification, yet their effectiveness on Vietnamese remains underexplored. This study evaluates four specialized decision models across 13 classification settings spanning six task groups, examining zero-shot performance, sensitivity to label-description language, and robustness to Vietnamese linguistic variations. The evaluation considers English, Vietnamese, and bilingual label descriptions, alongside common linguistic perturbations involving teencode, typographical errors, and diacritic removal. Under English label descriptions, JEV achieves the strongest overall performance, ranking first in 11 classification settings. The effects of label-description language vary across models and datasets, with bilingual descriptions providing no consistent improvement. Robustness experiments reveal that diacritic removal causes the most substantial performance degradation, reducing mean macro-$F_1$ by 9.51--15.47 points across model configurations, considerably more than teencode or typographical errors. These findings highlight the importance of label-description choices and Vietnamese orthographic variation when evaluating specialized decision models for zero-shot text classification.

papers.title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $\pi_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.

papers.title: Predictable performance is suboptimal, and what it means for model routing
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) differ in capabilities and costs, motivating routing methods that adaptively choose a model for each query. These methods rely on performance prediction: given a query, estimate whether a model will answer it correctly. Most routing methods train separate predictors of candidate models' performance to guide model selection. Our work shows that performance prediction only beats a simple baseline when the candidate model is suboptimal on the task or the performance predictor adds significant capacity relative to the candidate model. Specifically, we take a model's self-confidence, the probability it assigns to its chosen answer, as a baseline and study how much a performance predictor can improve on it. First, we show that any performance predictor that outperforms a model's self-confidence can be used to improve the model's loss: the predictor's advantage transfers exactly in log loss through recalibration. Second, accounting for the predictor's additional parameters, we bound its advantage by the model's suboptimality plus the gain from those parameters. Third, we extend our theoretical results to two-model cascades, which route queries to a more capable model when the first model is predicted to fail. Experiments with 16 language models on four benchmarks show that predictors gain a larger advantage over self-confidence on more suboptimal models. This advantage shrinks as models improve through finetuning. Cascading exhibits the same two patterns: predictor-based routing offers larger gains over confidence-based routing for more suboptimal models, and these gains diminish after finetuning.
papers.summary: Model-routing systems usually train a separate predictor to guess whether a candidate language model will answer a query correctly. The authors compare such predictors against a simple baseline: the model's own self-confidence, meaning the probability it assigns to its chosen answer. They prove that any predictor beating self-confidence can be turned into a recalibration that improves the model's own log loss. That advantage is bounded by the model's suboptimality plus the extra capacity the predictor adds, and the result extends to two-model cascades. Experiments with 16 language models on four benchmarks confirm that **predictors help most on more suboptimal models, and their edge shrinks as models are finetuned**.

papers.title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models
papers.abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.
papers.summary: Video models are increasingly used as world models, but existing evaluations rarely show where and when a generated video breaks physical expectations. `PhysTrace` is a training-free framework that has a multimodal LLM generate physical expectations from a video's history, then matches them against later windows to find violations in time and describe them in plain language. The authors also release `IntPhys2-Timing`, which adds violation intervals to `IntPhys2`. `PhysTrace` reaches **a Hit Rate of up to 70.7%** across physical principles and beats the compared methods at telling possible from impossible videos. Applied to diffusion and flow-based video models, it shows that where violations appear depends on the physical attribute and the noise level.

papers.title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
papers.abstract: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.
papers.summary: Classical analyses of the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (`ULA`) in Wasserstein-2 distance predict bias and mixing times that grow with dimension. The authors instead measure bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and low-dimensional marginals that practitioners usually estimate. For ridge-separable models built from i.i.d. data, they prove a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points N varies against the dimension d. Complexity depends on N rather than d in the overparameterized regime and becomes dimension-free for large N, but **dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general near the proportional regime where N is comparable to d**.

papers.title: Drift Says When, Budget Says How Much: Rate-Controlled KV Re-selection for Long-Form Multimodal Generation
papers.abstract: KV cache compression for multimodal LLMs usually selects the visual tokens to keep once, at prefill, and reuses that selection for the whole generation. We show that this one-shot selection is severely limited on long-form generation: on detailed image description, even an oracle that selects with the attention of the uncompressed answer reaches only 0.44-0.52 ROUGE-L agreement with the uncompressed output, because the evidence the model reads moves as the description unfolds. Re-selecting whenever attention drifts out of the kept set is the natural remedy, but we find that a fixed drift threshold fails systematically: drift magnitudes are not comparable across samples, so low-drift samples are almost never refreshed although they benefit the most. We propose Rate-Controlled Refresh (RCR), which lets drift decide when and where to re-select while a per-sample controller regulates how often, combined with a low-rank drift detector, candidate-restricted re-selection, and a decision that stays on the GPU. With one setting for all models and tasks, RCR outperforms the per-step retrieval method InfiniGen by 1.6-3.8 ROUGE-L points on five of six model-task settings with no significant difference on the sixth, while staying within 1.7 points of exact per-step re-selection, with comparable estimated data movement per step and a 4x smaller GPU-resident detector. On DetailCaps, drift-chosen timing beats random timing at the same refresh rate and periodic timing even at a higher rate, by 2.0-5.0 points. On pre-registered video description, where drift is homogeneous across samples, RCR is on par with InfiniGen on Qwen2-VL and exceeds it on Qwen3-VL but no longer beats a fixed threshold at the nearest tested rates, consistent with the diagnosis; object-level evaluation shows that RCR achieves higher object F1 against the uncompressed output than InfiniGen on two of three models.
papers.summary: KV-cache compression for multimodal LLMs usually picks which visual tokens to keep once, at prefill. The authors show this fails on long-form generation: even an oracle one-shot selection reaches only 0.44-0.52 ROUGE-L agreement with uncompressed output on detailed image description. Their method, Rate-Controlled Refresh (`RCR`), uses attention drift to decide when and where to re-select tokens, while a per-sample controller sets how often to refresh. A low-rank drift detector keeps the cost low. With a single setting for all models and tasks, `RCR` **beats the per-step retrieval method `InfiniGen` by 1.6-3.8 ROUGE-L points on five of six settings**, stays within 1.7 points of exact per-step re-selection, and uses a 4x smaller GPU-resident detector.

papers.title: Conservative Meta-Agent Search: Architecture Adaptation under Non-Stationarity
papers.abstract: Automated agentic-system design is typically evaluated on static task suites with immediate scalar rewards. Deployed systems face persistent shift, delayed dependent feedback, correlated component failures, and costly architecture changes. We formalize meta-agent architecture search as sequential incumbent replacement with switching costs and hard risk constraints and introduce Conservative Meta-Agent Search (CMAS). CMAS retrieves archived architectures and proposes typed graph edits, then scores each against the incumbent by paired shadow replay under common random numbers, with interventional component credit. Promotion requires an empirically calibrated, variance-penalized simultaneous score above a pre-specified margin, and is followed by a simulated canary stage and pre-specified rollback. Since backtests cannot certify meta-level skill, we introduce MetaInvest-Bench, a regime-switching simulator whose specified worker competence makes a surrogate-optimal architecture computable, with leakage-controlled replay, adversarial governance tracks, and five negative controls. Financial streams serve as a risk-sensitive testbed for meta-level generalization; we claim no alpha. Across 96 streams, CMAS cuts normalized mean surrogate dynamic-oracle regret from 0.116 to 0.104 and raises held-out utility from 0.44 to 0.48 over the strongest adaptive baseline; when extra workers add no value, it contracts to near-single-agent teams. Its deployment inference cost is ~6% lower, though its search-inclusive token cost is the highest of the methods compared. The observed per-update false-promotion rate is 3.4% against a nominal 5% target, and 4.8% in a sealed rerun. The calibration is empirical: it concerns an update-level replay statistic on an author-designed benchmark, and guarantees neither full-utility improvement, nor absence of simulated canary-stage harm, nor sequence-level error control.
papers.summary: Automated design of agentic systems is usually tested on static task suites, while deployed systems face ongoing distribution shift, delayed feedback, and costly architecture changes. Conservative Meta-Agent Search (`CMAS`) treats architecture search as replacing a running incumbent: it proposes typed graph edits, scores them against the incumbent by paired shadow replay, and promotes a change only if a calibrated, variance-penalized score clears a margin, followed by a simulated canary stage with rollback. On `MetaInvest-Bench`, a regime-switching financial simulator the authors built, `CMAS` **cuts normalized regret from 0.116 to 0.104** and raises held-out utility from 0.44 to 0.48 over the strongest adaptive baseline. It shrinks to near-single-agent teams when extra workers add no value, though its search phase has the highest token cost of the methods compared.

papers.title: DIAL: Steerable Language Models with Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels
papers.abstract: When a user says "Keep it short", how short should the LLM's response be? More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study "steerable language models" that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM's hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM's hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting, and training requires only instruction and request text. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98, 625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following.
papers.summary: Prompting gives users no reliable way to control how strongly an LLM follows an instruction such as keeping a response short. `DIAL` (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) offers numerical control over adherence. It uses classifier-free guidance on a frozen LLM to produce training signals for on-policy distillation into a lightweight steering adapter. The adapter's text-conditioned classifier sets a per-token steering edit in closed form, so one shared adapter can handle new instructions without per-instruction fitting. Across several LLM families, **concept scores increase monotonically with the requested adherence level** while fluency stays competitive. The authors also release `SteerIF`, a dataset of 98,625 instructions.

papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction and Alternative Tokenization Improve Learning Latent Multi-Hop Graph Search at Scale
papers.abstract: Given an unseen graph, a start node, $s$, and an end node, $t$, can a language model generate the shortest path from $s$ to $t$? Prior work has found that models fail to learn this task as the graphs scale. We show that this failure has two causes: the supervision signal and the tokenization. First, we theoretically establish and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-token prediction (MTP), and show that the benefits of MTP are topologically agnostic. Second, we introduce alternative tokenizations and show that the two causes are orthogonal. Using these methods, we break through the scaling wall observed by prior work, consistently and stably learning to solve the task at scales far beyond previous limits.
papers.summary: Prior work found that language models fail to learn shortest-path search on unseen graphs once the graphs get large. The authors trace this failure to two independent causes: the supervision signal and the tokenization. They show theoretically and empirically that multi-token prediction (MTP) helps regardless of graph topology, and they introduce alternative tokenizations that address the second cause. Combining the two lets models **consistently learn the task at scales far beyond the previously observed scaling wall**.

papers.title: How Different, or Different How? Stance Granularity in Viewpoint Selection for Dialog Systems that Engage Users with Alternative Views
papers.abstract: Systems that aim to help a user engage with viewpoints other than their own have to decide how different those viewpoints should be. Viewpoints are mainly represented on a scalar scale, too coarse to distinguish viewpoints that disagree with the user about different things. We introduce a selection policy in which a bandit sets how far viewpoints may sit from the user, and the policy selects the most novel viewpoint within that bound. We vary only its stance encoder, comparing a scalar score with Perspectivized Stance Vectors, which break a position into separate stances on concepts. We integrate it inside a dialog system and run a between-subjects study (N=63). Concept-level stance produces more varied exposure sequences and broader coverage of the topic's positions, but does not change how deeply users justify viewpoints or how accurately they reconstruct them. Finally, we analyze user--viewpoint relations at the concept level, showing that users reconstruct a viewpoint least accurately on concepts that one side took no position on, rather than on concepts where the two disagreed. Our findings open up opportunities for dialog systems that support engagement with alternative viewpoints by acting on which concepts a user and a viewpoint disagree on, rather than on distance alone.
papers.summary: Dialog systems that expose users to other viewpoints must decide how different those viewpoints should be, and they usually represent viewpoints on a single scalar scale. The authors build a selection policy in which a bandit sets the allowed distance from the user and the most novel viewpoint within that bound is chosen. They compare a scalar stance encoder with `Perspectivized Stance Vectors`, which record a separate stance for each concept. In a between-subjects study with 63 participants, concept-level stance produced more varied exposure and broader topic coverage, but **did not change how deeply users justified or how accurately they reconstructed viewpoints**. Users reconstructed viewpoints least accurately on concepts that one side took no position on.

papers.title: Adaptive Skill Granularity for Coding Agents: Runtime Routing and Macro-to-Micro Recovery
papers.abstract: Reusable skills allow large language model agents to package task-specific procedures, tool affordances, and execution guidance into modular units. Prior work has largely studied how agents retrieve, compose, or synthesize skills before execution. In coding agents, however, execution poses an additional runtime control problem: the same task may be solved through primitive tool calls, macro skills, or hybrid execution that starts with a macro and falls back to micro-level recovery. We introduce Adaptive Skill Granularity, a framework that treats skill granularity as an action-abstraction policy conditioned on task structure, execution state, and macro-skill failures. The system combines a feature-based granularity controller and a finite-state recovery executor. We evaluate the framework with a deterministic coding-agent protocol using verifier-defined success, total cost, and process metrics such as macro adoption, failure recovery, route match, and transition correctness. Results show that fixed macro execution is efficient when applicable but brittle under mismatch, while runtime routing and explicit macro-to-micro recovery improve robustness and recover controlled macro failures that fixed-granularity execution leaves unresolved. Our findings suggest that skill libraries for coding agents should be treated not only as retrievable resources, but also as controllable, verifiable, and recoverable execution abstractions.
papers.summary: Coding agents can complete a task with primitive tool calls, with reusable macro skills, or with a hybrid that starts with a macro and falls back to step-by-step recovery. `Adaptive Skill Granularity` treats this choice as a runtime policy that depends on task structure, execution state, and macro failures. It combines a feature-based granularity controller with a finite-state recovery executor. On a deterministic coding-agent evaluation protocol, fixed macro execution is efficient when it fits but brittle when it does not, while **runtime routing with explicit macro-to-micro recovery fixes macro failures that fixed-granularity execution leaves unresolved**.

papers.title: RheOPT: Few-Shot Non-Newtonian Flow Prediction via Newtonian Pretraining of RheOFormer
papers.abstract: Despite advances in numerical methods, non-Newtonian flow simulations remain computationally expensive because velocity and stress must be advanced together through rate- and history-dependent constitutive dynamics. Neural-operator surrogates reduce inference cost after training, but their training data require the same expensive simulations they aim to replace, making data-efficient learning essential when only a few non-Newtonian simulations can be afforded. Here, we introduce the Rheological Operator Pretrained Transformer (RheOPT), which pretrains a transformer-based neural operator on inexpensive Newtonian simulations and fine-tunes it on a small number of non-Newtonian samples. Rather than transferring the Newtonian constitutive response itself, RheOPT reuses geometry-conditioned transport structure that remains useful after the stress model changes. We evaluate RheOPT in two geometry-matched settings: a $4{:}1$ contraction channel for Giesekus, Oldroyd-B, and Bingham fluids, and the oscillatory wake behind a triangular obstacle for Oldroyd-B flow. In the contraction, Newtonian pretraining substantially improves few-shot prediction, and a model fine-tuned on four target samples can match or exceed a from-scratch model trained on four times as many. This benefit is reliable under reversible instance normalization (RevIN) but dataset dependent under Global normalization, a difference we trace to the dynamic range of each fluid's velocity and stress fields. In the wake, where relative $L_2$ error alone cannot verify that vortex shedding is recovered, phase-insensitive diagnostics show that pretraining recovers the shedding frequency and wake fluctuation amplitude that are suppressed by the from-scratch model in the few-shot regime. Overall, RheOPT establishes Newtonian simulation as a physically grounded pretraining source for data-efficient non-Newtonian operator learning.
papers.summary: Training neural-operator surrogates for non-Newtonian flows requires the same expensive simulations they are meant to replace. `RheOPT` pretrains a transformer neural operator, `RheOFormer`, on cheap Newtonian simulations and fine-tunes it on a few non-Newtonian samples, reusing geometry-dependent transport structure rather than the constitutive response. In a 4:1 contraction channel with Giesekus, Oldroyd-B, and Bingham fluids, **a model fine-tuned on four samples matches or beats a from-scratch model trained on four times as many**, with the benefit reliable under reversible instance normalization (`RevIN`). In an oscillatory wake, pretraining recovers the vortex-shedding frequency and amplitude that from-scratch few-shot models suppress.

papers.title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
papers.abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.
papers.summary: Turning structured health records from wearables into patient-friendly text with LLMs risks semantic drift, where simplification distorts clinical meaning. Focusing on menstrual health monitoring, the authors combine structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in a prompt-based constrained generation framework. They evaluate the summaries with Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality, and readability metrics. Across three LLMs and 4,500 summaries, explicit grounding constraints **consistently improve clinical alignment, especially the preservation of uncertainty**, but make the text harder to read and heavier in medical terminology.

papers.title: Measuring the Verifier's Floor: How Much Apparent Rare-Word Text-to-Speech Error Is ASR Error?
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) is usually evaluated by transcribing its output with an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system, so the word error rate also counts recognizer errors. We measure these errors on human recordings of the test sentences. On LibriSpeech and FLEURS, the evaluation recognizer misses 33-67% of very rare words even in human speech, and all three recognizers miss 22-42%. Checking every word with two more recognizer families lowers the apparent TTS error on words that at least one recognizer hears two- to three-fold (very rare LibriSpeech words: from 10-13% to 3-5%), yet very rare words remain the hardest. Ignoring words the recognizer misses in human speech is biased: the other recognizers find TTS errors far more often on these words (4-6% vs. 0.2-0.3%) and overturn about half of the errors this mask keeps. As half of the remaining adjudicated errors may be spelling variants, a listening test is needed.
papers.summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are usually scored by transcribing their output with an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system, so recognizer mistakes are counted as TTS errors. Running recognizers on human recordings of the same sentences in `LibriSpeech` and `FLEURS`, the authors find that the evaluation recognizer **misses 33-67% of very rare words even in human speech**. Checking each word with two additional recognizer families cuts apparent TTS error on very rare `LibriSpeech` words from 10-13% to 3-5%. Simply ignoring words the recognizer misses in human speech introduces bias, and because about half of the remaining errors may be spelling variants, the authors conclude that a listening test is still needed.

papers.title: MoG-VLM: Efficient Video Anomaly Detection through Motion-Guided Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame-level inference makes them impractical for real-time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG-VLM a motion-adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content-aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual-stream design in which dense multi-frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor-triggered context-window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC-ROC on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero-shot, training-free setting. On XD-Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content-aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG-VLM.
papers.summary: Running vision-language models (VLMs) on every frame is too slow for real-time video anomaly detection, and uniform frame sampling either wastes compute on static scenes or misses brief anomalies. `MoG-VLM` uses a cheap motion signal, Temporal Gradient Magnitude (`TGM`), to decide when VLM inference is needed. It switches to dense multi-frame VLM reasoning only around frames that look anomalous and then fuses those semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. In the zero-shot, training-free setting it reaches 91.91% AUC-ROC on `XD-Violence`, 84.30% on `UCF-Crime`, 87.88% on `MSAD`, and 78.96% on `ShanghaiTech`. That **sets a new state of the art on three of the four benchmarks**, with a 1.31x speedup on `XD-Violence`.

papers.title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
papers.abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.
papers.summary: Most LLM inference optimizations are built and validated on server NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving, yet Apple Silicon is one of the most common platforms for local inference. The authors test KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization on four Apple machines under single-request decoding, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons. KV-cache pruning gives up to 1.75x throughput on Apple but can slow down desktop NVIDIA GPUs, and **every speculative decoding method tested reduced throughput on Apple** despite reported 2-6x gains on servers. CUDA kernel ideas transfer only partly because public Metal lacks asynchronous copy. The authors conclude that a speedup depends jointly on the technique, runtime, hardware, and workload rather than on the technique alone.

papers.title: Training Small Language Models for Transferable Tool Selection
papers.abstract: As LLM agents operate over corpora of more than ten thousand tools, selecting the right tool for a complex multi-step user instruction becomes a central bottleneck. Tool descriptions cannot all fit in context, and relevance-based retrievers only rank tools without knowing which are actually needed. Recent work instead leverages proprietary commercial LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT to drive a retriever, decomposing the instruction and selecting over retrieved candidates. We show that a small, open model can be trained via reinforcement learning to perform the same functionality. On ToolBench, a Qwen3-8B model post-trained with our recipe outperforms Llama-4-Maverick (402B). In addition, the trained model transfers directly to different retrievers and generalizes to new tool corpora in different domains.
papers.summary: When LLM agents can choose from more than ten thousand tools, picking the right ones for a multi-step instruction becomes a bottleneck, and recent systems rely on proprietary LLMs to decompose the instruction and select from retrieved candidates. The authors show that a small open model can learn this job through reinforcement learning. On `ToolBench`, **`Qwen3-8B` post-trained with their recipe outperforms the 402B-parameter `Llama-4-Maverick`**. The trained model also works with different retrievers and generalizes to new tool corpora in other domains.

papers.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
papers.abstract: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ greatly exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using a finite-horizon schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. A recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bounding refitting cost by $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.
